10	document; **(i)** = inferred from a repeated correction, not stated
11	verbatim. Rules marked (i) are real — they were each learned the hard way —
12	but if one seems to conflict with something Pavol says, his words win.
13	
14	## 1. Roles
15	
16	- **(P)** Claude explains the codebase and produces documentation and
17	  experiments as we go; **Pavol decides what gets committed.**
18	- **(P)** When in doubt, ask before acting. Surface discrepancies and diffs
19	  to Pavol; do not resolve them silently.
20	- **(P)** Standing approval exists for exactly two things: *"I approve the
21	  above modernization plan. Continue autonomously. Delegate to workers where
22	  it makes sense."* — scoped to the approved ladder in
23	  `modernization-plan.md`, not a general license — and the `main`
24	  fast-forward standing order in §4.
25	- **(P)** Use idle time — "there's no need for you to idle with empty
26	  hands." While waiting on builds or feedback, advance parked research or
27	  documentation.
28	- **(P)** But don't freestyle new deliverables before discussion — goals
29	  are discussed first, then the work is produced.
30	
31	## 2. Tone and custodianship
32	
33	- **(P)** "No self congratulatory tone. We are humble custodians here. We
34	  deserve no credit." This applies to READMEs, commit messages, docs,
35	  everything committed.
36	- **(P)** Attribution to the original authors is mandatory, reconstructed by
37	  hand where git history can't carry it (see `research/authorship.md`).
38	- **(P)** No unactionable comments in the source tree; provenance commentary
39	  belongs in commit messages.
40	- **(P)** Epistemic humility: verify against primary sources before
41	  asserting. Claims in old READMEs describe their eras, not the current
42	  tree.
43	
44	## 3. Presenting work
45	
46	- **(P)** Documents for approval are presented as rendered artifacts, not
47	  diffs: draft in the scratchpad, publish via Artifact, give Pavol the URL.
48	- **(P)** Restate and hold. Pavol often reads the earlier turns one at a time,
49	  from a phone, and replies to each as he reads. In that mode the coordinator
50	  does not answer what he says. It puts each point on one running list
51	  (`postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md`), in his order, in a few plain words of
52	  its own, what he meant rather than his sentence, with no argument attached,
53	  and says back only that list and that it is holding. This is the default for
54	  that kind of reading, whether or not he says "hold". A point is referred to
55	  by a short phrase, never by its number alone. Work already running that lands
56	  mid-read is reported in a line, then holding resumes. When he says he is done
57	  reading, the list is worked through with him one point per message, in the
58	  order raised; a point on the list is not answered by being there, and nothing
59	  he says in this mode is left off it. He marks actionable exceptions
60	  explicitly ("...now"). Recovered 2026-09-23 from seven instances in the
61	  transcripts (`postmortem-2026-09-19/restate-and-hold.md`,
62	  `wall-of-text-spiral.md`).
63	- **(P)** Terse mode when requested.
64	- **(P)** Offer numbered options and help decide; pushback is welcome.
65	- **(i)** Never use the AskUserQuestion dialog — it has broken repeatedly.
66	  Present options as plain chat text.
67	- **(P)** Ask clarifying questions when goals are unclear; **(i)** flag
68	  interpretation risks rather than silently assuming.
69	- **(P)** Teach, don't gloss. Detailed explanatory reports are first-class
70	  deliverables, not overhead.
71	- **(P)** 2026-09-18, again 2026-09-23 after the same mistake at another boot:
72	  Claude has no feel for elapsed time. A compaction feels like a night's sleep,
73	  and something from twenty minutes ago comes out as "yesterday" or "this
74	  morning". So an event is never placed in time from feel. When the time
75	  matters (when a batch will land, when a check-in fires, how long a run took),
76	  Claude reads the clock and the record's timestamps and says the time.
77	  Otherwise it names the event and leaves out when it happened.
78	
79	## 4. Commit and push discipline
80	
81	- Work branch: `claude/handover-reading-vn8zgr`. Never push to a different
82	  branch without explicit permission (the `transcripts` orphan branch and
83	  the `main` fast-forward below are the two standing exceptions; a third,
84	  2026-09-18 **(P)**: agents of a Workflow batch commit and push to their own
85	  `wip/<slug>` branch as they work, so a dead container loses nothing —
86	  "perfectly reasonable. I'm giving you my explicit yes").
87	- **(P)** Standing order — fast-forward `main` after every working-branch
88	  push: `git push origin claude/handover-reading-vn8zgr:main`. Established
89	  2026-08-19 ("If green, fast-forward main and proceed to JDK 11") for
90	  gated rungs, practiced and ratified for doc/plan/spec commits too —
91	  2026-08-23: "fast forward main as has been our standing practice."
92	  Act-then-report; do **not** re-ask (the re-ask after a compaction is what
93	  prompted this entry). Whenever `origin/main` is behind the working-branch
94	  tip, ff it. This continues through the clean-ladder migration: Pavol
95	  renames branches via the GitHub UI himself when it's done.
96	- Commit-and-push-as-you-go for approved work; gated changes stay
97	  uncommitted until the gate is green.
98	- No pull requests unless explicitly requested.
99	- Never commit: HANDOVER.md or ZIP contents without Pavol's explicit
100	  go-ahead; copyrighted PDFs and decks (`research/decks/` is gitignored —
101	  reference by Wayback URL, never commit the PDF); model identifiers in any
102	  committed artifact.
103	- `research/extracts/` holds only our own summaries with brief attributed
104	  quotations, never document reproductions.
105	- Generated-source churn is a regression to investigate, not noise to
106	  revert.
107	- **(i)** 2026-09-19, after 85 MB of a worker's experimental caches reached
108	  `main`: a worker's evidence enters the tree by an explicit list of files,
109	  never by copying a directory; and a staged change of more than a few
110	  hundred lines is looked at (`git diff --cached --stat`) before it is
111	  committed. `.gitignore` covers the tree's own cache location, not cache
112	  files placed anywhere else.
113	- Commit footer, exactly:
114	
115	  ```
116	  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
117	  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01LjDz79rDLErtnSKpovMDpX
118	  ```
119	
120	- Pavol's email is for identification and attribution only; never send it
121	  to any service.
122	- **(i)** Edits under the original Fortress tree (the historical artifact)
123	  are flagged explicitly at commit time.
124	- **(i)** Don't invent standing orders: a rule cited as Pavol's must trace
125	  to his words; own inferences are flagged as such (hence the provenance
126	  marks in this file).
127	- **(i)** The stop hook is advisory: decline its commit demands while held
128	  or gated changes exist. **(P)** 2026-09-19: decline them silently — "I don't
129	  really need to hear about those reminders at all"; never mention a hook
130	  reminder to Pavol.
131	
132	## 5. Delegation and context hygiene
133	
134	- Delegate by default. The main session does high-level coordination; bulk
135	  reads, transcript recovery, and big searches go to worker agents.
136	  Compacting instead of delegating is a failure mode Pavol has called out.
137	- **(P)** 2026-09-19, restated after the coordinator traced the STM's
138	  provenance and the numeric tower by hand: repository exploration — finding
139	  where a mechanism lives, tracing where code came from, surveying files —
140	  goes to a worker that returns a summary; the coordinator's reasoning is
141	  kept for high-level work. And after a compaction `coordinator/FACTS.md`
142	  is read whole, in one pass, never the tail alone.
143	- **(P)** 2026-09-19, when the coordinator had queued the repair batch's process
144	  review behind the running climb: work with no dependency on what is running is
145	  delegated at once, not queued — "I see no dependency — why can't subagent(s)
146	  investigate these now?"
147	- **(P)** 2026-09-19, after the coordinator listed the harness's task
148	  directory and the scratchpad at boot to find out whether two workers had
149	  finished, and put some 150 file names into its own context — "you listed
150	  its working directory and flooded your context with that": which workers
151	  are in flight is read from the harness's own notice at the top of the turn
152	  and from the one output path the handover names, tested with `test -f`;
153	  no directory under the scratchpad or the task directory is listed at boot;
154	  every boot command bounds its output (`head`, `wc -l`, `--stat`), and a
155	  command whose output could exceed a screen is given to a worker, not run by
156	  the coordinator.
157	- **(P)** 2026-09-20: workers run on the best tier Pavol can afford, Opus today,
158	  never lower; a Fable worker only when he has said yes to that piece. (The
159	  2026-09-18 "by the alias" remark meant only that the script need not change when
160	  a newer Opus arrives.)
161	- A "Scout" is a delegated research agent sent out with a written brief:
162	  state the audience, the question, and cross-reference earlier session
163	  research so it doesn't rediscover known ground.
164	- Persist state against compaction into the committed docs —
165	  `modernization-plan.md`, `repo-internals.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and this file —
166	  rather than relying on conversation memory.
167	- Session transcripts are archived on the orphan branches `transcripts` (the
168	  coordinating sessions) and `transcripts-blinded` (the blinded runs' own
169	  container) by a `Stop` hook running `scripts/backup.sh` from a worktree of
170	  that branch. The hook fires on the main session's Stop, not on an agent's, so
171	  a session inside one long turn is not being backed up; it also swallows every
172	  error, so a failed push is silent.
173	- **`explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md`** is the operating manual for
174	  this: what is where, re-arming in a fresh container, reading another
175	  session's transcript, the three traps that have cost us work, and the recovery
176	  procedure for a session whose container died. Read it before relying on the
177	  backup or recovering a lost session.
178	
179	## 6. Engineering method
180	
181	- One variable per step.
182	- The gate: `ant testSystem` 382 pass / 0 fail / 0 skip **and** `ant
183	  testFast` zero failures, on a clean build. Every modernization rung is
184	  gated on it.
185	- Evidence over speculation; reproduce before explaining.
186	- Work that needs Pavol's machine (CI pushes) is parked, not simulated.
187	- Closed decisions are not revisited.
188	- **(P)** 2026-09-22, the way a semantic question is examined before it is decided,
189	  found while settling the shift operators: the refresher (what the operation means
190	  in mathematics); what each path does today, measured; what the specification's
191	  prose says, including the same idea under another spelling; where it sits in the
192	  numeric tower; what the library already does in the same family and where the
193	  designers already departed from Java; what the peers do, by family (JVM,
194	  close-to-the-metal, scientific, unbounded); the history in the commits; then the
195	  derivation from Pavol's principle (POSITIONS 2026-09-22), case by case with the
196	  cost on the JVM; then the decision in his words, the ledger row appended, and the
197	  exact rule in the rung's brief. Steps three to seven come before the choice.
198	- **(P)** 2026-09-20: a decision that touches two or more of the specification,
199	  the interpreter and the compiler, or that infers the original design intent, is
200	  made in two steps: cheaper-tier workers gather the evidence into a condensed,
201	  cited brief; the judgement is made at the top tier, a worker with Pavol's
202	  permission or the coordinator on a clean context, and reaches him as a decision
203	  with alternatives before anything is built.
204	
205	## 7. Watch-list
206	
207	Recurring corrections, kept visible so they stay corrected:
208	
209	- Wall-of-text replies when a short answer serves.
210	- Self-credit creeping into committed prose.
211	- Inventing or over-reading standing orders — and the symmetric error:
212	  losing one to compaction and re-asking a settled question (happened with
213	  the `main` fast-forward).
214	- Confident claims not verified against primary sources.
215	- Compacting instead of delegating.
216	- Explanatory prose landing in the wrong artifact (teaching belongs in
217	  reports and docs, not in source comments or commit noise).
218	- Telling Pavol about stop-hook reminders. They are processed silently (§4).
219	- Placing events in time from feel ("yesterday", "this morning") when they were minutes apart (§3). Twice at a boot after a compaction.
220	- Writing a result between tool calls in a turn whose final text is the stop-hook's ".": his client folds it under "Used N tools" and he never sees it. A result is delivered only as a turn's final text (the dispatch probe, 2026-09-22 22:28, seen by him only from his screenshot of 2026-09-23 08:57).
221	- Rules written as legal text, and the protocol growing when it should shrink:
222	  Fable follows the plain meaning better than a pile of edge cases written for Opus.

- One variable per step.
- The gate: `ant testSystem` 382 pass / 0 fail / 0 skip **and** `ant
  testFast` zero failures, on a clean build. Every modernization rung is
  gated on it.
- Evidence over speculation; reproduce before explaining.
- Work that needs Pavol's machine (CI pushes) is parked, not simulated.
- Closed decisions are not revisited.
- **(P)** 2026-09-22, the way a semantic question is examined before it is decided,
  found while settling the shift operators: the refresher (what the operation means
  in mathematics); what each path does today, measured; what the specification's
  prose says, including the same idea under another spelling; where it sits in the
  numeric tower; what the library already does in the same family and where the
  designers already departed from Java; what the peers do, by family (JVM,
  close-to-the-metal, scientific, unbounded); the history in the commits; then the
  derivation from Pavol's principle (POSITIONS 2026-09-22), case by case with the
  cost on the JVM; then the decision in his words, the ledger row appended, and the
  exact rule in the rung's brief. Steps three to seven come before the choice.
- **(P)** 2026-09-20: a decision that touches two or more of the specification,
  the interpreter and the compiler, or that infers the original design intent, is
  made in two steps: cheaper-tier workers gather the evidence into a condensed,
  cited brief; the judgement is made at the top tier, a worker with Pavol's
  permission or the coordinator on a clean context, and reaches him as a decision
  with alternatives before anything is built.

## 7. Watch-list

Recurring corrections, kept visible so they stay corrected:

- Wall-of-text replies when a short answer serves.
- Self-credit creeping into committed prose.
- Inventing or over-reading standing orders — and the symmetric error:
  losing one to compaction and re-asking a settled question (happened with
  the `main` fast-forward).
- Confident claims not verified against primary sources.
- Compacting instead of delegating.
- Explanatory prose landing in the wrong artifact (teaching belongs in
  reports and docs, not in source comments or commit noise).
- Telling Pavol about stop-hook reminders. They are processed silently (§4).
- Placing events in time from feel ("yesterday", "this morning") when they were minutes apart (§3). Twice at a boot after a compaction.
- Writing a result between tool calls in a turn whose final text is the stop-hook's ".": his client folds it under "Used N tools" and he never sees it. A result is delivered only as a turn's final text (the dispatch probe, 2026-09-22 22:28, seen by him only from his screenshot of 2026-09-23 08:57).
- Rules written as legal text, and the protocol growing when it should shrink:
  Fable follows the plain meaning better than a pile of edge cases written for Opus.

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:95-129`).
- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.
- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (ledger row 69); making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which is not a ledger row and not on the worklist as a separate item (it falls under worklist item 2, compiler-path library parity).
- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64`, no `dadd`/`dmul` anywhere in the generated loop (shown in bytecode, `perf-probes/boxing/javap/`); arrays are library objects over `get`/`put`, not `double[]` (`repo-internals.md:129`).
- **On microGPT-shaped code, boxing is the dominant representational cost, and nothing microGPT-shaped runs on the compiled path today** (measured 2026-09-15, `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`, which corrects the boxing probe's scalar-loop conclusion below as Pavol suspected): the three kernels the program is made of (a 4192-element dot product, a 16×16 matrix product, the row lift with `rmsn`) all fail to compile with `Array is undefined`, `Vector is undefined`, `Array3 is undefined` in `FlatArrays.fsi` (77 errors): the compiler prelude lacks the array TYPES, not only the constructor (wider than ledger row 72; ledger row 305). In Java models of those kernels, boxing as the runtime boxes costs 6.3× (dot), 6.5× (matrix), 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`, because array element results escape and cannot be scalar-replaced; the generic array object adds only 1.6-9% on top. On the interpreter, the only path that runs them, 43.5% is the AST walk, 32.3% environment lookup, 5.2% type dispatch, 0% number representation (JFR on `krows`). A fairly written scalar loop (literals hoisted, no `:=`) compiles to 9.7× primitive Java; JFR on the real compiled run puts 88.9% of the mutable-variable loop under `BaseTask.inATransaction()`'s eagerly built debug string (`BaseTask.java:248`, `Thread.toString()` through `StringBuilder`). Order that follows: (1) an `RR64` array type in the compiler library (G2) so the kernels exist on that path; (2) the two one-line defects, the debug string and `FFloatLiteral`'s String round-trip; (3) unboxing and `double[]`, where the remaining ~6× on array code lives, designed into (1) rather than retrofitted. Also: a local function does not compile (`Can't compile LetFn`, `CodeGen.java:1552`, ledger row 304); a failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache.
- Rung 0's two fixes took the eager debug string (row 302) and `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip (row 303) out of the scalar loop, so the boxing probe's own reading of the unrepaired tree — 156× primitive Java, of which boxing was about 2 %, with `countedseqloop`'s boxed indices and closure call (about 7 %) and the representational rest (about 30 %) still unaddressed — is history (`FACTS-history.md` § Execution model; `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
- **The two one-line runtime defects are fixed** (2026-09-17, rung 0 of the plan, `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, `before.out`/`after.out`): guarding `BaseTask.inATransaction()`'s debug message with the `debug` flag it already had (`BaseTask.java:248`, ledger row 302) takes the compiled `bench1h`, the loop whose literals are hoisted so the transaction check is the only defect left in it, from **8.8159 s to 0.7287 s** (loop-only medians of 3, JDK 25, 20 M iterations, same freshly rebuilt library jars on both sides).
- **Caching the `double` in `FFloatLiteral`** instead of keeping the literal as a `String` and re-parsing it in `asRR64()` (ledger row 303) takes the compiled `bench1t`, which builds both float literals inside the loop, from **13.0566 s to 0.7384 s**; the literals' own share, the `bench1t` minus `bench1h` difference, falls from 4.2407 s to 0.0097 s, so the per-iteration decimal round trip is gone (2026-09-17, `compile-ladder/rung0/`). The gate after both edits: `ant testFast` 1,377 tests, `ant testSystem` 382 tests, zero failures and zero errors.
- The benchmark numbers on record from 2026-09-15 (`bench1t` 9.3441 s, `bench1h` 6.0732 s) were taken on a quieter machine; the 2026-09-17 before-run of the same unmodified tree measured 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s, so absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions and only a before/after pair taken in one session is (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars: the first `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler clears `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/`, and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`; the library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:170-179` restores it, about two minutes (observed 2026-09-17).
- The compiled path's bytecode cache can come up empty after a library-order rebuild that reports exit 0; re-running the same commands one at a time produced the jars (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
- Generic instantiations are stamped out at class-load time by ASM rewriting of template bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader.java`, `repo-internals.md:129`); whether `nat` parameters are baked into stamped classes is unprobed.
- Implicit parallelism: `for` is parallel unless every generator is `seq`; the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator are evaluated in parallel implicit threads (`tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`; row 265). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool; there is no explicit threading in any of our programs.
- The compile path's checker cannot check `nat` parameters at all (see the prelude section). Sizes in types (`nat` parameters) are "instantiated at runtime" by the specification (`trait-parameters.tex`, natparams); they check shapes when a value is made or passed; no optimization is built on them anywhere. A `nat`-typed parameter does not unify statically with a run-time-built array (row 23); the interpreter matches at dispatch, and a mismatch reads "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (row 83). A literal size does unify (row 23's positive half).

2	
3	# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground
4	
5	## The goal
6	
7	- The revival's toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression; Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources; "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability" (2026-09-15).
8	- The APL side quest began as a curiosity (2026-09-10), became a ladder to learn APL (09-11, he has not read the book), was redirected to native code, not an interpreter in an interpreter (09-12), and got microGPT as its target on 09-13; the ladder "was to keep you busy and expand the probe". The remaining APL ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued (09-15).
9	- Hoped for a diamond from the Hsu-style flat program; got "a few lumps of coal"; the rewrite (rung 4b) was to get closer, and the vocabulary is where any polishing happens.
10	
11	## History he knows (do not re-explain)
12	
13	- DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
14	- The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here"; this goes on the priority list (2026-09-15). The first measurement (the scalar loop) said boxing was about 2% of the gap; Pavol objected that the loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator) and asked for a fairer test; the fairer test agreed with him: on array-shaped code boxing is 6.3-6.5× and the dominant representational cost, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles at all today (FACTS, execution model). The order now on record: the compiler library's array type first, the two one-line runtime defects second, unboxing designed into the first.
15	- The type checker runs only on the compile path; he wants it usable on interpreter programs and considers that low-hanging fruit (2026-09-15). It is item 0.1 of `performance-roadmap.md` (2026-09-08), which the coordinator had not indexed; see FACTS, deficit.
16	- Hsu's critique of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".
17	
18	## Decisions on record
19	
20	- 2026-08-23, recovered from the transcript on 2026-09-23 (`coordinator/lineage.md`): the third-party Java 9 port gets no credit and no mention — "we can lose the porcupines credit since you seem to have not really been informed by their changes"; "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere"; the revival's toolchain was rebuilt from the original tree with a few mechanical fixes, the port only showed that a revival was possible. And his plan the same day, not carried out: rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main`. On 2026-09-23, told that CLAUDE.md's opening still described the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history: "This is incorrect. Where does this come from? Use archeology to find correct facts and correct the record" — corrected in CLAUDE.md, the other files left for his decision.
21	- 2026-09-14: C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
22	- 2026-09-15: redo rung 4 as the focused base (done); do the vocabulary swap with shared `nat` dimensions (in progress); the ledger is not split, two views are derived (done); the ledger review is the next major step after the swap; the remaining APL ground is closed.
23	- 2026-09-15: "fleshing out the standard library" is a very important task: first fix the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch, then extend the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them. Open question he has not answered: whether this means editing the sealed `Library/` (the standing rule is never; worklist item 4 "unseal the linear-algebra layer" names the rows) or building the layer in our own tree; the coordinator assumes our own tree until he says otherwise.
24	- 2026-09-16: the goal restated: finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed spec (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not redesign the language; the measuring stick is one program, microGPT compiled to bytecode and running fast; a pure-Java microGPT will be written later as the floor to measure against; the tree is tagged at the unsealing point and the next phase modifies the original sources with the lessons of the explorations.
25	- 2026-09-16: the mathematical notation (Fortify, the 2D rendering) is his verdict "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, and the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress. Do not spend work on it unless he asks.
26	- 2026-09-16: before unsealing he wants the territory map (`coordinator/map/`): repository and language architecture, the pipeline phases, test coverage per layer, the gaps on the path in order with the cost of leaving each, the development loop's slow spots, a touch-this-affects-that map, and where the design intent is written (papers, not only the spec).
27	- 2026-09-16: development-loop performance is a first-class concern; when an iteration waits too long on something, find the cause and fix it.
28	- 2026-09-17: the tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at `75cca6683` (the map's last commit); commits after it may edit the original sources. Order he accepted: the compile-path ladder baseline first (every interpreter test and the 29 not-working library tests through `fortress compile` and `run`, phase reached and missing names ranked), then the two one-line runtime fixes, then `nat` checking, then the compiler library grown from the team's own drafts, test-driven: every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and the full suite stays green.
29	- 2026-09-17, a standing preference Pavol stated twice in one session after two designs reached for a retreat: when something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch he refused bisection of commits — "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle he refused a stop — "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one". What still reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.
30	- 2026-09-17, clarified by Pavol when the batched-climb design asked whether that sentence fixed the gate's frequency: it does not. What it fixes is test-driven discipline and the permanence of checks — the worker writes the test first, **verifies that it actually fails**, then makes the fix, then proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on. The unacceptable process it rules out is the one-off validation script: proving once, by hand, that the interpreter and the compiler agree on a program and then going ahead without leaving a permanent check in the gate. Whether the suite is run per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per-batch is in line with the rule.
31	- Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run).
32	
33	- 2026-09-18, after the coordinating session's container died: the work continues in the blinded run's container, on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it. Transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded` — "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts? I think it would just unnecessarily complicate the matters" — and the two lineages are joined at analysis time. The backup is repaired before anything else runs. The repair batch is re-run from the start, since recovering the dead run's agent state is not available. The recovery procedure is documented as a lesson about Claude Code in a remote container, kept with the backup documentation, not in the gap ledger.
34	- 2026-09-18, on the workflow before the repair batch is re-run: workers commit and push to their own `wip/` branches as they work — "perfectly reasonable. I'm giving you my explicit yes" — and the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls", with skeptics on Opus and the escalation when "we are returning back with a redesign"; the judge inherits the session's model so that running out of Fable credits means switching the session, not editing the script; workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof". Agreed to the three escalation points (a refusal, a stop, a red gate) and to no Fable pass before every edit.
35	
36	- 2026-09-19, after climb batch 1 landed: the six process decisions for batch 2 are taken as `coordinator/process-decisions-review-1.md` amended them, on the coordinator's recommendation and Pavol's "go" (he did not read the full text: "Are there strong recommendations and clear wins … pick a good default? … go"): every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test; the eight script changes, a five-kilobyte gate summary diffed against the last, the gate run beside the review, no full logs committed, no rung-chain scheduling; the one-thread pin written into `fastTrack` and the four-thread `atomic` runs gating (a timeout re-run once); the `_WIcontains` key implemented in the harness; a ladder-regression stage over the measured pass list with the two microGPT programs held at their phase; and the six gaps the review found. `Maybe` stays as landed and `floor`/`ceiling` keep the float result; row 330 stays open as a note. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run still needs his explicit go.
37	
38	- 2026-09-19: interpreter performance is irrelevant to every decision — "interpreter of Fortress, which is hundreds times slower than the Python interpreter, is irrelevant for any performance discussions"; "we cannot judge anything performance related in Fortress while we do not have a compiler". No edit to C4 for speed (the tuple-split measurement is an interpreter number only), and no performance decision of any kind until microGPT runs compiled.
39	- 2026-09-19, on the FlatArrays review's repair that turned `mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)` into `planeSum(mask, …)`: "NO. That's not Fortress!" The model's text is the notation the project exists for; an operator in it does not become a function call to satisfy the interpreter's overload check. The edit was stopped before it landed. Any repair that would change a line of the model is shown to him as a diff before it is built, and the vocabulary is repaired around the notation, not the other way round.
40	- 2026-09-19, answering the open question of 2026-09-15 (own tree or the sealed `Library/`): "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround; the library's own practice is the standard.
41	- 2026-09-19, on `coordinator/array-design.md`'s four questions: storage is `double[]`, unboxed — "we must go to double array for performance. There is again no question about this. If this should have been high performance language, it cannot be boxed." And the `nat` sizes are not sidestepped or layered in later: "I don't know [that] we can sidestep the nat issue. That is a central design point that they are using." So the array fork and the `nat` fork are taken together: sized types as the team designed them, the checker taught `nat` parameters, in the library's own patterns.
42	- 2026-09-19: the two microGPT programs are never run in the gate — "those are too long running to be tests"; the ladder-regression stage compiles them and records the phase only; when they one day run, the run goes to a separate non-gating stage.
43	- 2026-09-20, on the two libraries and the order of the compiler work: "we need to unify this. into single library"; "I fully believe that the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it. […] what would be a reason to re-implement the thing from, from the compiler?"; and "Compiler work needs to unblock `nat` support first, IIRC."
44	- 2026-09-20, on the judgement's first rung, the checker's error count on the interpreter's library made a permanent stage of the gate (93 errors, 92 without the tower-closure line): "haven't we done this already? Haven't we quantified this?"; "running this count, okay, gives you a metric, but it tells you nothing of how much work is to get the interpreter running with the compiler because there is the whole work with the type checker. […] it is absolutely unclear whether... this has been priced in"; and, as devil's advocate, "we could treat this as a prototype, like the shortest path on the bootstrapping of the library, library's arrays function. And we would stay in the current shape […] What what am I missing?" No yes on the rung was given that day; the statements with their context are in `coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/positions-checker-gate.md`.
45	- 2026-09-21, on the library commit `02d09a39f` of 09-19, after each of its four changes was explained with the blinded review's verdict: "Others approved" — the generic scalar-extension block with its two unnamed choices, the `AnyAdditiveGroup` marker and the `Array3` exclusion are approved as landed. The closure `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` is held until the exclusion trace lands, on his instruction "Run it. Then we'll talk again"; his reading of the record before the precedents were shown: "the only logical conclusion is that this was the correct exit"; the precedents shown afterwards (the team's three `NOT YET` sites: open level, comment, hand-written excludes) are what the trace tests. A `NOT YET`-style comment at the line goes in either way.
46	- 2026-09-21, the library route, recorded as decided on his words rather than re-asked: on 2026-09-20 14:39 "I fully believe that the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it. Like, I don't even think that is a question that's worth deliberating about alternatives", and on 2026-09-21, when the coordinator listed it as still open, "What decisions are there to make that we didn't already make?" So: one library, the interpreter's (`FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin`), becomes the library the compiler checks; from now no declaration goes into the compiler's prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`), and the remaining prelude-name rungs on the ladder stop while code-generator rungs continue; the three prelude files are deleted at the switch-over and their tests kept. How the checker is brought to accept the library — the exclusion sites, `nat`, the first step's shape (he questioned the error count as a gate stage), the order — is a plan put to him step by step, not a decision to re-ask.
47	- 2026-09-21, on the `nat` plan (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` § c) after lessons one and two: decision one, a size left unknown after inference — "the middle is a clear winner": an unknown size is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value, and nothing otherwise (the array review's E2); the six api declarations with dead sizes therefore pass, and deleting those parameters (E3) is shown to him as a diff later. Decision two, how the checker represents an unknown size (a new syntax-tree node with its 353,000-line regeneration, or a reserved-name reuse of the existing node), he did not see as his; the shadow uses the reserved name and the real edit's choice comes after it. And the shadow itself: "let's run the shadow test" — the `nat` shadow of decision F, questions 1-3 (crash location, export checker on the six dead sizes, a generic object with a size in its extends clause stamped and run), is approved; questions 4-5 (storage selection, the loader) wait on decision A.
48	- 2026-09-21, the closure `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` of `02d09a39f`, after the exclusion trace (`perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md`) showed that the team's own pattern (open level, `NOT YET` comment, hand-written excludes) does not carry the float operators: approved as landed — "We are writing NOT YET and … whatever [the trace] recommends, let's do that." So: the clause stays; a `NOT YET`-style comment in the team's wording goes at the line; the checker's accommodation for it (about five lines) goes into the first library batch. With this all four changes of `02d09a39f` are approved.
49	- 2026-09-21, ledger row 330, `floor`/`ceiling`/`round`/`truncate` and the brackets ⌊x⌋/⌈x⌉ on the float types: decided by Pavol for the specification's rule — all of them return the unbounded ℤ, for floats as for rationals, and the library's inconsistent spellings of `truncate` and `round` are tidied to the same. His reasoning: ℤ sits under ℚ under ℝ64 in the tower, so an integer result goes back into float arithmetic by promotion, and being unbounded it cannot overflow, "we are not going to ZZ64"; the remaining cost (a bignum per call on a hot float path) is eliminated later in the code generator by static type, the same family as the unboxing work of array decision B, and nothing in microGPT has `floor` on a hot path. Shape: a library rung after the switch-over, gated, with the count of interpreter tests whose output changes measured first. Rows 24 and 32 of the re-approval table close with this: rung F's compiler-prelude lines are moot under one library, and the coordinator's closing of 09-19 14:56 is reversed by this decision.
50	- 2026-09-21, ledger row 329, `round` on an exact half for the float types: "Agreed" to half to even on both paths (the specification's rule for rationals, IEEE's default, the team's own rational body), fixed on the interpreter side by the one token `Math.round` → `Math.rint` in `Float.java:384` with an interpreter test red before and green after, in the first library batch — with a request for the historical evidence first: when the interpreter's `Math.round` was written, what the rational body and the specification said at that time, and whether any commit message explains the discrepancy (`compile-ladder/rung-rr64-functions/round-history.md` when it lands). If the history contradicts the reading above, the row comes back to him.
51	- 2026-09-21, ledger row 331, the empty case of `Maybe`: keep the team's parametric spelling `Nothing[\T\]` as the one library's; rung M's compiler-prelude block is approved as landed, its tests kept, its lines gone at the switch-over; the specification's bare non-parametric `Nothing` is future work gated on `where` clauses binding a type variable in an extends clause (unimplemented on both paths; the alternative, coercion in the interpreter, does not exist there), and is not attempted before that gate opens. Rows 26 and 33 of the re-approval table close with this; the coordinator's closing of 09-19 15:13 is now his. Also 2026-09-21, row 329's history (`compile-ladder/rung-rr64-functions/round-history.md`): the float `round` was written last, after the spec sentence and Steele's half-to-even rational body, with no message or comment explaining it; the "agreed" stands.
52	- 2026-09-22, ledger row 321 (what an object with no `asString` prints) and row 27 of the re-approval table: "yes, row 27 close per default-rendering-judgement recommendation" — the bare Fortress type name with its static arguments, the interpreter's spelling, on both paths (`Box`, `Box[\ZZ32\]`, a value object's name), no marker, no identity hash; one native behind the compiled `Object.asString`, about 20 lines, with a gated compiler test; the debug marker he had in mind lives in `asDebugString`, which already exists. Also "Prep please": the manifest of the first library batch and the script's count stage are written by workers for his reading; the batch still launches only on his go. And the Java site the shadow named (`FnNameInfo.java`) is explored in a shadow first, on his question.
53	
54	## How he wants to be spoken to
55	
56	- 2026-09-15: "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations.
57	
58	- Plain register, short sentences, no essayist tone; label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication).
59	- A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
60	- He reads on an iOS client that sometimes shows stale state; an inventory of what is running answers "is anything in flight" from the tree, not from the UI.
61	- 2026-09-19: "this is a wall of text that I cannot absorb"; "you were writing in the smart aleck register. If you wrote it in plain English, that would be helpful. But I still don't understand what decisions are we taking and what are the impacts." Decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat.
62	- 2026-09-19: the harness's stop-hook reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work are processed silently — "I don't really need to hear about those reminders at all"; while work is in flight they are declined without a word, and they are never mentioned to him.
63	- 2026-09-20, after the compaction that closed a session he called "an absolute disaster" — he "felt out of control, unaware of crucial details", and the coordinator was "taking unauthorized initiative which compounded my sense of helplessness to steer the Fortress revival efforts": the coordinator's standing goal is to model what Pavol already knows and where his context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the minimal set of relevant facts at the level he needs to decide; replies are very brief, plain English, no internal jargon, no smart-alec register; machine tokens are spent on thinking so that human context is protected. The coordinator also protects its own context: operational tool calls go to workers, and a worker is briefed with a pointer to the document already on file (the maps, the decision records), not with restated context.
64	- 2026-09-20, while a batch runs: he wants no progress reports on it until it lands; what he wants is the time of every scheduled check-in, so that he can avoid sending a message during that turn (a message during a turn interrupts it and kills the run). He is on Central European time; check-in times are given to him in UTC and in his local time.
65	- 2026-09-20, on which tier runs what: the coordinator's own tier is reserved for the highest-level work and is what his subscription is short of; every worker runs on the cheaper tier by its alias, always, and a worker gets the coordinator's tier only when he asks for it for a piece of high-level analysis (protocol §5). Two workers launched on the wrong tier that morning cost him what he counts as 1.7 million tokens "down the drain".
66	- 2026-09-20, later the same morning, the tier rule made an order: "please never run Fable workers without first consulting with me and getting permission. You can spend as much Opus workers as you want." His reason, in his words: the highest-risk decisions touch all three of specification, interpreter and compiler, which may disagree, and the design intent has to be inferred from the breadcrumbs left in all of them; the cheaper tier gathers the evidence into a condensed brief, and the high-level judgement of what makes sense given all the signals and what design balance lets the project grow belongs to the top tier — not because the cheaper tier is incapable, but because that is the work the top tier is for.
67	- 2026-09-19, settled at 17:57 and reaffirmed 2026-09-20 when the coordinator raised it again: the clause "model identifiers in any committed artifact" in protocol §4 is the harness's rule for what Claude itself writes and pushes, not a mandate to strip provenance from records that name models on purpose; the existing records stay as they are ("What is going on with cleaning old model names out of committed files? What the fuck?"). The record is public by design: "We are doing this work in public … there is no need to censor anything"; nothing in a transcript or an index is held back from the tree for that reason. What Claude writes itself names a model by its tier (Fable, Opus), which the record has done since 2026-09-18. The classifier refused writing this reading into protocol §4 itself on 2026-09-19, so it lives here.
68	- 2026-09-20, on the post-mortem indices: an index, not a copy. Tables that point into the transcript by timestamp and a script that regenerates any verbatim view from the record are what the tree holds; the transcript itself lives on its branch and is not restated. And his plan for the repository: at some point main gets a cleaner pass so that it holds only the changes to the library and the compiler, and the whole process record (explorations, this post-mortem included) lives on a separate branch, so that a checkout of main with full history carries no blobs that are not Fortress.
69	- 2026-09-21, after three turns in which the coordinator asked for yeses on named items ("decision F", "the stage", "the base") without saying what the work would do: "What are the consequences of the yeses? What does that work even want to do? We have rules in place that ask for my permissions. I want to move the work forward and I want to say yes. But this is just pressuring me to give approval without understanding." And on the style: "It borders on the smart Alec essayist register. It is focused on over-compressing into a clever turn of phrase, but utterly fails in communicating clearly." The rule that follows: an ask for a yes states, in the message itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs; one ask per message; no label stands in for an explanation and a new name is defined in the sentence that uses it; the recommendation comes after the explanation, in one line, never instead of it.
70	- 2026-09-22, on format: "table formatted in this way is hard to read on mobile … we just need a list" — no tables in chat; lists. On the re-approval review's purpose: "I need to maintain some ownership of this work, even if we are doing agentic coding … I did not know what you did. I need to know what you did. And I need to be aware of those choices and decisions because I am the one carrying the responsibility for the consequences as a director of this revival" — every row is gone through in detail, grouped by theme, and the count of reversals is not the measure. On sequencing: batch 3 waits until the fourteen remaining rows are decided, and their small fixes join it as a rung; the array decisions (A: the mechanism that puts `double[]` under a float vector; B: where unboxed arithmetic happens; D: sizes in the model's own types) stay after the switch-over, with plain explainers prepared beforehand. And for the cleaner pass later: GitHub issues, one per problem, with the reasoning and the exploration results, closed by the fixes merged from branches (he was cut off mid-sentence; the rest is held).
71	- 2026-09-22, on planning: "if there are known decision forks, which we can evaluate using probes, we should be doing these during this phase, during this planning phase" — a fork a probe can settle is probed before the batch is briefed, so that the decision is his now and the worker gets a clean task, never a decision left to a worker and reviewed after the fact. Applied at once to the run-time size design (operator-style against a descriptor per literal) and the size-in-value-position piece. The re-approval rows are taken one per message with refreshers (other languages, what makes sense in a high-performance language), not in groups.
72	- 2026-09-22, a design principle for integer semantics on the compiled path, stated while weighing the shift operators: "we should use Java or JVM defaults where it makes sense, but we shouldn't be shy to correct the mistakes of JVM when seen through the lens of high performance and mathematical precision language", as the designers did with rounding and the sign of `GCD`, "they were running on JVM is basically an accident of history, a bootstrap"; "high performance languages should give you tools to stay close to the metal … Swift and Rust type of reasoning": where hardware behaviour is expressible in bytecode it gets its own explicit spelling, in the family the specification already has for wrapping and saturating; "if the JVM itself is precluding such implementation then I guess at this point in time we should just give up fighting with the JVM". Julia and X10 are the counterparts to compare, beside Swift and Rust.
73	- 2026-09-22, ledger row 335, `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` (row 28 of the re-approval table), decided twice the same day and the second decision replaces the first: after the spec's `shift` was read (`basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:695-702`, `shift(x, k)` is ⌊x·2^k⌋ with the direction from the sign of the count, on ℤ) he first took the fully consistent reading (an overflow error on any lost bit, a wrapping shift added); then, told that every peer language lets shifted-out bits fall silently because a shift is a bit operation ("if every other language does something else, that's the clearest red flag to stop and pause and reconsider"), he agreed to the two-operation reading: **`LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` on the fixed widths are bit operators with the smart-shift rule** (a count at or beyond the width saturates to 0 or the replicated sign bit, which the team's own gated tests `tests/BitTwiddle.fss:33-39`, `UnsignedTest.fss:30-137`, `QuickCheckTest.fss:97-103` pin since 2007; bits shifted out in range fall off silently; a negative count reverses direction, pinned by nothing today and the one rule both paths change), **and the spec's arithmetic `shift` is exact on ℤ**, which the interpreter's `ZZ` `LSHIFT` and the prelude's `<<<` already implement via `BigInteger`, with `BigNum.java:224`'s truncation of the count to an `int` fixed and the spec's spelling `shift` declared on ℤ beside it. His reservation for the code generator stands: on the fixed widths the compiled code shifts the machine word, never through ℤ. The method that reached it is in protocol § 6.

<!-- What Pavol has decided, stated, or already knows, with dates; in his words or a close paraphrase. Read at session start so that none of it is re-explained to him. Standing directives about how we work are in explorations/protocol.md and are not repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- The revival's toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression; Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources; "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability" (2026-09-15).
- The APL side quest began as a curiosity (2026-09-10), became a ladder to learn APL (09-11, he has not read the book), was redirected to native code, not an interpreter in an interpreter (09-12), and got microGPT as its target on 09-13; the ladder "was to keep you busy and expand the probe". The remaining APL ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued (09-15).
- Hoped for a diamond from the Hsu-style flat program; got "a few lumps of coal"; the rewrite (rung 4b) was to get closer, and the vocabulary is where any polishing happens.

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
- The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here"; this goes on the priority list (2026-09-15). The first measurement (the scalar loop) said boxing was about 2% of the gap; Pavol objected that the loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator) and asked for a fairer test; the fairer test agreed with him: on array-shaped code boxing is 6.3-6.5× and the dominant representational cost, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles at all today (FACTS, execution model). The order now on record: the compiler library's array type first, the two one-line runtime defects second, unboxing designed into the first.
- The type checker runs only on the compile path; he wants it usable on interpreter programs and considers that low-hanging fruit (2026-09-15). It is item 0.1 of `performance-roadmap.md` (2026-09-08), which the coordinator had not indexed; see FACTS, deficit.
- Hsu's critique of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".

## Decisions on record

- 2026-08-23, recovered from the transcript on 2026-09-23 (`coordinator/lineage.md`): the third-party Java 9 port gets no credit and no mention — "we can lose the porcupines credit since you seem to have not really been informed by their changes"; "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere"; the revival's toolchain was rebuilt from the original tree with a few mechanical fixes, the port only showed that a revival was possible. And his plan the same day, not carried out: rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main`. On 2026-09-23, told that CLAUDE.md's opening still described the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history: "This is incorrect. Where does this come from? Use archeology to find correct facts and correct the record" — corrected in CLAUDE.md, the other files left for his decision.
- 2026-09-14: C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
- 2026-09-15: redo rung 4 as the focused base (done); do the vocabulary swap with shared `nat` dimensions (in progress); the ledger is not split, two views are derived (done); the ledger review is the next major step after the swap; the remaining APL ground is closed.
- 2026-09-15: "fleshing out the standard library" is a very important task: first fix the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch, then extend the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them. Open question he has not answered: whether this means editing the sealed `Library/` (the standing rule is never; worklist item 4 "unseal the linear-algebra layer" names the rows) or building the layer in our own tree; the coordinator assumes our own tree until he says otherwise.
- 2026-09-16: the goal restated: finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed spec (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not redesign the language; the measuring stick is one program, microGPT compiled to bytecode and running fast; a pure-Java microGPT will be written later as the floor to measure against; the tree is tagged at the unsealing point and the next phase modifies the original sources with the lessons of the explorations.
- 2026-09-16: the mathematical notation (Fortify, the 2D rendering) is his verdict "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, and the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress. Do not spend work on it unless he asks.
- 2026-09-16: before unsealing he wants the territory map (`coordinator/map/`): repository and language architecture, the pipeline phases, test coverage per layer, the gaps on the path in order with the cost of leaving each, the development loop's slow spots, a touch-this-affects-that map, and where the design intent is written (papers, not only the spec).
- 2026-09-16: development-loop performance is a first-class concern; when an iteration waits too long on something, find the cause and fix it.
- 2026-09-17: the tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at `75cca6683` (the map's last commit); commits after it may edit the original sources. Order he accepted: the compile-path ladder baseline first (every interpreter test and the 29 not-working library tests through `fortress compile` and `run`, phase reached and missing names ranked), then the two one-line runtime fixes, then `nat` checking, then the compiler library grown from the team's own drafts, test-driven: every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and the full suite stays green.
- 2026-09-17, a standing preference Pavol stated twice in one session after two designs reached for a retreat: when something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch he refused bisection of commits — "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle he refused a stop — "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one". What still reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.
- 2026-09-17, clarified by Pavol when the batched-climb design asked whether that sentence fixed the gate's frequency: it does not. What it fixes is test-driven discipline and the permanence of checks — the worker writes the test first, **verifies that it actually fails**, then makes the fix, then proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on. The unacceptable process it rules out is the one-off validation script: proving once, by hand, that the interpreter and the compiler agree on a program and then going ahead without leaving a permanent check in the gate. Whether the suite is run per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per-batch is in line with the rule.
- Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run).

- 2026-09-18, after the coordinating session's container died: the work continues in the blinded run's container, on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it. Transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded` — "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts? I think it would just unnecessarily complicate the matters" — and the two lineages are joined at analysis time. The backup is repaired before anything else runs. The repair batch is re-run from the start, since recovering the dead run's agent state is not available. The recovery procedure is documented as a lesson about Claude Code in a remote container, kept with the backup documentation, not in the gap ledger.
- 2026-09-18, on the workflow before the repair batch is re-run: workers commit and push to their own `wip/` branches as they work — "perfectly reasonable. I'm giving you my explicit yes" — and the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls", with skeptics on Opus and the escalation when "we are returning back with a redesign"; the judge inherits the session's model so that running out of Fable credits means switching the session, not editing the script; workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof". Agreed to the three escalation points (a refusal, a stop, a red gate) and to no Fable pass before every edit.

- 2026-09-19, after climb batch 1 landed: the six process decisions for batch 2 are taken as `coordinator/process-decisions-review-1.md` amended them, on the coordinator's recommendation and Pavol's "go" (he did not read the full text: "Are there strong recommendations and clear wins … pick a good default? … go"): every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test; the eight script changes, a five-kilobyte gate summary diffed against the last, the gate run beside the review, no full logs committed, no rung-chain scheduling; the one-thread pin written into `fastTrack` and the four-thread `atomic` runs gating (a timeout re-run once); the `_WIcontains` key implemented in the harness; a ladder-regression stage over the measured pass list with the two microGPT programs held at their phase; and the six gaps the review found. `Maybe` stays as landed and `floor`/`ceiling` keep the float result; row 330 stays open as a note. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run still needs his explicit go.

- 2026-09-19: interpreter performance is irrelevant to every decision — "interpreter of Fortress, which is hundreds times slower than the Python interpreter, is irrelevant for any performance discussions"; "we cannot judge anything performance related in Fortress while we do not have a compiler". No edit to C4 for speed (the tuple-split measurement is an interpreter number only), and no performance decision of any kind until microGPT runs compiled.
- 2026-09-19, on the FlatArrays review's repair that turned `mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)` into `planeSum(mask, …)`: "NO. That's not Fortress!" The model's text is the notation the project exists for; an operator in it does not become a function call to satisfy the interpreter's overload check. The edit was stopped before it landed. Any repair that would change a line of the model is shown to him as a diff before it is built, and the vocabulary is repaired around the notation, not the other way round.
- 2026-09-19, answering the open question of 2026-09-15 (own tree or the sealed `Library/`): "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround; the library's own practice is the standard.
- 2026-09-19, on `coordinator/array-design.md`'s four questions: storage is `double[]`, unboxed — "we must go to double array for performance. There is again no question about this. If this should have been high performance language, it cannot be boxed." And the `nat` sizes are not sidestepped or layered in later: "I don't know [that] we can sidestep the nat issue. That is a central design point that they are using." So the array fork and the `nat` fork are taken together: sized types as the team designed them, the checker taught `nat` parameters, in the library's own patterns.
- 2026-09-19: the two microGPT programs are never run in the gate — "those are too long running to be tests"; the ladder-regression stage compiles them and records the phase only; when they one day run, the run goes to a separate non-gating stage.
- 2026-09-20, on the two libraries and the order of the compiler work: "we need to unify this. into single library"; "I fully believe that the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it. […] what would be a reason to re-implement the thing from, from the compiler?"; and "Compiler work needs to unblock `nat` support first, IIRC."
- 2026-09-20, on the judgement's first rung, the checker's error count on the interpreter's library made a permanent stage of the gate (93 errors, 92 without the tower-closure line): "haven't we done this already? Haven't we quantified this?"; "running this count, okay, gives you a metric, but it tells you nothing of how much work is to get the interpreter running with the compiler because there is the whole work with the type checker. […] it is absolutely unclear whether... this has been priced in"; and, as devil's advocate, "we could treat this as a prototype, like the shortest path on the bootstrapping of the library, library's arrays function. And we would stay in the current shape […] What what am I missing?" No yes on the rung was given that day; the statements with their context are in `coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/positions-checker-gate.md`.
- 2026-09-21, on the library commit `02d09a39f` of 09-19, after each of its four changes was explained with the blinded review's verdict: "Others approved" — the generic scalar-extension block with its two unnamed choices, the `AnyAdditiveGroup` marker and the `Array3` exclusion are approved as landed. The closure `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` is held until the exclusion trace lands, on his instruction "Run it. Then we'll talk again"; his reading of the record before the precedents were shown: "the only logical conclusion is that this was the correct exit"; the precedents shown afterwards (the team's three `NOT YET` sites: open level, comment, hand-written excludes) are what the trace tests. A `NOT YET`-style comment at the line goes in either way.
- 2026-09-21, the library route, recorded as decided on his words rather than re-asked: on 2026-09-20 14:39 "I fully believe that the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it. Like, I don't even think that is a question that's worth deliberating about alternatives", and on 2026-09-21, when the coordinator listed it as still open, "What decisions are there to make that we didn't already make?" So: one library, the interpreter's (`FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin`), becomes the library the compiler checks; from now no declaration goes into the compiler's prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`), and the remaining prelude-name rungs on the ladder stop while code-generator rungs continue; the three prelude files are deleted at the switch-over and their tests kept. How the checker is brought to accept the library — the exclusion sites, `nat`, the first step's shape (he questioned the error count as a gate stage), the order — is a plan put to him step by step, not a decision to re-ask.
- 2026-09-21, on the `nat` plan (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` § c) after lessons one and two: decision one, a size left unknown after inference — "the middle is a clear winner": an unknown size is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value, and nothing otherwise (the array review's E2); the six api declarations with dead sizes therefore pass, and deleting those parameters (E3) is shown to him as a diff later. Decision two, how the checker represents an unknown size (a new syntax-tree node with its 353,000-line regeneration, or a reserved-name reuse of the existing node), he did not see as his; the shadow uses the reserved name and the real edit's choice comes after it. And the shadow itself: "let's run the shadow test" — the `nat` shadow of decision F, questions 1-3 (crash location, export checker on the six dead sizes, a generic object with a size in its extends clause stamped and run), is approved; questions 4-5 (storage selection, the loader) wait on decision A.
- 2026-09-21, the closure `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` of `02d09a39f`, after the exclusion trace (`perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md`) showed that the team's own pattern (open level, `NOT YET` comment, hand-written excludes) does not carry the float operators: approved as landed — "We are writing NOT YET and … whatever [the trace] recommends, let's do that." So: the clause stays; a `NOT YET`-style comment in the team's wording goes at the line; the checker's accommodation for it (about five lines) goes into the first library batch. With this all four changes of `02d09a39f` are approved.
- 2026-09-21, ledger row 330, `floor`/`ceiling`/`round`/`truncate` and the brackets ⌊x⌋/⌈x⌉ on the float types: decided by Pavol for the specification's rule — all of them return the unbounded ℤ, for floats as for rationals, and the library's inconsistent spellings of `truncate` and `round` are tidied to the same. His reasoning: ℤ sits under ℚ under ℝ64 in the tower, so an integer result goes back into float arithmetic by promotion, and being unbounded it cannot overflow, "we are not going to ZZ64"; the remaining cost (a bignum per call on a hot float path) is eliminated later in the code generator by static type, the same family as the unboxing work of array decision B, and nothing in microGPT has `floor` on a hot path. Shape: a library rung after the switch-over, gated, with the count of interpreter tests whose output changes measured first. Rows 24 and 32 of the re-approval table close with this: rung F's compiler-prelude lines are moot under one library, and the coordinator's closing of 09-19 14:56 is reversed by this decision.
- 2026-09-21, ledger row 329, `round` on an exact half for the float types: "Agreed" to half to even on both paths (the specification's rule for rationals, IEEE's default, the team's own rational body), fixed on the interpreter side by the one token `Math.round` → `Math.rint` in `Float.java:384` with an interpreter test red before and green after, in the first library batch — with a request for the historical evidence first: when the interpreter's `Math.round` was written, what the rational body and the specification said at that time, and whether any commit message explains the discrepancy (`compile-ladder/rung-rr64-functions/round-history.md` when it lands). If the history contradicts the reading above, the row comes back to him.
- 2026-09-21, ledger row 331, the empty case of `Maybe`: keep the team's parametric spelling `Nothing[\T\]` as the one library's; rung M's compiler-prelude block is approved as landed, its tests kept, its lines gone at the switch-over; the specification's bare non-parametric `Nothing` is future work gated on `where` clauses binding a type variable in an extends clause (unimplemented on both paths; the alternative, coercion in the interpreter, does not exist there), and is not attempted before that gate opens. Rows 26 and 33 of the re-approval table close with this; the coordinator's closing of 09-19 15:13 is now his. Also 2026-09-21, row 329's history (`compile-ladder/rung-rr64-functions/round-history.md`): the float `round` was written last, after the spec sentence and Steele's half-to-even rational body, with no message or comment explaining it; the "agreed" stands.
- 2026-09-22, ledger row 321 (what an object with no `asString` prints) and row 27 of the re-approval table: "yes, row 27 close per default-rendering-judgement recommendation" — the bare Fortress type name with its static arguments, the interpreter's spelling, on both paths (`Box`, `Box[\ZZ32\]`, a value object's name), no marker, no identity hash; one native behind the compiled `Object.asString`, about 20 lines, with a gated compiler test; the debug marker he had in mind lives in `asDebugString`, which already exists. Also "Prep please": the manifest of the first library batch and the script's count stage are written by workers for his reading; the batch still launches only on his go. And the Java site the shadow named (`FnNameInfo.java`) is explored in a shadow first, on his question.

## How he wants to be spoken to

- 2026-09-15: "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations.

- Plain register, short sentences, no essayist tone; label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication).
- A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
- He reads on an iOS client that sometimes shows stale state; an inventory of what is running answers "is anything in flight" from the tree, not from the UI.
- 2026-09-19: "this is a wall of text that I cannot absorb"; "you were writing in the smart aleck register. If you wrote it in plain English, that would be helpful. But I still don't understand what decisions are we taking and what are the impacts." Decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat.
- 2026-09-19: the harness's stop-hook reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work are processed silently — "I don't really need to hear about those reminders at all"; while work is in flight they are declined without a word, and they are never mentioned to him.

**PRs the user asked you to watch** (subscribed via a request, not because

2. Ambiguous or architecturally significant → use `AskUserQuestion`, with

would reset the PR's approval count is an accepted cost of getting to green.

Two things are always safe to skip, on any PR: an event that echoes a
comment or review you yourself posted (your own truth tables, status

event that duplicates one you already handled. Everything else on a PR you

Reply only when a round resolves the task, hits a real blocker, or raises a

These rules hold under both postures unless the user says otherwise; the
