tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file outside the working directory that you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

schema.name: Write
schema.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file outside the working directory that you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a task suggestion you queued earlier with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion has gone stale: the issue was fixed in this session (by you or the user), it turned out not to be a problem after all, or you have queued a better-scoped replacement — in that case queue the replacement with spawn_task first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only a suggestion the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn. If they already started or dismissed it, the result says so and nothing changes; that answer is final, so don't retry or re-flag it.

Only a suggestion the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn. If they already started or dismissed it, the result says so and nothing changes; that answer is final, so don't retry or re-flag it.

reason.description: Optional short note on why the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34". It doesn't change the outcome.

task_id.description: The task_id from the spawn_task result that queued the suggestion (of the form task_1a2b3c4d).

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Suggest a separate task for something you noticed that is outside the scope of your current work.

Call this when you come across something that deserves fixing but doesn't belong in this change — dead code, stale docs, a missing test, a confirmed TODO, a bug or security issue spotted in passing. Don't use it for trivial fixes you can make inline, for anything the user asked you to do, for vague code-smell impressions or unverified hunches, or to split off parts of your own task. The call only queues a suggestion and returns; carry on with your current work.

The user sees a "Suggested task" card in the Claude desktop app with your title and tldr, can open the full prompt, and with one click starts it as a new session — on their machine in their local clone of this repository (optionally a fresh worktree of it), or in the cloud — sends it to this session, or dismisses it. A new session starts from your prompt alone, on a checkout that may not have this session's changes, so the prompt has to stand alone: what to change and why, the files involved by repository-relative path, and any context from this conversation it depends on. Absolute paths and other state of this environment may not exist there. If the find involves a secret or credential, say where it is rather than copying the value, since the prompt is stored and displayed.

The result carries a task_id; if the suggestion later becomes moot, withdraw it with dismiss_task.

prompt.description: The opening message of the new session: the goal, the files involved by repository-relative path, the context it needs from this conversation, and what done looks like. The user can read it in full before starting; markdown is fine. Keep it to what the task needs (hard limit 32000 characters) — the new session can read the code itself.

title.description: The card's heading and the new session's title: a short imperative phrase starting with a verb, under 60 characters, that makes sense on its own — e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option".

tldr.description: One or two plain sentences on what the task would do and why it is worth doing. Shown on the card under the title; it is what the user reads when deciding whether to start it, so no file paths or code.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__add_repo
tools.description:
Add a GitHub repository to the current session so you can read, clone, or operate on it alongside the repos already in the session. Call this whenever you need a repository the session does not have — including when someone only asks a question about one, rather than asking for it to be attached. Prefer attaching a repository over reporting that you cannot reach it. 

IMPORTANT — DO NOT PRE-CHECK THE REPO BEFORE CALLING THIS TOOL. Do not curl github.com, do not run `gh repo view`, do not run `git ls-remote` to verify the repo exists. Unauthenticated requests to private repos return 404 ("Not Found") even when the repo is real and your session has authorized access to it. Those preemptive 404s will mislead you into skipping the tool. Instead: call add_repo with the owner/repo exactly as you have it. The backend performs the real reachability + authorization check and returns a structured error you can act on. If the repo genuinely doesn't exist or isn't accessible, the tool response will tell you — report that to the user. If it does exist, the tool response will include a clone command you can then run. Do not report success until the tool has actually been called and returned. 

WHEN ACCESS IS DENIED: if the tool returns an authorization or policy error — the repo exists but isn't enabled for this workspace/project/organization, or the GitHub App isn't installed or linked — relay the tool's exact reason to the user. The response names the remedy: if Claude doesn't have GitHub access for this organization at all, the user should reconnect GitHub under claude.ai Settings → Connectors; if the repo is simply not in the allowed set, a Claude.ai organization owner can grant access in the settings page the response points to. Do not add settings URLs beyond those provided here or in the tool response. Do not retry the same repo. You may remind the user which repositories are already available in this session, and offer to help them request access. Do not guess, infer, or list repositories you cannot see in the tool res… [truncated]

access.description: What access this session needs. "read" (default): fetch/clone only — when the repository is public, git read access is often already served by the session's git proxy with nothing to attach, and the tool says so instead of attaching. "push": the session must push commits, open PRs, or use GitHub API tools against the repository, so it is attached with credentials after the full repository-access checks.

owner.description: GitHub owner (user or organization) of the repo to add, e.g. "anthropics".

repo.description: GitHub repo name, e.g. "claude-code". Do not include the owner prefix — pass owner and repo as separate fields.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__archive_session
tools.description: Archive a Claude Code Remote session. Transitions the session to read-only archived state and releases its container. Use this when a child session has finished its work or is stuck (PR merged, task complete, session failed to initialize) and a human has already acknowledged they're done with the session.

session_id.description: The target session ID to archive.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_session
tools.description: Create a new Claude Code Remote session. Returns the new session's ID and status. If environment_id is omitted, the new session inherits the calling session's environment. Combine with send_message for fan-out orchestration: spawn a sibling and send it a task. Where enabled, this session receives a <child-session-event> turn if the new session's turn fails or its worker restarts and drops background tasks; a session that finishes cleanly does not report back, so check on it with get_session (status_bucket reads 'failed' for a turn that errored, where status alone reads 'idle' either way) and list_events.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_session
schema.description: Create a new Claude Code Remote session. Returns the new session's ID and status. If environment_id is omitted, the new session inherits the calling session's environment. Combine with send_message for fan-out orchestration: spawn a sibling and send it a task. Where enabled, this session receives a <child-session-event> turn if the new session's turn fails or its worker restarts and drops background tasks; a session that finishes cleanly does not report back, so check on it with get_session (status_bucket reads 'failed' for a turn that errored, where status alone reads 'idle' either way) and list_events.

append_system_prompt.description: Text appended to the new session's system prompt.

blob_limit_kb.description: Optional. Files larger than this many KB are left out of the checkout; git fetches one on demand when a command reads it. Requires source_url. Set it for very large repositories, whose sessions otherwise fail to start for lack of disk space. Ignored when sparse_checkout_paths is set.

clone_depth.description: Optional number of commits of history to fetch (default 50). Requires source_url. Lower it for very large repositories.

environment_id.description: Environment ID — a tagged ID starting with 'env_' (or 'ccpool_' for self-hosted pools). Defaults to the calling session's environment. Do NOT invent a value — call list_environments to get the user's real environment_ids. When this resolves to the remote_cowork environment (explicitly or via inheritance), a Claude Cowork session is spawned — the account's enabled skills, plugins and the Cowork system prompt are assembled server-side, and only prompt, title, model and tags are read (source_url, extra_allowed_tools, append_system_prompt and environment_variables are ignored so the caller cannot widen the tool surface).

extra_allowed_tools.description: Extra tool names pre-approved without a user permission prompt. Entries the calling session does not itself have pre-approved are dropped — the child never carries a grant its parent lacks.

model.description: Model ID for the new session. Defaults to the calling session's model.

outcome_branch.description: Optional branch name to push changes to. When set, the session pushes directly to this branch (no session-derived suffix appended).

permission_mode.description: Initial permission mode for the new session. Cannot be more permissive than the calling session's mode; omit to inherit it. 'plan' makes the agent propose a plan and then BLOCKS waiting for human approval via the claude.ai/code web UI — do NOT use 'plan' for autonomous child sessions that no human is watching, as they will stall indefinitely at the approval prompt.

prompt.description: Optional initial message to send to the new session.

source_revision.description: Optional git branch, tag, or commit to check out. Requires source_url. Defaults to the repo's default branch.

source_url.description: Optional git repository URL to check out.

sparse_checkout_paths.description: Optional directories, relative to the repository root. The checkout holds only these, plus the files directly in their parent folders and at the root. Requires source_url. Set it to work in part of a very large repository.

tags.description: Free-form tags to categorize the session (e.g. ["remote-agents-project:frontend"]). Editable later via set_session_tags.

title.description: Optional session title.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_trigger
tools.description: Create a Routine (scheduled trigger). Three targeting modes: (1) default — fires into THIS SESSION, resuming the same conversation each time; (2) persistent_session_id set — fires into a SPECIFIC OTHER SESSION you name (must be in your account); (3) create_new_session_on_fire=true — spawns a FRESH SESSION in this environment on each firing. Use mode 1 for recurring work you want to pick back up yourself; mode 2 for waking a sibling session you created; mode 3 when each firing should start from a clean slate. If the result warns that the Routine stores no connectors, say so plainly when you confirm the Routine to the user and pass on the remedy it names; never report such a Routine as simply created.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_trigger
schema.description: Create a Routine (scheduled trigger). Three targeting modes: (1) default — fires into THIS SESSION, resuming the same conversation each time; (2) persistent_session_id set — fires into a SPECIFIC OTHER SESSION you name (must be in your account); (3) create_new_session_on_fire=true — spawns a FRESH SESSION in this environment on each firing. Use mode 1 for recurring work you want to pick back up yourself; mode 2 for waking a sibling session you created; mode 3 when each firing should start from a clean slate. If the result warns that the Routine stores no connectors, say so plainly when you confirm the Routine to the user and pass on the remedy it names; never report such a Routine as simply created.

connectors.description: Optional list of connector names the Routine's fired sessions may use, e.g. ["Gmail", "linear"]. Pass ONLY connectors the user explicitly asked this Routine to use — the stored grant applies to every future firing. Names resolve against the user's connected claude.ai connectors; when calling from inside a CCR session the list is further limited to connectors that session itself holds (it can only narrow that set, never widen it). Any name that cannot be resolved fails the call. Pass [] to store no connectors. Omit to keep the default behavior for this surface. The grant attaches the connectors only — individual tool calls from fired sessions still go through runtime permission checks.

create_new_session_on_fire.description: If true, each firing creates a fresh session in the calling session's environment instead of resuming an existing one. Default false. Mutually exclusive with persistent_session_id.

cron_expression.description: Standard 5-field cron expression (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week), evaluated in UTC. Convert local times to UTC first, using the offset currently in effect. If the conversion crosses midnight, shift the day fields that are set, day-of-week and/or day-of-month (e.g. weekdays at 5pm in UTC-07:00 is 0 0 * * 2-6). Minimum interval is normally hourly (some projects allow shorter); a too-frequent schedule is rejected and the error names the minimum. For hourly or every-N-hours schedules, use minute 0 (e.g. '0 * * * *', '0 */4 * * *'): the server anchors it to the creation minute ('hourly starting now'), so Routines spread across the hour instead of all firing at :00. All other schedules are stored verbatim. Mutually exclusive with run_once_at. Omit both for a poke-only Routine that never fires on its own schedule.

environment_id.description: Environment ID — a tagged ID starting with 'env_' (or 'ccpool_' for self-hosted pools). Defaults to the calling session's environment. Required when calling from outside a CCR session (no session context to inherit from). Do NOT invent a value — call list_environments to get the user's real environment_ids.

initiation.description: Who wanted this: human_request — a person asked you to set this up now; human_schedule — a schedule a person set (e.g. an earlier firing) told you to; own_followup — your own check-in or follow-up on work you are already doing; own_initiative — you decided on your own that this should exist.

name.description: Human-readable Routine name.

notifications.description: Completion notifications for this Routine. push sends to the owner's phone when a run finishes with something noteworthy; email sends the same summary to their inbox. If omitted, the setting stays unset and the server default applies at fire time. Passing this sets an explicit per-Routine choice, so list every channel you want on ({push:true, email:true} for both; {email:true} alone means email-only, push off). Pass {} to opt out of all channels. Only fresh-session-per-fire Routines (create_new_session_on_fire=true) take this; the server rejects it for self-bind or persistent_session_id Routines.

persistent_session_id.description: Optional session ID to fire into instead of this one. Must belong to the same account — the server rejects sessions you don't own. Omit to fire into this session (default). Mutually exclusive with create_new_session_on_fire.

prompt.description: The message the Routine sends on each firing. When binding to an existing session (modes 1-2), write it assuming past context — the conversation continues. In fresh-session mode (mode 3), write it as a complete standalone instruction since each firing starts from nothing.

run_once_at.description: RFC3339 timestamp for a one-shot fire (e.g. 2026-04-20T17:00:00Z). Must be in the future. Mutually exclusive with cron_expression — set one or the other, not both. After the one-shot fires the Routine disables itself with ended_reason=run_once_fired.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__delete_trigger
tools.description: Delete a Routine (scheduled trigger). The Routine must belong to the calling session's account — deleting another account's Routine fails with not-found. Use this to undo a create_trigger call or to clean up Routines whose work is done. A bad cron or wrong prompt does not need deletion — update_trigger fixes those in place, keeping the Routine's run history. On success, the result usually echoes the deleted Routine's last state (including its name) in the response's trigger field — callers without stored-data read access get a plain-text confirmation instead. Either way the Routine no longer exists once this returns.

On success, the result usually echoes the deleted Routine's last state (including its name) in the response's trigger field — callers without stored-data read access get a plain-text confirmation instead. Either way the Routine no longer exists once this returns.

trigger_id.description: The Routine's trigger ID to delete (starts with 'trig_'). Returned by create_trigger in the response's trigger.id field, or by list_triggers.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__fire_trigger
tools.description: Fire a Routine (scheduled trigger) immediately, outside of its schedule. The Routine must belong to the calling session's account. Use this to kick off a Routine on demand — e.g. after noticing a condition the Routine is meant to handle, or to re-run a Routine whose last scheduled run failed. Optionally include a text message that is appended as an extra user turn after the Routine's configured prompt, so you can pass run-specific context (an error message, a PR link, a diff) into that one firing.

text.description: Optional text appended as an extra user message after the Routine's configured prompt. Use this to pass run-specific context into the Routine. Bounded to 64 KiB.

trigger_id.description: The Routine's trigger ID (starts with 'trig_'). Returned by create_trigger in the response's trigger.id field, or by list_triggers.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__get_session
tools.description: Get details for a specific Claude Code Remote session by ID. Returns the session's title, status, status_bucket (working / blocked / review_ready / completed / failed — 'failed' means its last turn errored), creation time, and context. Every returned session carries three model fields: configured_model is the model stored at creation, echoed as stored (it may be an alias or carry a context-window suffix, so normalize before comparing); session_context.model is the model the session is currently set to run (the creation-time model, or a later switch or refusal fallback); external_metadata.last_served_model is the model the CLI ran the latest turn on, which also reflects turn-scoped fallbacks (overload or unavailable) that do not change session_context.model. To detect a switch or fallback in a child session, compare configured_model against both session_context.model and external_metadata.last_served_model; the fallback notices in list_events give the reason. Omit session_id to describe this session.

To detect a switch or fallback in a child session, compare configured_model against both session_context.model and external_metadata.last_served_model; the fallback notices in list_events give the reason. after_id.description: Pagination cursor: return sessions older than this session ID. Pass the last_id from a previous response to get the next page.

before_id.description: Pagination cursor: return sessions newer than this session ID. Pass the first_id from a previous response to get the previous page.

limit.description: Maximum number of sessions to return (default 20, max 100).

mine.description: Filter to sessions started by the same account as the calling session. Use this for 'my recent sessions' in shared bot contexts. In personal accounts the list is already scoped to you, so mine has no additional effect. Returns an error if the calling session has no resolvable originating account.

tags.description: Filter to interactive sessions carrying ANY of these tags. Cowork sessions are tagged "cowork-local" or "cowork-remote" and are excluded from the default (untagged) listing — pass those tags here to list them. Scheduled/trigger-fired runs are not included (same as the REST default). Max 16 tags. Only available to OAuth callers; returns an error for in-session and toolbox callers.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__list_triggers
tools.description: List Routines (scheduled triggers) owned by this account. Use it to find trigger IDs (trig_...) for update_trigger and delete_trigger. From a thread in a Slack channel, only Routines that fire into that thread's session are listed unless all_in_channel is true. Each entry has the Routine's id, name, cron_expression, run_once_at, enabled state, ended_reason, next_run_at, created_at, persistent_session_id, and last_run. last_run is the most recent recorded run {status, fired_at, finished_at, session_id}. It is absent when no run was recorded (e.g. never fired). For a Routine that wakes an existing session, last_run records that the wake was delivered (SUCCEEDED) or failed to deliver, not how the turn went, unless run tracking covers that session. A FAILED or repeatedly non-SUCCEEDED last_run means the Routine is not doing its job. ended_reason says why a disabled Routine is permanently disabled. suspension_reason (e.g. subscription_paused) marks a temporary hold that lifts when the owner's subscription resumes. Both empty means user-paused. One-shot Routines that already fired (e.g. delivered send_later reminders) and Routines moved to a project are hidden unless include_completed is true. Scheduled tasks stored locally by the Cowork desktop app are not listed.

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:95-129`).
- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.
- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (ledger row 69); making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which is not a ledger row and not on the worklist as a separate item (it falls under worklist item 2, compiler-path library parity).
- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64`, no `dadd`/`dmul` anywhere in the generated loop (shown in bytecode, `perf-probes/boxing/javap/`); arrays are library objects over `get`/`put`, not `double[]` (`repo-internals.md:129`).
- On microGPT-shaped array code boxing is the dominant representational cost, 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]` in Java models of the program's three kernels, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles: the compiler prelude lacks the array types, with `Array`, `Vector` and `Array3` undefined in `FlatArrays.fsi` (row 305, wider than row 72). On the interpreter, the only path that runs the kernels, 43.5% is the AST walk, 32.3% environment lookup, 5.2% type dispatch and 0% number representation (JFR on `krows`). The order that followed: an `RR64` array type in the compiler library (G2); the two one-line runtime defects (rows 302, 303, since fixed by rung 0); unboxing and `double[]`, designed into the first. A failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache (`258105b3e`; `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The boxing probe's scalar-loop reading, 156× primitive Java with boxing about 2% of it, is of the tree before rung 0's two fixes (rows 302, 303; `53362cb88`); of the costs it named, `countedseqloop`'s boxed indices and closure call (about 7%) and the representational rest (about 30%) are unaddressed (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed: the message is built only under the `debug` flag (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:248`; row 302; `53362cb88`; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip is fixed: the literal caches its `double` instead of re-parsing its text in `asRR64()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`; row 303; `53362cb88`; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The benchmark numbers on record from 2026-09-15 (`bench1t` 9.3441 s, `bench1h` 6.0732 s) were taken on a quieter machine; the 2026-09-17 before-run of the same unmodified tree measured 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s, so absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions and only a before/after pair taken in one session is (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars: the first `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler clears `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/`, and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`; the library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:170-179` restores it, about two minutes (observed 2026-09-17).
- The compiled path's bytecode cache can come up empty after a library-order rebuild that reports exit 0; re-running the same commands one at a time produced the jars (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
- Generic instantiations are stamped out at class-load time by ASM rewriting of template bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader.java`, `repo-internals.md:129`); whether `nat` parameters are baked into stamped classes is unprobed.
- Implicit parallelism: `for` is parallel unless every generator is `seq`; the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator are evaluated in parallel implicit threads (`tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`; row 265). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool; there is no explicit threading in any of our programs.
- The compile path's checker cannot check `nat` parameters at all (see "The checker and the one library" below). Sizes in types (`nat` parameters) are "instantiated at runtime" by the specification (`trait-parameters.tex`, natparams); they check shapes when a value is made or passed; no optimization is built on them anywhere. A `nat`-typed parameter does not unify statically with a run-time-built array (row 23); the interpreter matches at dispatch, and a mismatch reads "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (row 83). A literal size does unify (row 23's positive half).
- **The specification's own declaration of `Nothing` compiles on neither path, and the reason is name resolution, not codegen.** `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification/basic-lib/convenience.tex:49`) gives the identical single error from `fortress compile` and from `fortress walk`, both rc=255: `T is undefined`, at the `T` inside the extends clause (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-maybe/probes/WhereClauseNothing.fss`, `.txt`). A where clause on an object declaration does not bind a type variable used in that declaration's extends clause in either implementation. `CodeGen.forObjectDeclPrePass` would refuse the declaration a second time at codegen — `header.getWhereClause().isNone()` is one of its `canCompile` conditions (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:4088`) — but nothing reaches it. This is the mechanism behind `FortressLibrary.fss:1340-1341`'s "when we get where clauses working", and it is why both worlds must spell the empty case some other way.
- **An exported function fails exactly as an exported variable does when a component's name differs from the api it exports, and the failure is the repository's, not codegen's** (2026-09-20, rung X). `probes/FnApi.fsi`+`FnLib.fss`+`FnMain.fss` dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: FnApi`, alongside `P8Api$shared` and `P9Api$shared` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-export-var/probes/probes-preedit.txt:29,96,163`). Through the real entry points the divergence never reaches codegen at all: `fortress link P8Main` and `walk` on each of the three main components print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" (`probes/link-and-walk-preedit.txt:4-9,45-60`), so both execution paths assume the api and its implementing component share a name. The assumption is `Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`'s fallback to the api's own name (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/linker/Linker.java:72-76`) when nothing has been registered in its persisted map, and only the user can register one, by hand, through `LinkShell`'s `alink`/`clink` verbs (`linker/LinkShell.java:41-70`; `linker/README:28-40` describes the intended design). `Specification/basic/components/overview.tex:33-35` settles it — a reference to an imported api is "resolved to a component that exports that api" — and the team reserved the codegen half of the repair in three comments in one file (`CodeGen.java:411-441`, `:1856`, `:6599-6606`). Gated as an expected failure by `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test`.
- **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it** (2026-09-22, rung C, `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/probes/SpanAbsorb.fss` and `SpanAbsorb.txt`; ledger row 359). `createSpan` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Fortress.rats:145-157`) trims back over space characters only. A declaration ending in `end` is unaffected. # Facts on record

## Execution model

- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:95-129`).
- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.
- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (ledger row 69); making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which is not a ledger row and not on the worklist as a separate item (it falls under worklist item 2, compiler-path library parity).
- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64`, no `dadd`/`dmul` anywhere in the generated loop (shown in bytecode, `perf-probes/boxing/javap/`); arrays are library objects over `get`/`put`, not `double[]` (`repo-internals.md:129`).
- On microGPT-shaped array code boxing is the dominant representational cost, 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]` in Java models of the program's three kernels, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles: the compiler prelude lacks the array types, with `Array`, `Vector` and `Array3` undefined in `FlatArrays.fsi` (row 305, wider than row 72). On the interpreter, the only path that runs the kernels, 43.5% is the AST walk, 32.3% environment lookup, 5.2% type dispatch and 0% number representation (JFR on `krows`). The order that followed: an `RR64` array type in the compiler library (G2); the two one-line runtime defects (rows 302, 303, since fixed by rung 0); unboxing and `double[]`, designed into the first. A failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache (`258105b3e`; `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The boxing probe's scalar-loop reading, 156× primitive Java with boxing about 2% of it, is of the tree before rung 0's two fixes (rows 302, 303; `53362cb88`); of the costs it named, `countedseqloop`'s boxed indices and closure call (about 7%) and the representational rest (about 30%) are unaddressed (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed: the message is built only under the `debug` flag (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:248`; row 302; `53362cb88`; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip is fixed: the literal caches its `double` instead of re-parsing its text in `asRR64()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`; row 303; `53362cb88`; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The benchmark numbers on record from 2026-09-15 (`bench1t` 9.3441 s, `bench1h` 6.0732 s) were taken on a quieter machine; the 2026-09-17 before-run of the same unmodified tree measured 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s, so absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions and only a before/after pair taken in one session is (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars: the first `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler clears `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/`, and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`; the library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:170-179` restores it, about two minutes (observed 2026-09-17).
- The compiled path's bytecode cache can come up empty after a library-order rebuild that reports exit 0; re-running the same commands one at a time produced the jars (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
- Generic instantiations are stamped out at class-load time by ASM rewriting of template bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader.java`, `repo-internals.md:129`); whether `nat` parameters are baked into stamped classes is unprobed.
- Implicit parallelism: `for` is parallel unless every generator is `seq`; the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator are evaluated in parallel implicit threads (`tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`; row 265). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool; there is no explicit threading in any of our programs.
- The compile path's checker cannot check `nat` parameters at all (see "The checker and the one library" below). Sizes in types (`nat` parameters) are "instantiated at runtime" by the specification (`trait-parameters.tex`, natparams); they check shapes when a value is made or passed; no optimization is built on them anywhere. A `nat`-typed parameter does not unify statically with a run-time-built array (row 23); the interpreter matches at dispatch, and a mismatch reads "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (row 83). A literal size does unify (row 23's positive half).
- **The specification's own declaration of `Nothing` compiles on neither path, and the reason is name resolution, not codegen.** `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification/basic-lib/convenience.tex:49`) gives the identical single error from `fortress compile` and from `fortress walk`, both rc=255: `T is undefined`, at the `T` inside the extends clause (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-maybe/probes/WhereClauseNothing.fss`, `.txt`). A where clause on an object declaration does not bind a type variable used in that declaration's extends clause in either implementation. `CodeGen.forObjectDeclPrePass` would refuse the declaration a second time at codegen — `header.getWhereClause().isNone()` is one of its `canCompile` conditions (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:4088`) — but nothing reaches it. This is the mechanism behind `FortressLibrary.fss:1340-1341`'s "when we get where clauses working", and it is why both worlds must spell the empty case some other way.
- **An exported function fails exactly as an exported variable does when a component's name differs from the api it exports, and the failure is the repository's, not codegen's** (2026-09-20, rung X). `probes/FnApi.fsi`+`FnLib.fss`+`FnMain.fss` dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: FnApi`, alongside `P8Api$shared` and `P9Api$shared` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-export-var/probes/probes-preedit.txt:29,96,163`). Through the real entry points the divergence never reaches codegen at all: `fortress link P8Main` and `walk` on each of the three main components print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" (`probes/link-and-walk-preedit.txt:4-9,45-60`), so both execution paths assume the api and its implementing component share a name. The assumption is `Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`'s fallback to the api's own name (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/linker/Linker.java:72-76`) when nothing has been registered in its persisted map, and only the user can register one, by hand, through `LinkShell`'s `alink`/`clink` verbs (`linker/LinkShell.java:41-70`; `linker/README:28-40` describes the intended design). `Specification/basic/components/overview.tex:33-35` settles it — a reference to an imported api is "resolved to a component that exports that api" — and the team reserved the codegen half of the repair in three comments in one file (`CodeGen.java:411-441`, `:1856`, `:6599-6606`). Gated as an expected failure by `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test`.
- **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it** (2026-09-22, rung C, `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/probes/SpanAbsorb.fss` and `SpanAbsorb.txt`; ledger row 359). `createSpan` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Fortress.rats:145-157`) trims back over space characters only. A declaration ending in `end` is unaffected. So a comment-only edit to the library is not neutral at the syntax-tree level: rung C's widened three spans (the scalar block's first `-` in both files, `SUFFIX_SUM` in the `.fsi`), besides shifting every position below each insertion, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics must map positions back first (`compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py`, `remap-lines.py`). No answer changed.
- **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees** (rung I, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md`, section 4.1): `throw new FortressError((FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(name))` from inside a `builtinPrimitive` method reaches `Evaluator.forTry` unchanged (`MethodClosure.java:85-86` has no `catch`) and matches `catch e IntegerOverflow`; `Int.overflow()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:256-259`) is the helper and `WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException` the name. Measured by the 25 `overflows(...)` assertions of `ProjectFortress/tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, whose helper catches nothing but `IntegerOverflow`. Before this rung no native raised one; the interpreter's mapping of every other Java exception is unchanged (`FunctionClosure.java:188-196`), so row 336's division by zero and row 347's `Int.rc` still end the run.

## The checker and the one library

- Only 211 of `FortressLibrary.fss`'s 4,518 lines (4.7%) are the 108 `builtinPrimitive` native bindings; the rest is plain Fortress. Whole interpreter library: 427 bindings across nine files. The interpreter's glue classes take the evaluator's boxed values and cannot be reused by the compiled path; the compiler's natives are static Java methods, and `nativeHelpers/` already ships 355 of them, covering about 79 of the 108 by another name. Source: `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`, measured 2026-09-16.
- `fortress compile Library/FortressLibrary.fss` as it is: 1,417 errors, all in DISAMBIGUATE, all name collisions because both preludes are in scope; an artifact. With `FortressLibrary` made the prelude (a driver over `Shell`'s public entry points, no tracked file changed): disambiguation passes with zero errors; the type checker then reports 92 errors in the library's own apis (36 `X excludes Y but it extends Y`, 26 `types exclude each other`, 26 `Integral[\I\]` bound failures, in the comparison and numeric tower) and then **crashes: `Not yet implemented`** in `STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` (STypesUtil.scala:546-559) for `nat`, `int`, `bool`, `dim` and `unit` static parameters. Desugar and codegen are never reached. Source: `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`, measured 2026-09-16.
- **The Scala type checker does not implement `nat` static parameters at all**: a six-line program with a `nat` parameter fails on the compile path (`Not yet implemented` inferred, `ClassCastException` explicit) and runs on the interpreter. The interpreter's library has 81 such declarations, C4's vocabulary 30; `CompilerLibrary` has one, the empty `Matrix`. So the sized-array vocabulary cannot pass the compile path's checker today, and the static dimension checking the `nat` design promises is not implemented anywhere. Source: `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`, measured 2026-09-16.
- **Between the interpreter's library and bytecode stands the checker, not desugaring or code generation** (2026-09-20, `perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen.md`, the library pushed through DESUGAR and CODEGEN with the checker's failures caught per top-level declaration, validated on `CompilerLibrary.fss` where the method reproduces the ordinary compile exactly): of `FortressLibrary.fss`'s 446 top-level declarations the checker passes 237 clean, reports errors on 97 and crashes on 112 (81 `makeInferenceArg` nyi, 29 `TraitType→IntExpr`, the `nat` gap); DESUGAR and OVERLOADREWRITE then report zero diagnostics on all of it; CODEGEN emits 275 and refuses 313, of which only **5 are on declarations the checker checked clean** (four a numeric static argument, one a method call on an intersection-typed receiver); the rest are missing annotations on unchecked declarations (227), the two missing visitors `Juxt` (53) and `Label` (1), `nat` static arguments (14), malformed overload sets (7); `canCompile` refused nothing and no native binding was missing. <!-- What Pavol has decided, stated, or already knows, with dates; in his words or a close paraphrase. Read at session start so that none of it is re-explained to him. Standing directives about how we work are in explorations/protocol.md and are not repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- The revival's toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression; Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources; "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability" (2026-09-15).
- The APL side quest began as a curiosity (2026-09-10), became a ladder to learn APL (09-11, he has not read the book), was redirected to native code, not an interpreter in an interpreter (09-12), and got microGPT as its target on 09-13; the ladder "was to keep you busy and expand the probe". The remaining APL ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued (09-15).
- Hoped for a diamond from the Hsu-style flat program; got "a few lumps of coal"; the rewrite (rung 4b) was to get closer, and the vocabulary is where any polishing happens.

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
- The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here"; this goes on the priority list (2026-09-15). The first measurement (the scalar loop) said boxing was about 2% of the gap; Pavol objected that the loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator) and asked for a fairer test; the fairer test agreed with him: on array-shaped code boxing is 6.3-6.5× and the dominant representational cost, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles at all today (FACTS, execution model). The order now on record: the compiler library's array type first, the two one-line runtime defects second, unboxing designed into the first.
- The type checker runs only on the compile path; he wants it usable on interpreter programs and considers that low-hanging fruit (2026-09-15). It is item 0.1 of `performance-roadmap.md` (2026-09-08), which the coordinator had not indexed; see FACTS, deficit.
- Hsu's critique of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".

## Decisions on record

- 2026-08-23, recovered from the transcript on 2026-09-23 (`coordinator/lineage.md`): the third-party Java 9 port gets no credit and no mention — "we can lose the porcupines credit since you seem to have not really been informed by their changes"; "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere"; the revival's toolchain was rebuilt from the original tree with a few mechanical fixes, the port only showed that a revival was possible. And his plan the same day, not carried out: rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main`. On 2026-09-23, told that CLAUDE.md's opening still described the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history: "This is incorrect. Where does this come from? Use archeology to find correct facts and correct the record" — corrected in CLAUDE.md, the other files left for his decision.
- 2026-09-14: C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
- 2026-09-15: redo rung 4 as the focused base (done); do the vocabulary swap with shared `nat` dimensions (in progress); the ledger is not split, two views are derived (done); the ledger review is the next major step after the swap; the remaining APL ground is closed.
- 2026-09-15: "fleshing out the standard library" is a very important task: first fix the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch, then extend the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them. Open question he has not answered: whether this means editing the sealed `Library/` (the standing rule is never; worklist item 4 "unseal the linear-algebra layer" names the rows) or building the layer in our own tree; the coordinator assumes our own tree until he says otherwise.
- 2026-09-16: the goal restated: finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed spec (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not redesign the language; the measuring stick is one program, microGPT compiled to bytecode and running fast; a pure-Java microGPT will be written later as the floor to measure against; the tree is tagged at the unsealing point and the next phase modifies the original sources with the lessons of the explorations.
- 2026-09-16: the mathematical notation (Fortify, the 2D rendering) is his verdict "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, and the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress. Do not spend work on it unless he asks.
- 2026-09-16: before unsealing he wants the territory map (`coordinator/map/`): repository and language architecture, the pipeline phases, test coverage per layer, the gaps on the path in order with the cost of leaving each, the development loop's slow spots, a touch-this-affects-that map, and where the design intent is written (papers, not only the spec).
- 2026-09-16: development-loop performance is a first-class concern; when an iteration waits too long on something, find the cause and fix it.
- 2026-09-17: the tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at `75cca6683` (the map's last commit); commits after it may edit the original sources. Order he accepted: the compile-path ladder baseline first (every interpreter test and the 29 not-working library tests through `fortress compile` and `run`, phase reached and missing names ranked), then the two one-line runtime fixes, then `nat` checking, then the compiler library grown from the team's own drafts, test-driven: every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and the full suite stays green.
- 2026-09-17, a standing preference Pavol stated twice in one session after two designs reached for a retreat: when something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch he refused bisection of commits — "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle he refused a stop — "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one". What still reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.
- 2026-09-17, clarified by Pavol when the batched-climb design asked whether that sentence fixed the gate's frequency: it does not. What it fixes is test-driven discipline and the permanence of checks — the worker writes the test first, **verifies that it actually fails**, then makes the fix, then proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on. The unacceptable process it rules out is the one-off validation script: proving once, by hand, that the interpreter and the compiler agree on a program and then going ahead without leaving a permanent check in the gate. Whether the suite is run per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per-batch is in line with the rule.
- Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run).

- 2026-09-18, after the coordinating session's container died: the work continues in the blinded run's container, on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it. Transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded` — "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts? I think it would just unnecessarily complicate the matters" — and the two lineages are joined at analysis time. The backup is repaired before anything else runs. The repair batch is re-run from the start, since recovering the dead run's agent state is not available. The recovery procedure is documented as a lesson about Claude Code in a remote container, kept with the backup documentation, not in the gap ledger.
- 2026-09-18, on the workflow before the repair batch is re-run: workers commit and push to their own `wip/` branches as they work — "perfectly reasonable. I'm giving you my explicit yes" — and the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls", with skeptics on Opus and the escalation when "we are returning back with a redesign"; the judge inherits the session's model so that running out of Fable credits means switching the session, not editing the script; workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof". Agreed to the three escalation points (a refusal, a stop, a red gate) and to no Fable pass before every edit.

- 2026-09-19, after climb batch 1 landed: the six process decisions for batch 2 are taken as `coordinator/process-decisions-review-1.md` amended them, on the coordinator's recommendation and Pavol's "go" (he did not read the full text: "Are there strong recommendations and clear wins … pick a good default? … go"): every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test; the eight script changes, a five-kilobyte gate summary diffed against the last, the gate run beside the review, no full logs committed, no rung-chain scheduling; the one-thread pin written into `fastTrack` and the four-thread `atomic` runs gating (a timeout re-run once); the `_WIcontains` key implemented in the harness; a ladder-regression stage over the measured pass list with the two microGPT programs held at their phase; and the six gaps the review found. `Maybe` stays as landed and `floor`/`ceiling` keep the float result; row 330 stays open as a note. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run still needs his explicit go.

- 2026-09-19: interpreter performance is irrelevant to every decision — "interpreter of Fortress, which is hundreds times slower than the Python interpreter, is irrelevant for any performance discussions"; "we cannot judge anything performance related in Fortress while we do not have a compiler". No edit to C4 for speed (the tuple-split measurement is an interpreter number only), and no performance decision of any kind until microGPT runs compiled.
- 2026-09-19, on the FlatArrays review's repair that turned `mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)` into `planeSum(mask, …)`: "NO. That's not Fortress!" The model's text is the notation the project exists for; an operator in it does not become a function call to satisfy the interpreter's overload check. The edit was stopped before it landed. Any repair that would change a line of the model is shown to him as a diff before it is built, and the vocabulary is repaired around the notation, not the other way round.
- 2026-09-19, answering the open question of 2026-09-15 (own tree or the sealed `Library/`): "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround; the library's own practice is the standard.
- 2026-09-19, on `coordinator/array-design.md`'s four questions: storage is `double[]`, unboxed — "we must go to double array for performance. There is again no question about this. If this should have been high performance language, it cannot be boxed." And the `nat` sizes are not sidestepped or layered in later: "I don't know [that] we can sidestep the nat issue. That is a central design point that they are using." So the array fork and the `nat` fork are taken together: sized types as the team designed them, the checker taught `nat` parameters, in the library's own patterns.
- 2026-09-19: the two microGPT programs are never run in the gate — "those are too long running to be tests"; the ladder-regression stage compiles them and records the phase only; when they one day run, the run goes to a separate non-gating stage.
- 2026-09-20, on the two libraries and the order of the compiler work: "we need to unify this. into single library"; "I fully believe that the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it. […] what would be a reason to re-implement the thing from, from the compiler?"; and "Compiler work needs to unblock `nat` support first, IIRC."
- 2026-09-20, on the judgement's first rung, the checker's error count on the interpreter's library made a permanent stage of the gate (93 errors, 92 without the tower-closure line): "haven't we done this already? Haven't we quantified this?"; "running this count, okay, gives you a metric, but it tells you nothing of how much work is to get the interpreter running with the compiler because there is the whole work with the type checker. […] it is absolutely unclear whether... this has been priced in"; and, as devil's advocate, "we could treat this as a prototype, like the shortest path on the bootstrapping of the library, library's arrays function. And we would stay in the current shape […] What what am I missing?" No yes on the rung was given that day; the statements with their context are in `coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/positions-checker-gate.md`.
- 2026-09-21, on the library commit `02d09a39f` of 09-19, after each of its four changes was explained with the blinded review's verdict: "Others approved" — the generic scalar-extension block with its two unnamed choices, the `AnyAdditiveGroup` marker and the `Array3` exclusion are approved as landed. The closure `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` is held until the exclusion trace lands, on his instruction "Run it. Then we'll talk again"; his reading of the record before the precedents were shown: "the only logical conclusion is that this was the correct exit"; the precedents shown afterwards (the team's three `NOT YET` sites: open level, comment, hand-written excludes) are what the trace tests. A `NOT YET`-style comment at the line goes in either way.
- 2026-09-21, the library route, recorded as decided on his words rather than re-asked: on 2026-09-20 14:39 "I fully believe that the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it. Like, I don't even think that is a question that's worth deliberating about alternatives", and on 2026-09-21, when the coordinator listed it as still open, "What decisions are there to make that we didn't already make?" So: one library, the interpreter's (`FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin`), becomes the library the compiler checks; from now no declaration goes into the compiler's prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`), and the remaining prelude-name rungs on the ladder stop while code-generator rungs continue; the three prelude files are deleted at the switch-over and their tests kept. Decision two, how the checker represents an unknown size (a new syntax-tree node with its 353,000-line regeneration, or a reserved-name reuse of the existing node), he did not see as his; the shadow uses the reserved name and the real edit's choice comes after it. And the shadow itself: "let's run the shadow test" — the `nat` shadow of decision F, questions 1-3 (crash location, export checker on the six dead sizes, a generic object with a size in its extends clause stamped and run), is approved; questions 4-5 (storage selection, the loader) wait on decision A.
- 2026-09-21, the closure `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` of `02d09a39f`, after the exclusion trace (`perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md`) showed that the team's own pattern (open level, `NOT YET` comment, hand-written excludes) does not carry the float operators: approved as landed — "We are writing NOT YET and … whatever [the trace] recommends, let's do that." So: the clause stays; a `NOT YET`-style comment in the team's wording goes at the line; the checker's accommodation for it (about five lines) goes into the first library batch. With this all four changes of `02d09a39f` are approved.
- 2026-09-21, ledger row 330, `floor`/`ceiling`/`round`/`truncate` and the brackets ⌊x⌋/⌈x⌉ on the float types: decided by Pavol for the specification's rule — all of them return the unbounded ℤ, for floats as for rationals, and the library's inconsistent spellings of `truncate` and `round` are tidied to the same. His reasoning: ℤ sits under ℚ under ℝ64 in the tower, so an integer result goes back into float arithmetic by promotion, and being unbounded it cannot overflow, "we are not going to ZZ64"; the remaining cost (a bignum per call on a hot float path) is eliminated later in the code generator by static type, the same family as the unboxing work of array decision B, and nothing in microGPT has `floor` on a hot path. Shape: a library rung after the switch-over, gated, with the count of interpreter tests whose output changes measured first. Rows 24 and 32 of the re-approval table close with this: rung F's compiler-prelude lines are moot under one library, and the coordinator's closing of 09-19 14:56 is reversed by this decision.
- 2026-09-21, ledger row 329, `round` on an exact half for the float types: "Agreed" to half to even on both paths (the specification's rule for rationals, IEEE's default, the team's own rational body), fixed on the interpreter side by the one token `Math.round` → `Math.rint` in `Float.java:384` with an interpreter test red before and green after, in the first library batch — with a request for the historical evidence first: when the interpreter's `Math.round` was written, what the rational body and the specification said at that time, and whether any commit message explains the discrepancy (`compile-ladder/rung-rr64-functions/round-history.md` when it lands). If the history contradicts the reading above, the row comes back to him.
- 2026-09-21, ledger row 331, the empty case of `Maybe`: keep the team's parametric spelling `Nothing[\T\]` as the one library's; rung M's compiler-prelude block is approved as landed, its tests kept, its lines gone at the switch-over; the specification's bare non-parametric `Nothing` is future work gated on `where` clauses binding a type variable in an extends clause (unimplemented on both paths; the alternative, coercion in the interpreter, does not exist there), and is not attempted before that gate opens. Rows 26 and 33 of the re-approval table close with this; the coordinator's closing of 09-19 15:13 is now his. Also 2026-09-21, row 329's history (`compile-ladder/rung-rr64-functions/round-history.md`): the float `round` was written last, after the spec sentence and Steele's half-to-even rational body, with no message or comment explaining it; the "agreed" stands.
- 2026-09-22, ledger row 321 (what an object with no `asString` prints) and row 27 of the re-approval table: "yes, row 27 close per default-rendering-judgement recommendation" — the bare Fortress type name with its static arguments, the interpreter's spelling, on both paths (`Box`, `Box[\ZZ32\]`, a value object's name), no marker, no identity hash; one native behind the compiled `Object.asString`, about 20 lines, with a gated compiler test; the debug marker he had in mind lives in `asDebugString`, which already exists. Also "Prep please": the manifest of the first library batch and the script's count stage are written by workers for his reading; the batch still launches only on his go. And the Java site the shadow named (`FnNameInfo.java`) is explored in a shadow first, on his question.

## How he wants to be spoken to

- 2026-09-15: "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations.

A shadow `checkP` implementing it takes the interpreter's library from 103 errors to 37, lifting 48 of the 61 exclusion errors (tower, comparisons, `Maybe`) and keeping the 13 on the `DistributesOver` markers, but only with the library's F-bound read as self-typed. The probes (`mie-probes/forest/`) show that the forest alone does not keep a specialisation at an inner level sound: generic code at the level below gets the specialisation's result (`IncompatibleClassChangeError`). It needs a return type rule over every level below, `comprises T` read covariantly, and dispatch ordered to match; so it is a third route that keeps the rule, the tower and specialisation, at more checker work than dropping the rule.

76	## The library's arrays and algebra
77	
78	- `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` are the only sized array traits; `Array3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, …\]` carries no algebraic trait (row 292; `FortressLibrary.fsi:1460, 1578, 1652`).
79	- `Vector` and `Matrix` inherit `+`, `-`, unary `-` and `zero` from `AdditiveGroup`, nothing else; `×` reaches no array by design because juxtaposition is the inner product and the array traits exclude `AnyMultiplicativeRing` (rows 64, 109, 293); a carrier that extends the ring is accepted unchecked, changes juxtaposition to elementwise and breaks `+` (vocabulary review v02, v02b).
80	- The library's products are declared with shared `nat`s (`Matrix[\T,n,m\]` × `Matrix[\T,m,p\]`, `FortressLibrary.fsi:1508-1516`); C4's own products were not, which is habit; the focused base's `FlatArrays2` states them (twelve declarations including the per-rank elementwise `×` and `/`, 25 of 29 nats agreeing; 39 declarations), and a wrong-shape call is refused at dispatch, uncatchable for an overloaded name (row 83), as a unification error naming the nat for an unoverloaded one (`apl/mg/checks/mismatch_probe.out`).
