- The compiled path's integer rules: `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` give `0` or the replicated sign for a count at or beyond the width and shift the other way by its magnitude for a negative count (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:353-362`, `simpleLongArith.java:322-331`; bodies `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:647-648`, `:736-737`), while `<<`, `>>` and `<<<` keep their old meanings; on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` only the minimum overflows or saturates, so `|0|`, `-0`, `0 DIV -1`, `DOTMINUS 0` and every zero factor on `ZZ64` answer `0`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD` and `LCM` do not throw on a zero quotient, and the long multiply, now `Math.multiplyExact`, answers a product equal to the minimum; `ZZ64.narrow` and `NN64.narrow` keep the low 32 bits (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:659`, `:879`), so `NN64` has no checked narrowing to `NN32` on this path, while the getter `asZZ32` still throws; the `ZZ`'s `<<<` refuses an unrepresentable left shift with a catchable `IntegerOverflow` before the JVM allocates it (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.java:93-102`, row 386). Gated by `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/IntSemanticsRungB.fss` and `ProjectFortress/library_tests/IntConversionsRungW.fss:43-45`, `:63-64`; row 379's `walk` half is an expected failure, `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXFixedWidthOverflowRungB.fss` (`ce0c7f453`, `c9faa7df4`; `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-compiled/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The interpreter's integer rules: `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64` saturate at the width and reverse on a negative count, the count read by the class of its value (an `NN64` count of `2^63` or more is beyond the width, a `ZZ` count is read exactly); the unbounded `ZZ`'s shift count is exact at any size, a negative one giving `0` or `-1` and an unrepresentable left shift a catchable `IntegerOverflow`, refused before the JVM allocates it (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/BigNum.java:247`); `GCD` and `LCM` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` are nonnegative and an unrepresentable result, `MIN GCD 0` and `MIN GCD MIN` included, is a catchable `IntegerOverflow`; `LCM` on the unbounded `ZZ` is nonnegative (`BigNum.java:176-192`); `0 LCM 0` is `0` on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ`, and on `NN32` and `NN64` since the review's repair (row 385); `ZZ64.narrow` keeps the low 32 bits; the specification's `shift` is declared on `ZZ` (next entry) and absent from the compiler prelude (row 383, expected failure `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXShiftDeclRungI.test`). Gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`. Not repaired (row 380): a `ZZ32` receiver shifted by a `ZZ`, `NN32` or `NN64` count is answered by `ZZ64`'s method at width 64 as a `ZZ64` (`3 LSHIFT big(widen(33))` is `25769803776 : ZZ64`), because `ZZ32`'s own pair takes exactly a `ZZ64` count (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:688-691`) though `Integral[\I\]` promises the receiver's type (`:637-638`); the repair, the pair declared with `b:AnyIntegral`, changes an existing declaration's type, which batch 3.5 reserved (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-3.5.md:57`), and no gated assertion pins the case (`d6faad28f`, `c9faa7df4`; `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- **Every functional-method name of the library is reserved in every program that imports it**: the disambiguator's `checkForShadowingVar` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala:745-763`) rejects a parameter or local named `even` or `numerator` with `Variable even is already declared.` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/probes/ShadowEven.txt`), and the specification forbids a parameter to shadow within the reach of a functional method, which is the whole component and every importer (`Specification/basic/declarations.tex:426-432`, `:435-436`, `:454-461`, `:533`). So declaring the spec's `shift(self, k)` on `ZZ` in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` alone stops every `walk` run on the library's own `Range` parameters named `shift`: 12 api sites, then 6 in `FortressLibrary.fss`, 30 in `RangeInternals.fss` and a local in `List.fss:311` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/probes/shift-collision-layer1.txt` to `layer4.txt`). Rung I (`d6faad28f`) landed it with the renames the specification requires, as ruled in `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/JUDGE.md`: `shift(self, k:AnyIntegral): ZZ` is declared on `trait ZZ` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:544`, the line after `even`; body `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:885-886`, after `RSHIFT` at `:883-884`, bound to `BigNum$LShift`), and the colliding parameters and the `List.fss:311` local are renamed to `amount` (4 sites in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, 6 in `FortressLibrary.fss`, 8 in `RangeInternals.fsi`, 30 in `RangeInternals.fss`, 1 in `List.fss`); the array-origin `.shift(` is unaffected (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/probes/harness-shift-landed.txt`). No other file in the tree binds `shift` (the only other `shiftLeft(shift: I)` is `CompilerLibrary/FortressLibrary.fsi:2061-2064`, on no source path), so a `walk` program may no longer bind it, as it may not bind `even`; the compiled path, with no prelude declaration, keeps no such reservation.
- `ProjectFortress/tests/RangePrototype.fss` computes its signed stride as `(this.stride DIV (this.stride GCD other.stride)) DOT other.stride` (`:66`, `:171`), since `LCM` is nonnegative; the library's `RangeInternals.fss` never depended on the sign (`d6faad28f`; `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).

## The library's arrays and algebra

- `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` are the only sized array traits; `Array3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, …\]` carries no algebraic trait (row 292; `FortressLibrary.fsi:1460, 1578, 1652`).
- `Vector` and `Matrix` inherit `+`, `-`, unary `-` and `zero` from `AdditiveGroup`, nothing else; `×` reaches no array by design because juxtaposition is the inner product and the array traits exclude `AnyMultiplicativeRing` (rows 64, 109, 293); a carrier that extends the ring is accepted unchecked, changes juxtaposition to elementwise and breaks `+` (vocabulary review v02, v02b).
- The library's products are declared with shared `nat`s (`Matrix[\T,n,m\]` × `Matrix[\T,m,p\]`, `FortressLibrary.fsi:1508-1516`); C4's own products were not, which is habit; the focused base's `FlatArrays2` states them (twelve declarations including the per-rank elementwise `×` and `/`, 25 of 29 nats agreeing; 39 declarations), and a wrong-shape call is refused at dispatch, uncatchable for an overloaded name (row 83), as a unification error naming the nat for an unoverloaded one (`apl/mg/checks/mismatch_probe.out`).
- Two declarations of one name differing only in the element type, or a rank-specialised declaration beside an index-generic one, are refused at load ("at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types"; `apl/mg/checks/model_run.out.0`, `elemwise_nat_probe.out.0`); two apis' overloads of one name are checked as one family, so two vocabularies cannot stand in one component (`diag_fwd_two_vocabularies_rejected.out.0`).
- The shipped `RR64` does not satisfy the specification's algebraic bound `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` (vocabulary review, probe `v04b_groupbound.out.0`); `T extends Number` is the bound that works for every element type and rank (row 295).
- The library's scalar-extension block for `+ - MIN MAX` over arrays is generic since `02d09a39f` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4511-4521`, `.fsi:2550-2560`); no reshape, plane, gather, outer product or ravel exists in the library (vocabulary review, section A).
- An array is a trait with `get`/`put`; a view is an object implementing it over other storage, the language's own idiom; the library's row slice `m[i,:]` costs 5× a six-line user view; a diagonal as a `Matrix` view costs 13-54× the operator (vocabulary review v20, v07).
- The element type is `Number` only for `Vector`/`Matrix` (row 24); irrelevant to numeric microGPT, decisive for Run B's autodiff value and for APL characters.

## The specification and the repository's lineage

- **Citing `Specification/library/apis/*.tex` as an independent standard is circular.** `Specification/library/structure.tex:25-31` says in the team's own words that Part Library "is largely automatically generated from the API code for the libraries themselves" and that the libraries are "presently in a state of flux", so `library/apis/CompilerBuiltin.tex` is a rendering of `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` and cannot justify an edit to that same file. Two rung reports cited it as the published api or the spec's shape. The prose chapters of `Specification/basic/` and `basic-lib/` are the standard; the api renderings are not. Sharper still (2026-09-19, batch 1's record worker): the rendered `library/apis/*.tex` files are not in the tree at all, they are generated at spec-build time from the `.fsi` sources (`Specification/library/default-libraries.tex:27,39`), so the `(api listing)` citations of ledger rows 314 and 316 and of `library_tests/IntLiteralArithRung7.fss:30-31` name paths that cannot be opened; the `(api listing)` convention should cite the `.fsi` line instead. Source: the conformance review of the eight rungs, 2026-09-17, `reviews/rung-conformance-1-4.md` and `-5-8.md`, verified in that session.
- The in-repo `Specification/` is the later draft with the implementers' notes; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is 1.0. Searches are made in the draft. Superseded 2026-09-16 by `map/spec-to-implementation.md` §1.2: the sources under `Specification-1.0-frozen/` are a byte-identical copy of the same draft in 202 of 208 files (the five differences are the revival's `fortress.tex` restyling, three `.pl` generators, and one stray `\tracingcommands` line); only `fortress.1.0.pdf` beside them is the 1.0 artefact. There is one prose to search, the draft, and it is 596 pages against the PDF's 262.
- `palimondo/fortress` is a 2018 GitHub fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository: 5,397 trunk commits, root `72ae6881b` (2007-01-04), tip `a874948ac` (2012-08-31), twelve relic branches, the `1.0` tag; the conversion cut 146 parent links (`research/authorship.md:14-22`). The third-party Java 9 port is one squashed commit (`eab48aa6d`) sharing no history with this tree; `8fe1daa8f` (2026-08-18) copied 1,506 of its files onto `a874948ac`, most of it since removed or redone; `clean-ladder` (`8332bd34f`) is a rebuild on `a874948ac` with no graft that never replaced `main`, so `main` still descends from `8fe1daa8f` (the work went on pushing the grafted line to `main` after the rebuild, no rename or merge ever happened) and its tree owes the port one running piece, the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (`clean-ladder` fixes it in two lines), plus dead files, cosmetic lines and the habit of tracking the generated sources (verified against `clean-ladder`, `lineage.md`). CLAUDE.md's opening sentence said otherwise from `446836590` until corrected; the files that still repeat it are listed in `lineage.md`.

## The territory map

- Tasks and transactions are implemented twice, `interpreter/evaluator/` and `runtimeSystem/`, independently (B.11). Row 302's fix is in the compiled world's copy only.
- `import java` also works on the interpreter path through `ForeignComponentWrapper` + `ClosureMaker`; no test uses it (B.12). Corrected 2026-09-20 (`perf-probes/prelude/import-java-interpreter.md`): wired and unfinished, it does not work; four gaps, all on the interpreter's side: `NamingCzar.fortLib` is fixed to the builtin api, which declares none of `ZZ32`/`RR64`/`JavaString` in that world (`NamingCzar.java:294-295`); a second `import java` from one package falls through `Driver.ensureApiImplemented` to a `ClassCastException` (`Driver.java:464-466`, "temp hack till we knit in natives properly"); the foreign name is never rewritten (`ForeignComponentWrapper.java:31,38`) and `BaseEnv.java:531-533` bugs on the qualified reference; and `ClosureMaker` emits a call into the compiler's `nativewrapper_cache`, which the interpreter neither writes nor loads. So one binding file cannot serve both worlds; the one-library variant is one shared text with one small builtin component per world behind a single api, which makes the api-to-differently-named-component link (ledger row 320's class-name half, `Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`) live work.
- Codegen refuses any declaration carrying a where clause or a contract (`CodeGen.java:2937, :2941, :4076, :4078, :4983, :4985`); not in the ledger (flagged, Pavol's call). `atomic <expr>` has no visitor, `atomic do … end` compiles; `spawn`, `label`/`exit`, object expressions, array literals and comprehensions, local function declarations have no visitor (`spec-to-implementation.md` §3).
- The checker (`IndexBuilder.scala:187-189`) refuses `type` aliases, `test` and `property` on both paths. Coercion is the one mechanism the compiler path has and the interpreter does not (no `Coercion`/`coerce` under `interpreter/`; row 19).
- **A generic object referenced without its static arguments is a static error on the compiled path, and the checker never consults the expected type for it** (2026-09-19, `explorations/compiler-probes/maybe-inference/inference.md`): `b: Box[\ZZ32\] = Box` fails with `Ill-formed type: Box`; a bare `Empty` as a call argument or a field default fails with `T is not in the kind env`, an internal `bug()` from `TypeAnalyzer.scala:766` reported at the declaration's span; the same forms with the static argument written compile and run on both paths. The decision is in the checker's `SVarRef` case, `typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:624-641`, whose `:639-640` keeps the uninstantiated type under the team's own `TODO: handle missing static args`; static-argument inference exists only for arrows (`STypesUtil.scala:912-930`, called from application and coercion), and a parametric empty case reached by `coerce` still fails bare. Under `walk` the same forms are `InterpreterBug: Couldn't figure out Empty[\T\](uninstantiated) <: Opt[\ZZ32\]`. Consequence for row 331: a parametric `Nothing[\T\]` would serve the corpus's `Nothing[\ZZ32\]` and never the specification's bare `= Nothing`; the non-parametric object plus `coerce` that the prelude uses is the only shape that compiles, so `Maybe` stays as landed. Incidental: `typecase` over a user-declared generic object crashes code generation (`Error trying to close method scope`, `CodeGen.java:2802`), row 340. Corrected the same day by the minimal reproducer (`compiler-probes/maybe-inference/probes/TcPlain.fss`): neither the generic object nor `typecase` alone is the trigger; a `typecase` used directly as a function or method body whose value needs an implicit coercion (`IntLiteral` to a declared `ZZ32`) makes ASM's stack-map frame computation fail (`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` under `MethodWriter.visitMaxs`, relabelled by the `catch (Throwable)` at `CodeGen.java:2801-2802`); wrapped in `do … end` the same body compiles, and every gated use of the shape returns `()` so never reaches the coercion.
- The gate: two corpora, hand-ported, sharing no file name; only `parser_tests/` is read by both; no test compares the paths on one program; interpreter tests pass on "no exception and no `fail` in output" (`FileTests.java:367-371`), compiler run tests on exit code plus `PASS`. `fortress.unittests.noopt=true` (`default_repository/configuration:51`) hides 226 tests and leaves the 43-file bytecode optimizer with zero. Every `testSystem` shard runs `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (`build.xml:1184`), so no gated test sees concurrency; `TransactionJUTest`'s multi-threaded half is commented out (`TestTask.java:43-44`). No `nat`-parameterised program is compiled or run; the cache round trip is not asserted (`ASTJUTest.java:654`). 121 `.fss` inside green directories are dark; `linker_tests`, `compiler_regressions`, `BirdyLib`, the `not_working_*` directories are orphaned (`map/test-coverage.md`).

## The container

- The process cost of the climbs and the batches — the eight-rung climb's wall clock and its gate share, the limits of parallelism on this box, and each batch's agents, tokens, tool calls and span — is measured in `explorations/coordinator/iteration-cost.md`, `coordinator/repair-batch-review.md` and the batch records; the conclusions it produced are in `POSITIONS.md` and in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, and the entries themselves are in `FACTS-history.md`.
- The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling kills long runs; check runs go under the `Monitor` tool (1800000 ms), sequential, nothing else running when a number is to be kept.
- The disk allowance fills with parser-generation temp directories: every run that imports a grammar generates a Rats! parser into a fresh `/tmp/fortress<random>rats` directory (`RatsUtil.getTempDir`, `syntax_abstractions/rats/RatsUtil.java:138-146`, via `IOUtil.createAndMarkTempDirectory`), 5.8 MB each, never deleted; 723 of them (4.2 GB) filled the allowance on 2026-09-15 and broke a worker's tool output mid-run ("no space left on device"). Deficit until fixed at the source (an edit under the sealed tree, or a `deleteOnExit`); mitigation in our tree: `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them when sourced, and `df` must be checked before any long run.
- The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling; `Monitor` for long runs (the microGPT-runs entry above).
- A container can be lost outright: the coordinating session of 2026-09-17 (`bdff267d-…`) died mid-workflow and could not be re-provisioned, because the branch it was created from was no longer found on the remote. Recovery moved into the blinded run's container, which already had the checkout and toolchain. Cost: four workflow agents (~798k tokens), their worktrees, and the 13 hours after the last transcript snapshot at 20:31. Everything through `2ab1d6d8` was pushed and safe, and `REPAIR-BATCH.md` kept the batch runnable. Mechanism, the three traps and the recovery procedure: `explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md`.
- The transcript backup fires on the main session's Stop, not on any agent's completion, and swallows all errors: a session inside one long turn is not being backed up and a failed push is silent. Workflow-agent transcripts were outside its globs until 2026-09-18; oversized transcripts now split at 64 MiB, and the wrapper packs loose objects because the clone ships `gc.auto=0`.
- **The Workflow harness runs two agents at once on this box** (measured 2026-09-18, four one-command agents in one `parallel()`: agents 0 and 1 started 19:14:08, agents 2 and 3 at 19:14:31 after the first pair finished at 19:14:23; `batched-climb-plan.md` §2). `model: 'opus'` in `agent()` resolves to a fixed model identifier, readable in each agent transcript's `message.model` field and not written here (protocol §4); an agent with no `model` inherits the session's. A subagent's floor is about 45k tokens before it does anything (183k for the four). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (33,022 tokens read by agents 1–3) and not the first user message (11,010 written by each), because a cache read lands only at a breakpoint the harness placed and a shared prefix inside one message is not one.
- The VM can be restarted under a live session with the disk intact: 2026-09-18 23:22 UTC, 25 minutes into the repair batch's re-run, kernel build string fc-v33 → fc-v37, one JVM running (16 GB, no swap, 4 CPUs: not a memory death). Worktrees, uncommitted edits and agent transcripts survived; the Workflow run and its agents did not, and a run is relaunched, never resumed; the `wip/` branches held every pushed milestone (`remote-container.md` § The 2026-09-18 restart).
- **A user interrupt of the coordinating session's turn kills a background Workflow run** (2026-09-19): climb batch 1's first run, `wf_a29fd04b-a9a`, launched 07:15 UTC, lost both its rung agents at 07:46:42, the second Pavol's interrupt cut the turn that a check-in trigger had just started; both agent transcripts end at that timestamp mid-work, no result line reached the journal, and the harness no longer knew the task. The Agent tool's workers are not affected (the review worker launched after the interrupt ran to completion). The `wip/` branches held F's three and M's three milestones and M's worktree its uncommitted report, so the relaunch at 08:25 from the same base continued under the prefix's continuation clause. Cost: about 40 minutes of two workers. Rule: while a Workflow runs, a check-in must not be interrupted mid-turn; and a batch is relaunched, never resumed, after any such death.
- **A manual compaction issued between turns leaves a running Workflow alive** (found 2026-09-19 by a worker in the archived transcript of session `bdff267d`, `transcripts` branch, parts file `001.jsonl`): the eight-rung climb's run `wf_73833dfb-d25` (launched 2026-09-17 06:00:57 UTC) survived two `/compact` commands, boundaries 10:47:33 (442,504 tokens before, 130 s) and 14:25:25 (177,831 tokens, 153 s), both typed while the session sat between turns; rung 5's commit landed 84 s after the first boundary, rungs 6-8 and the final re-run followed, and the run's completion notification arrived 14:39:09 with all eight rungs. This container's three compactions (09-18 18:38, 22:54; 09-19 06:38) coincided with no run. So the rule is: compact between turns, never send during a turn; the 09-19 death was a mid-turn interrupt, not a compaction. Caveat: that run's journal and agent transcripts are not in the backup, so the agents' survival is inferred from their commits and the session's own status turns.
- **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` is the one script every probe and gate runner sources, and it is verified from its new home** (2026-09-24, after `7bc8177a3` moved `experiment/` under `explorations/`): it derives `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own location two levels up, and re-running the two shadow experiments that source it, `reviews/mie-probes/forest/forest-run.sh` (423 s) and `perf-probes/nat/runtime/run-all.sh` (669 s), reproduced every committed count and probe output (`checker-count.txt`'s six counts, stock 103 and forest 37 among them, and captures r1-r5 byte-identical); the only differences were dates, timings and line numbers shifted by the library commits `c2b4e2c95` and `d6faad28f` made after the captures. astra's scripts keep their own `experiment/` paths, which name astra's tree.

## The ledger

- Rows are never renumbered or moved, and the reports cite them by number; the counts by kind are derived by script in the ledger's counts (`fortress-gap-ledger.md:714`), and the revival worklist (46 items, `fortress-gap-ledger.md:574`) and `apl/lessons.md` are the two derived views. Five cost rows sit in section 15; whether they get a section of their own is Pavol's call.

# The C series and the APL side quest: state and what comes next

## Where the work stands

The goal is to finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed specification (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not to redesign the language, with one program as the measuring stick: microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast (the root `CLAUDE.md` § Project goal; `coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-16).

The live thread is the one library. The interpreter's library (`FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`) is to become the library the compiler checks, and the work is to bring the compiled checker to accept it (`coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-21). Between that library and bytecode stands the checker, not desugaring or code generation; it reports 103 errors on the library, the count since climb batch 3, and a batch's count may only fall from it or declare its rise (`coordinator/FACTS.md` § The checker and the one library). Two decisions are in front of Pavol. First, the route on the checker's multiple instantiation exclusion, the rule that no type may be two different instantiations of one generic, which 61 of the 103 errors come from: route A keeps the rule and flattens the library's numeric tower, with the interpreter taught coercion; route B drops the rule; route C takes the forest rule of the group's 2012 patents; the brief recommends A (`reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md` § 1 and § 5). Next after it, how a `nat` size is carried at run time: design A, the path the run time already takes for an `opr` argument, against design B, a small class stamped per size literal; the probe note's labelled default is A (`perf-probes/nat/runtime.md` § 2).

Decided, in `coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the goal and its measuring stick (2026-09-16); test first, the test written and seen failing before the fix and kept in the corpus from then on (2026-09-17); the workflow, with workers pushing to their own `wip/` branches, the script in the repository and the higher tier called only at a refusal, a stop or a red gate (2026-09-18), narrowed to a judge's second ruling on the same rung or tree (2026-09-24); unboxed `double[]` storage and the `nat` sizes taken together, as the team designed them (2026-09-19); the tier rule, workers on the cheaper tier and a worker on the top tier only with his permission (2026-09-20); one library, the interpreter's, with no new declaration in the compiler prelude and its three files deleted at the switch-over (2026-09-21).

## Boot note to the resumed coordinator

**Update, 2026-09-24 07:10 UTC, written for the compaction Pavol asked for.** No batch runs before the weekly usage reset (Friday 12:00 CEST; his report of about 05:30 UTC: all models 90 %, Fable 89 %). Landed since the 04:55 note, all on `main` and the container branch: the workflow script's judge tier on his reading of the redesign note's option (c), a judge's first ruling on a rung or the merged tree on Opus and a second on the session's tier (`343ad91df`); the review's judge ruling while the gate runs on and the gate's outputs under `tmp/` until the commit stage (`9ed2a2109`, his "Yes to both"); CLAUDE.md made timeless (`8c1472ebf`); FACTS gardened to the current state by area with the narrative in `FACTS-history.md` (`2f105225a`; the rule is in the coordinator README); POSITIONS corrected on the redesign's option (b), never put to him (`87ad36c6e`); and this commit: the handover's first section rewritten as the current state with the landings moved verbatim to `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover-history.md`, the older boot notes moved to the end of this file, protocol § 4's dead branch and session lines replaced, the script's FACTS-section instruction repointed. His ruling of the day on boot: `INDEX.md` is read whole at every boot and `coordinator/check-index.sh` run; skipping it to save tokens is not acceptable. Done in the commit after `201834fa8`, on his "does this make sense" and the coordinator's yes: `git mv experiment explorations/experiment` by an Opus worker, with every executable reference (`env.sh` sourced by the three workflow scripts and their shared prefix, `setup.sh`, the goldens if a check program reads them by relative path, the CI gate file) re-pointed in the same commit and the prose citations in records left as history; `env.sh` derives `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own location and is verified after the move. The order after boot: (1) his calibration check; (2) the exclusion route: he leans A, not decided; his two additions of the day are recorded in POSITIONS (the cost of switching to C later, answered: one library rung in reverse, C's checker half additive, C probeable as a shadow; and that the specification is revised with the decision and a decision record preserves the original text, the reasoning and route C, the spec edit flagged as an original-tree edit, the frozen copy untouched); (3) the run-time size design through the nine steps (`perf-probes/nat/runtime.md`); (4) batch 4's manifest for his go, three rungs sharing no file (interpreter coercion, the spec rung, the size wall's first rung), launched after the reset; (5) the one workflow ask still owed, option (b) of `climb-batch-3-redesign.md`; (6) rows 379, 380/381, 383, then the ten re-approval rows (30, 39-42, 44-48) and the four ledger homes (374-377), one per message; (7) the inventory's move list (`experiment/` moved on 2026-09-24 as its group E; the four groups under `explorations/` remain), once he has read `coordinator/explorations-inventory.md`; (8) the lineage cleanup, the GitHub issues plan, the cleaner pass of `main`. The remote `wip/rung-int-semantics-*` branches are still his to delete in the GitHub UI.

## The decisions in front of him, in the order agreed

1. **Which library** (his item 18). The judge's ruling (`coordinator/library-route-judgement.md`): nothing on record argues for keeping the compiler's second library; make the interpreter's library the compiler's, retire the three compiler prelude files, no new declaration into them from now on, code-generator rungs continue. First rung: the checker's error count on the library becomes a stage of the gate, no library line changed, stop condition two identical runs. Evidence: `coordinator/two-libraries.md` (the split born 2008-12-19 as a "stripped-down minimalist library for first crack at compilation", "hopefully temporary hack"; 93 checker errors at 48 sites), `perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen.md` (desugaring clean, code generation refuses 5 of 446 cleanly checked declarations; the checker is the wall: the `nat` crash on 112 declarations, the `extends Object` pre-desugaring that adds 712 of 960 api errors by rejecting generics at tuple types, and an overload dispatch generator that does not terminate on the library), `perf-probes/prelude/import-java-interpreter.md` (the interpreter's Java import is wired and unfinished at four points, so the natives are one shared text plus one small binding component per world behind one api, which makes the linker's api-to-component lookup live work, ledger row 320's class-name half). His stated belief: "the compiler's second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it." Waiting on his yes; after it, record it in POSITIONS and the plan. Decided 2026-09-21 on his words of 09-20 (POSITIONS 2026-09-21); what remains is the plan for the first step, after the exclusion trace.

2. **The six array decisions** A to F of `reviews/array-design-review.md` §3, one per turn. Verdict on the design as written: unsound, sound only under these. His leans on record: A, the team's own direction, specialising in the class loader, unless a clear reason appears; C is decision 1 above. D: sizes into the model's own text (the specification's shape; changes model lines; diff shown first) against the vocabulary over unsized arrays (model unchanged, no static shape check). B: natives first (measured to buy nothing) against unboxing by static type in generated code (the team's precedent). E: an unconstrained size is an error when used, not 0. F: a shadow rung answering five questions before the checker rung, with stop conditions.

3. **The four findings on yesterday's library commit**, each with a one-page explainer in `postmortem-2026-09-19/library-findings-explained.md`: the tower closure (the probe `reviews/library-scalar-extension-review-probes.md` found no spelling the checker accepts: 92 errors without the clause, 93 with it, 93 with the team's repair beside it; choice: keep and carry one more known checker error, or remove and re-house the interpreter's acceptance of the generic block; the explainer's default B is corrected in its appended note); the rank-3 exclusion (two futures: user operators between a matrix and a rank-3 array, or rank-3 arrays that may join the algebra as vectors and matrices do; default keep but place on `Rank3` with the reason commented); the two unnamed choices in the scalar block (reversed subtraction, unsized result; default keep and comment); exclusion between static-parameter bounds (the team's open question, `future.tex:264-265`; default one probe then a position). The blinded review is `reviews/library-scalar-extension-review.md`; its test-quality note was wrong and is retracted in an appended correction (a printed `fail` does fail the suite, `compile-ladder/gate-baseline/fail-word-probe/`). State on 2026-09-21: three of the four changes approved as landed (POSITIONS 2026-09-21); the closure held for the exclusion trace, which is running. Later on 2026-09-21: the closure approved as landed after the trace; all four changes of the commit are approved; the comment and the checker accommodation are batch work.

4. **The re-approval table**, `postmortem-2026-09-19/decisions-for-reapproval.md`, 25 rows: every decision that was his and was taken without him, from 2026-09-19 06:38 to batch 2's landing, with what reverting takes. He approves or reverts each. The post-mortem closes when this is done and the protocol is simplified (next item).

5. **The protocol, shorter, not longer.** Protocol §5's two entries of today are lawyerly and wrong in spirit; he wants the plain meaning: workers on the best tier he can afford, Opus now, never Sonnet; the "alias" remark of 09-18 was only about not renaming when a newer Opus arrives; Fable for a worker only with his permission. And fewer rules overall: Fable follows common sense better than a pile of edge-case constraints written for Opus. He accepted this wording for the design rule: a decision that touches two or more of specification, interpreter and compiler, or that infers the original design intent, is made in two steps, cheaper-tier workers gather the evidence into a condensed cited brief, the judgement is made at the top tier with his permission or by the coordinator only on a clean context, and it reaches him as a decision with alternatives before anything is built. Done in the evening of 2026-09-20 (`a0924cd6c`): the tier rule in plain words, the two-step design rule, and a watch-list line against legal text; the wider shortening of the protocol is part of the skill-extraction session (item 10).

6. **The recovery shape for work that landed without him**: review, re-approve or revert, amend the process. Executed for the library commit up to the review and the probes; the re-approval is item 4.

7. **Knowing what we already know.** The index missed 42 of 118 notes (`coordinator/check-index.sh` prints them). Fix: the check as a gate, and every brief for a plan or a review told to search the index and `reviews/` for prior work first. Today's failure: the array-design reviewer was not given `reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` until he noticed.

8. **The explorations cleanup**, `coordinator/explorations-inventory.md`: eight parallel patterns, ten `git mv` lines, 139 citations to fix, `apl-probes/` left to him. One-time chore, on his word, after he has read it.

9. **Two explanations he asked for**: the takeaway of the script-changes-against-the-turn table (`postmortem-2026-09-19/script-vs-tactics.md`: the six process decisions were taken in one word and built before the direction turned; only test-first was used by the array work; the rest first ran in batch 2; the batch machinery keeps its value for the library route's batches, the fork-free name rungs do not); and the fifteen review shapes (`postmortem-2026-09-19/review-patterns.md`), which he found too terse.

10. **A dedicated session later** to extract a coordinator skill and an architect role. Not now.

## The research he asked for, answered

Was the compiler-library direction chosen without pricing the array re-implementation, and why: yes. `postmortem-2026-09-19/direction-history-documents.md` and `direction-history-transcripts.md`. The direction was fixed in four steps (08-24 framing, 09-15 step one, 09-16/17 plan and accepted order, 09-19 the design's one line); he proposed one library himself on 09-15 at 23:51 and the probe favoured it; the coordinator's recommendation of 09-17 01:19 inverted that evidence and priced its own route at nothing; the fork was "reserved, yours" at every batch and never put to him with both prices; the next-climb analysis of 09-17 said the decision was not which name to add next and it was never answered. Not wasted: runtime and code-generator repairs, the map, the measurements, the batch machinery, yesterday's library repair. Wasted: the library-name rungs of the eight-rung climb, batch 1, and rungs W and B of batch 2.

input.description: Run-time size design brief
input.prompt:
You are a worker in the Fortress revival repository at /home/user/fortress (read the root CLAUDE.md first, then explorations/protocol.md sections 2, 3 and 6). You write a decision brief for Pavol, the project's director; you do not decide. Reading only: another worker is running experiments in this tree, so run no build, no probe and no test, edit no tracked file, and commit and push nothing. Every claim comes from a file, cited by path and line; a claim that would need a run is marked unprobed.

The decision. Fortress types can carry a size as a static parameter (a "nat" parameter: Vector[\T, nat n\] is a vector of n elements, with n a type-level natural number). The compiled path's checker cannot check them today and its run time cannot carry one; a shadow built over 2026-09-21 and 09-22 showed both halves working. On the run-time half two designs were built and both run the same programs: design A, where a size argument follows the path the run time already has for an operator argument (an opr parameter: exempt from needing a run-time type descriptor class, 4 files, 28 code lines); and design B, a small descriptor class stamped per size literal (about 60 lines). A third piece, a size in value position (using n as a number inside a method body), was built in 25 lines and works under both; a fourth gap (a size read inside a method of a sized object) is found and not built. Pavol decides A or B, and how the two remaining pieces are taken. On 2026-09-22 he ruled that forks a probe can settle are probed before a batch is briefed, so the decision is his now and the worker of the next batch gets a clean task.

Read these before anything else, in this order, and do not rediscover them:
- explorations/perf-probes/nat/runtime.md, and the patches and captures under explorations/perf-probes/nat/runtime/ (design-a.patch, value-position.patch, captures r1-r8)
- explorations/perf-probes/nat/java.md, REPORT.md, followup.md, zero.md, triage.md (the checker half, the Java site, the counts)
- explorations/reviews/nat-checking-plan.md (the team's intended design, the plan's minimal design)
- explorations/coordinator/map/compile-path-walkthrough.md, the nat section (what the checker and the loader each lack, four outside precedents) and the glossary
- explorations/coordinator/array-design.md and explorations/reviews/array-design-review.md (the array decisions A-F; the size design touches decision D, sizes in the model's own types, and unboxed storage)
- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md: section "Execution model" (the entry on nat parameters and the specification's "instantiated at runtime"), section "The checker and the one library" (the five shadow entries dated 2026-09-21 and 2026-09-22), section "The library's arrays and algebra"
- explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md: the entries dated 2026-09-19 (double[] and the nat sizes taken together, as the team designed them), 2026-09-21 (the nat plan's two decisions and the shadow), 2026-09-22 (forks probed before briefing; his design principle for the compiled path: JVM defaults where they make sense, corrected where high performance and mathematical precision need it, close to the metal in the Swift and Rust way)
- explorations/protocol.md section 6, the nine-step method (dated 2026-09-22) and the two-step rule for decisions touching the specification, the interpreter and the compiler
- Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex (the nat parameter passages, "instantiated at runtime", makeVector) and where Vector and Matrix are declared in Library/FortressLibrary.fsi
- explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md rows that name nat parameters (grep for "nat" in the row texts; rows 23, 83, 292, 295 among them)
- ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/ (Naming.isOprKind, the RTTI reference sites the notes cite, MethodInstantiater) and ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java, only at the lines the notes cite, to verify the citations still hold

The brief follows the nine steps of protocol section 6, adapted from a semantic question to a representation question: (1) the refresher, what a static size parameter is and what "carried at run time" means, defined for a reader who knows Scala, Swift, Kotlin and Rust and not Fortress; (2) what each path does today, from the measurements on file (the interpreter matches sizes at dispatch; the compiled path's checker and loader); (3) what the specification's prose says, including the same idea under another spelling; (4) where a size sits in the type system beside the other static-parameter kinds and how the run time treats each today; (5) what the library already does with sizes (the sized traits, the shared nats in the products, the 85 literal sites, the 25 declarations with dead sizes) and where the team's own drafts departed from it; (6) what the peers do, by family: the JVM languages (Java none, Scala literal and singleton types, Kotlin none), close to the metal (C++ non-type template parameters, Rust const generics with monomorphisation, Swift's integer generic parameters if landed), scientific (Chapel, Fortran, X10's constrained types, Julia's Val), and the typed functional family (Haskell DataKinds, Idris), each in a sentence with what it costs at run time and cited to a URL or a document, not from memory alone; (7) the history in this tree's commits: when nat parameters were designed, what the team built and left (the checker's Not yet implemented, isOprKind as the one run-time kind, the RTTI stamping), found by git log -S and git blame on the cited lines, bounded searches only; (8) the derivation from Pavol's principles, case by case: A against B on start-up cost, dispatch (both distinguish Vec[3] from Vec[4]), class count, the value-position piece, the fourth gap, the loader's substitute-at-load channel, unboxed double[] storage under each, and what each forecloses; (9) the decision written for him as: what we do, what it changes, a default he can accept without reading the argument, the ledger rows it touches, and the exact rule as it would go into the rung's brief.

Also answer, from the notes, whether the size wall's first rung (the checker half of the nat plan: seven Scala files, about 225 lines, plus FnNameInfo.java; FACTS 2026-09-21 and 09-22) depends on the A-or-B decision at all; if it does not, say so on the first page, because then the decision can be taken while that rung runs.

Deliverable: explorations/reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md. Its first line is an HTML comment whose first sentence says what the note is, in the style of the other notes' headers (it becomes the index line). Then a plain first page: the decision in plain words, the default and what it changes, whether the first rung waits on it, in under a page. Then the nine steps. Then the options with what each forecloses and what is unsettled. Then the recommendation in one line, after the explanation and never instead of it. Then the open questions, each with its cost. Plain register, short sentences, a term defined in the sentence that first uses it, no self-credit, no model names, no estimates in days or weeks (sizes in files, lines, rungs). Keep it under about 400 lines. When done, run git status --short and confirm only the new file appears. Your final message to the coordinator: the default in one line, whether the first rung waits on the decision, the open questions in one line each, and the file path.

Both workers are running, and the record carries the go and their output paths (`c7fd0f13a`, pushed to both branches). The rows now, one per message.

**Row 379: under `walk`, fixed-width integer arithmetic wraps silently.**

What it is. On `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, an addition, subtraction, negation, absolute value, division or multiplication whose result does not fit wraps around under the interpreter: `ZZ32 MAX + 1` prints the most negative value. The compiled path throws a catchable `IntegerOverflow` for every one of those cases since rung B. The specification settles it in one sentence, in the operators chapter: for integer results, overflow throws `IntegerOverflow`, and wraparound and saturation have their own operator spellings. So the interpreter is the one that departs from the spec, and the two paths disagree today. Batch 3.5 pinned the defect as an expected failure test, so the gate knows it.

The refresher. Java and the JVM wrap silently, which is where the interpreter's one-line natives got it. Swift traps on overflow and spells the wrapping version `&+`. Rust panics in a debug build and wraps in release, with checked and wrapping method families beside. Julia wraps. The specification's shape is Swift's: an error by default, wrapping and saturating written explicitly. That matches your principle of 09-22, JVM defaults corrected where mathematical precision needs it, and it is what the compiled path already does.

What a yes does. One small interpreter rung: an overflow check in each of the ten natives in the interpreter's `Int` and `Long` glue classes, raising the catchable `IntegerOverflow` rung I made available, and the expected-failure test turned into a plain gated test. It touches two Java files under the interpreter's glue and one test file, and nothing the coercion rung touches as far as the record says, so it can ride in batch 4 as a fourth rung if the manifest confirms no shared file, otherwise in the next interpreter batch. The rung's worker measures first how many interpreter tests change output, per your rule of 09-21, and the count comes to you before the edit if it is not zero. What a no costs: the divergence stays, pinned as an expected failure; microGPT is unaffected either way, since it is float arithmetic.

My recommendation: yes, the specification's rule on `walk`, as a rung in batch 4 if it shares no file, else the next batch.

Row 379 is recorded (`accaf9a0b`, pushed).

**Rows 380 and 381: a `ZZ32` shifted by a count of another width.**

What it is. Under `walk`, shifting a `ZZ32` by a count that is a `ZZ`, an `NN32` or an `NN64` lands on `ZZ64`'s method: the shift is done at width 64 and the answer comes back as a `ZZ64`, so `3 LSHIFT 33` with a `ZZ` count prints a large number, while the same shift with a `ZZ64` count prints `0 : ZZ32`. The cause is one declaration's type: `ZZ32`'s own shift pair takes exactly a `ZZ64` count, while the `Integral` trait promises a shift by any integral count that answers in the receiver's type, and `ZZ64`'s pair takes any integral count. Row 381 is the compiled side of the same declaration: the compiler prelude's `ZZ32` pair takes a `ZZ32` count, so a `ZZ64` count there also goes to `ZZ64`'s method, and the two paths disagree on that one case today. The specification names neither operator, so this is your receiver-width rule of 09-22 applied to the declaration's type. Batch 3.5 reserved it because the repair changes an existing declaration's type.

The refresher. Every peer answers a shift in the receiver's width whatever the count's type: Java masks the count and keeps the receiver's type, Swift and Rust take any integer count and answer in the receiver's type. The width-64 answer is the odd one out.

What a yes does. Four lines in the library's two files: `ZZ32`'s shift pair declared with any integral count, bound as now to the natives that already read any count; and `ZZ64`'s pair made to say the same in the api as it already does in the component, which is a mismatch of the kind row 345 records. A gated assertion in the interpreter's integer test pins the case. The checker count is declared by the rung. Row 381 then closes at the switch-over, when the compiled path checks this same library; until then it stays a probe under a silent specification, its home today. Placement as for row 379: batch 4 if it shares no file with the batch's other rungs, else the next batch. What a no costs: a `ZZ32` shifted by a `ZZ` count keeps answering as a `ZZ64` under `walk`, against the library's own contract.

My recommendation: yes, the receiver-width rule in the declaration, with 381 closing at the switch-over.

# Carrying a size at run time: a decision brief

## The decision in plain words

- A `nat` parameter puts a number into a type: `Vector[\RR64, 16\]` is a vector of sixteen `RR64`s. The compiled path lacks two halves. Its checker cannot compare sizes; that is the size wall's first rung, already in batch 4's manifest (`microgpt-run-c-handover.md:9, 13`). - Every compiled generic already gets its own class per instantiation, made when first loaded, and the size is already in that class's name: `Box⟦3⟧`. What is missing is the size's place in the run-time type descriptor, the object a running program asks "is this a `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]`?".
- Design A: a size goes where an operator argument already goes, into the descriptor class's name, with no object of its own. 4 files, 28 code lines, built and measured (`perf-probes/nat/runtime.md § 1`).
- Design B: a size gets a small descriptor object, as a type argument does, from one tiny class per distinct literal. About 60 lines in 3 files; the 17-line descriptor class is written and works, the loader code that would make the per-literal classes is not (`perf-probes/nat/java.md § 2`).
- Measured: the two run the same programs, stop at the same places, both tell `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]` from `Vec[\ZZ32,4\]`, and start-up is within noise. A also passes a size in an `extends` clause, the library's `Rank1 extends Rank[\1\]` shape; B needs about 10 more lines for it (`runtime.md § 2`).
- What A gives up: a size can no longer be read off a value through its descriptor, only out of a class name. By reading, unprobed: an overloaded function with an arm generic in a size (`f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` beside `f(x: RR64)`, ledger row 214; the library's `DOT` family) is handled by neither design when the call is dispatched at run time. Under B its fix would follow the type-argument path; under A it would read the class name, as the run time already does for an operator.
- Two further pieces are needed under both designs. A size used as a number in a body (value position): built, 25 lines, works under both. A size read inside a method of a sized object (the fourth gap): found, not built. The library's own `getter size():ZZ32 = s0` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2022`) has the fourth gap's shape.

## The default, and what it changes

- Default: design A, with the value-position piece in the same rung (53 code lines, in the four files A touches). Before that rung is briefed, one shadow session probes the fourth gap and a size-generic dispatch arm. If that arm needs more under A than reading a size out of the value's descriptor class name, the choice comes back to him.
- What it changes: every sized descriptor class is renamed (`Box❮3❯$RTTIc`), so every cache is rebuilt, the prelude's included; the heavy-angle name channel, which only operators used, carries numbers; a size has no field or getter in its descriptor; `XXXNatArgRungS` should leave the expected failures (its printed name is checked in the rung). By reading, the three lines A needed for its own first failure also fix ledger row 366 (an object with an operator parameter), whose expected failure `XXXOprParamRungS` would then pass; unprobed.

## Does the first rung wait on it?

- No. The first rung (seven Scala files, about 225 code lines, and nine lines in `FnNameInfo.java`; FACTS:32, :34) touches no file either design touches: A touches `Naming`, `MethodInstantiater`, `CodeGen`, `OverloadSet` (`runtime/design-a.patch`), B a new `RTTIsize`, the loader and `CodeGen` (`java.md § 2`). The checker behaved identically under both: the compile half of the A run is line for line the checker shadow's own (`runtime.md § 1`), and the A and B captures differ only in their flag lines (`runtime/r1-probes-A.out` against `r2-probes-B.out`). The one thing the halves share, a sized method's generated name, is fixed by the first rung and used unchanged by both designs (`java.md § 1`).
- One condition goes into the first rung's brief: its run tests stop at compile and link, or are written as expected failures that fail at load with `3$RTTIc`, as `XXXNatArgRungS` does today. A sized program that the first rung makes compile cannot run until the run-time rung lands, under either design.
- So he can decide while the first rung runs. The decision is needed before the run-time rung is briefed.

---

## 1. The refresher

- A **static parameter** is what stands between Fortress's white brackets in a declaration, `[\T, nat s0\]`; a **static argument** is what fills it at a use, `[\RR64, 16\]`. A **`nat` parameter** takes a natural number instead of a type (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:68-81`). In Rust it is `const N: usize`, in Swift 6.2 `let N: Int`, in C++ `size_t N`; in Scala the nearest thing is a literal type such as `3` used as a type argument.
- "Carried at run time" asks what, in the running program, still says "this vector has 3 elements". Languages give four answers: nothing, the size was erased (Java, Kotlin); a constant inside a copy of the code made per size (C++, Rust); an entry in a run-time type descriptor that unspecialised code reads (Swift's type metadata, Haskell's `KnownNat` dictionary, Scala's `ValueOf` argument); or a field in each object (X10's properties, Fortran's `LEN` parameters). Sources in § 6.
- Fortress's compiled path keeps generics at run time. The code generator writes one **template** class per generic, and the class loader **stamps** a class per instantiation the first time it is used, by rewriting the template's names (FACTS:18; `runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java`). The arguments are in the stamped class's name between **oxford brackets**: `Box⟦3⟧`. So every sized class already exists once per size, like a Rust copy, made at load time instead of compile time.
- Beside each class the run time keeps **RTTI** (run-time type information): a descriptor class per generic, `Box$RTTIc`, whose objects answer type tests and hand dispatch the static arguments of a value (`runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:94-139`; `reviews/mie-probes/dispatch-and-route-c.md § 1`). For a type argument the descriptor holds the argument's own descriptor, in a field with a getter. An **`opr` parameter** (an operator symbol as a static argument, `trait-parameters.tex:156-176`) gets none of that: its symbol is written into the descriptor class's name between **heavy angles**, `Op❮+❯$RTTIc` (`runtimeSystem/Naming.java:207-210, 1053-1066`).
- So the question is narrow. The size is already in the stamped class's name under both designs. The question is only whether the size's descriptor is a name (A) or an object (B).

A symbol needs none: the template names `Box⟦k⟧$RTTIc`, and substitution fills in the size (`java.md § 2`).
- The code generator: a size in an `extends` clause falls through an empty branch into `CompilerError("Only emitting RTTI for types right now")` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:5784, 5793`); a size read as a value compiles to a static field of a class that does not exist, `pNatVec$s0` (`java.md § 3`; `CodeGen.java:5969-5996`).

## 3. What the specification says

- "These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values" (`trait-parameters.tex:82`; the same sentence for `bool`, `:111`). A nat "may be used to instantiate other nat parameters, or to appear in any context that a variable of type ℕ32 can appear, except that it cannot be assigned to" (`:83-86`). The chapter opens "Non-type static parameters and static expressions are not yet supported" (`:15-17`). Its one example, `makeVector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]():Vector[\T,s0\] = vector[\T,s0\]` (`SpecData/examples/basic/StatParam.Nat.fss`, quoted at `:94-97`), never reads `s0` as a value (`runtime.md § 3`).
- The same idea under other spellings, three times. Static expressions: "Conceptually, a static expression is not evaluated while a program is running … Given instantiations of all static parameters … the value of the static expression can be determined statically", and a nat parameter "denotes a value that has type NaturalStatic" (`Specification/basic/expressions/constant.tex:17-25, 95-97`). Read with `:82`: the value is fixed per instantiation, and the instantiation happens at run time, which is what a load-time stamping loader does under either design. Operator parameters: "Unlike other static parameters, operator parameters may be used in both type context and value context" (`trait-parameters.tex:172-175`), a sentence the nat section contradicts (`:83-86`); the run time carries an operator by name, design A's model. And the factories: `array[E](size)` for a "runtime-determined size" beside `array1[E,n]()` for a "statically determined size" (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex:42-48`).

## 4. Where a size sits beside the other kinds

- Six kinds: type; `nat` and `int`; `bool`; `dim` and `unit`; `opr` (`trait-parameters.tex:36-176`).
- The checker: inference variables exist for types and, since 2011, operators (`STypesUtil.scala:546-559`). The first rung adds sizes as a third track modelled on the operator track: equality only, solved by unification, no subtyping, no variance (`REPORT.md § 2`; `nat-checking-plan.md § c`, "the op track's `oEquivalent` … with an int flavour"). To the checker, a size behaves like an operator.
- The run time has one kind predicate, "is this an operator?" (`Naming.java:95-109`). A type argument gets a descriptor object, a field, a getter and a factory argument (`CodeGen.java:5261-5272, 5317-5328`); an operator gets none, is written into the descriptor's name, is pushed as null in the factory call (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:2684-2691`), and is read back off the name (`RTHelpers.java:18-45`).
- A size has a tag, `intnat` (`Naming.java:213`), recorded in the side file (`Naming.java:87-93`) and read by nothing. - So A makes the run time agree with the checker's model of a size, a value compared by equality like an operator. B makes it agree with the code generator's count and with the interpreter, where a size is a type object.

## 5. What the library already does with sizes

- The sized traits: `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]`, `Array2`, `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]`, `Array3` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1440, 1465, 1542, 1583, 1657`).

Every `DOT` arm is generic in its sizes: the family is an overload set of size-generic arms, the shape of the dispatch question in § 8.
- Literals: 4 distinct size literals (0, 1, 2, 3) written as static arguments in 85 places, 78 of them `0`; 244 nat parameters declared (`runtime/r7-lib-literals.txt`). Under B that is four descriptor classes in all; under A one descriptor class and interface per sized type used.
- Dead sizes: 25 api declarations carry a size that occurs in no domain, range or body (`REPORT.md § 2`); the checker lets them pass by decision E2 (POSITIONS:47). Neither design meets them unless a dead size reaches a name (`REPORT.md § 11`).
- Sizes read as numbers inside sized traits: `getter size():ZZ32 = s0` and `opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0` in `ReadableArray1` (`FortressLibrary.fss:2022, 2036`); `s0 s1` in `Array2` (`:2299, 2320`); `s0 s1 s2` in `Array3` (`:2680, 2712`); `o::m#s` and `o-b0` in `subarray` (`:2127-2128`). This is the fourth gap's shape; whether a trait's default method meets it exactly as `NatExtends1`'s object method does is unprobed.

Design A's one `continue` is the branch they reach (measured on `NatExtends2`, which writes a symbol; the literal case is by reading).

## 6. The peers, by family

- JVM. Java: a type parameter is an identifier with an optional bound, erased (JLS § 8.1.2, https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-8.html#jls-8.1.2); "Unlike generic types in other languages such as C# and Java, C++ templates support non-type parameters" (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/cpp/templates-cpp). Nothing is carried, so nothing costs; a size is a field.
- JVM. Kotlin: `typeParameter: [typeParameterModifiers] simpleIdentifier [':' type]`, no value parameter (https://kotlinlang.org/spec/syntax-and-grammar.html). As Java.
- JVM. Scala: literal types, `val one: 1 = 1`, and `ValueOf[T]` with `valueOf[T]`, "yielding the unique value of types with a single inhabitant" (SIP-23, https://docs.scala-lang.org/sips/42.type.html). On the erasing JVM the value reaches generic code as an implicit argument: a descriptor passed per call.
- Close to the metal. C++: a non-type argument "is passed in as a template argument at compile time and must be const or a constexpr expression", and each instantiation is its own class (Microsoft Learn, above). Nothing at run time; the size is a constant in the class's code.

- Scientific. Nothing was built, run or probed for it; every number is a note's or a cited file's, and a claim that would need a run says unprobed. Designs A and B here are not the nat plan's options A/B for the inference variable, the array review's decisions A-F, or the exclusion brief's routes A-C. -->
2	
3	# Carrying a size at run time: a decision brief
4	
5	## The decision in plain words
6	
7	- A `nat` parameter puts a number into a type: `Vector[\RR64, 16\]` is a vector of sixteen `RR64`s. The compiled path lacks two halves. Its checker cannot compare sizes; that is the size wall's first rung, already in batch 4's manifest (`microgpt-run-c-handover.md:9, 13`). And its run time has nowhere to keep a size, so a compiled sized object dies when its class loads with `NoClassDefFoundError: 3$RTTIc`. A gated expected-failure test shows exactly this today (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNatArgRungS.fss`; `compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/probes/xxx-skeptic-defects.txt:74-80`).
8	- Every compiled generic already gets its own class per instantiation, made when first loaded, and the size is already in that class's name: `Box⟦3⟧`. What is missing is the size's place in the run-time type descriptor, the object a running program asks "is this a `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]`?".
9	- Design A: a size goes where an operator argument already goes, into the descriptor class's name, with no object of its own. 4 files, 28 code lines, built and measured (`perf-probes/nat/runtime.md § 1`).
10	- Design B: a size gets a small descriptor object, as a type argument does, from one tiny class per distinct literal. About 60 lines in 3 files; the 17-line descriptor class is written and works, the loader code that would make the per-literal classes is not (`perf-probes/nat/java.md § 2`).
11	- Measured: the two run the same programs, stop at the same places, both tell `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]` from `Vec[\ZZ32,4\]`, and start-up is within noise. A also passes a size in an `extends` clause, the library's `Rank1 extends Rank[\1\]` shape; B needs about 10 more lines for it (`runtime.md § 2`).
12	- What A gives up: a size can no longer be read off a value through its descriptor, only out of a class name. By reading, unprobed: an overloaded function with an arm generic in a size (`f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` beside `f(x: RR64)`, ledger row 214; the library's `DOT` family) is handled by neither design when the call is dispatched at run time. Under B its fix would follow the type-argument path; under A it would read the class name, as the run time already does for an operator.
13	- Two further pieces are needed under both designs. A size used as a number in a body (value position): built, 25 lines, works under both. A size read inside a method of a sized object (the fourth gap): found, not built. The library's own `getter size():ZZ32 = s0` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2022`) has the fourth gap's shape.
14	
15	## The default, and what it changes
16	
17	- Default: design A, with the value-position piece in the same rung (53 code lines, in the four files A touches). Before that rung is briefed, one shadow session probes the fourth gap and a size-generic dispatch arm. If that arm needs more under A than reading a size out of the value's descriptor class name, the choice comes back to him.
18	- What it changes: every sized descriptor class is renamed (`Box❮3❯$RTTIc`), so every cache is rebuilt, the prelude's included; the heavy-angle name channel, which only operators used, carries numbers; a size has no field or getter in its descriptor; `XXXNatArgRungS` should leave the expected failures (its printed name is checked in the rung). By reading, the three lines A needed for its own first failure also fix ledger row 366 (an object with an operator parameter), whose expected failure `XXXOprParamRungS` would then pass; unprobed.
19	
20	## Does the first rung wait on it?
21	
22	- No. The first rung (seven Scala files, about 225 code lines, and nine lines in `FnNameInfo.java`; FACTS:32, :34) touches no file either design touches: A touches `Naming`, `MethodInstantiater`, `CodeGen`, `OverloadSet` (`runtime/design-a.patch`), B a new `RTTIsize`, the loader and `CodeGen` (`java.md § 2`). The checker behaved identically under both: the compile half of the A run is line for line the checker shadow's own (`runtime.md § 1`), and the A and B captures differ only in their flag lines (`runtime/r1-probes-A.out` against `r2-probes-B.out`). The one thing the halves share, a sized method's generated name, is fixed by the first rung and used unchanged by both designs (`java.md § 1`).
23	- One condition goes into the first rung's brief: its run tests stop at compile and link, or are written as expected failures that fail at load with `3$RTTIc`, as `XXXNatArgRungS` does today. A sized program that the first rung makes compile cannot run until the run-time rung lands, under either design.
24	- So he can decide while the first rung runs. The decision is needed before the run-time rung is briefed.
25	
26	---
27	
28	## 1. The refresher
29	
30	- A **static parameter** is what stands between Fortress's white brackets in a declaration, `[\T, nat s0\]`; a **static argument** is what fills it at a use, `[\RR64, 16\]`. A **`nat` parameter** takes a natural number instead of a type (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:68-81`). In Rust it is `const N: usize`, in Swift 6.2 `let N: Int`, in C++ `size_t N`; in Scala the nearest thing is a literal type such as `3` used as a type argument.
31	- "Carried at run time" asks what, in the running program, still says "this vector has 3 elements". Languages give four answers: nothing, the size was erased (Java, Kotlin); a constant inside a copy of the code made per size (C++, Rust); an entry in a run-time type descriptor that unspecialised code reads (Swift's type metadata, Haskell's `KnownNat` dictionary, Scala's `ValueOf` argument); or a field in each object (X10's properties, Fortran's `LEN` parameters). Sources in § 6.
32	- Fortress's compiled path keeps generics at run time. The code generator writes one **template** class per generic, and the class loader **stamps** a class per instantiation the first time it is used, by rewriting the template's names (FACTS:18; `runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java`). The arguments are in the stamped class's name between **oxford brackets**: `Box⟦3⟧`. So every sized class already exists once per size, like a Rust copy, made at load time instead of compile time.
33	- Beside each class the run time keeps **RTTI** (run-time type information): a descriptor class per generic, `Box$RTTIc`, whose objects answer type tests and hand dispatch the static arguments of a value (`runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:94-139`; `reviews/mie-probes/dispatch-and-route-c.md § 1`). For a type argument the descriptor holds the argument's own descriptor, in a field with a getter. An **`opr` parameter** (an operator symbol as a static argument, `trait-parameters.tex:156-176`) gets none of that: its symbol is written into the descriptor class's name between **heavy angles**, `Op❮+❯$RTTIc` (`runtimeSystem/Naming.java:207-210, 1053-1066`).
34	- So the question is narrow. The size is already in the stamped class's name under both designs. The question is only whether the size's descriptor is a name (A) or an object (B).

81	## 6. The peers, by family
82	
83	- JVM. Java: a type parameter is an identifier with an optional bound, erased (JLS § 8.1.2, https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-8.html#jls-8.1.2); "Unlike generic types in other languages such as C# and Java, C++ templates support non-type parameters" (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/cpp/templates-cpp). Nothing is carried, so nothing costs; a size is a field.
84	- JVM. Kotlin: `typeParameter: [typeParameterModifiers] simpleIdentifier [':' type]`, no value parameter (https://kotlinlang.org/spec/syntax-and-grammar.html). As Java.
85	- JVM. Scala: literal types, `val one: 1 = 1`, and `ValueOf[T]` with `valueOf[T]`, "yielding the unique value of types with a single inhabitant" (SIP-23, https://docs.scala-lang.org/sips/42.type.html). On the erasing JVM the value reaches generic code as an implicit argument: a descriptor passed per call.
86	- Close to the metal. C++: a non-type argument "is passed in as a template argument at compile time and must be const or a constexpr expression", and each instantiation is its own class (Microsoft Learn, above). Nothing at run time; the size is a constant in the class's code.
87	- Close to the metal. Rust: `const N: usize` may be used "as a value in any runtime expression" and in types; an argument is a literal, a single-segment path or a braced const expression; `N + 1` in a type is refused (https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/generics.html). The compiler "stamps out a different copy of the code of a generic function for each concrete type", paid in compile time and binary size (https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/backend/monomorph.html). Nothing at run time.
88	- Close to the metal. Swift: SE-0452, "Implemented (Swift 6.2)": a reference to an integer generic parameter "evaluates the parameter as a value of type `Int`", and the runtime must "encode and interpret them as part of type metadata" (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0452-integer-generic-parameters.md). Specialised code sees a constant; unspecialised code reads the metadata. That is B's shape, and Swift needs it because unspecialised generic code exists.
89	- Scientific. Chapel: a `param` field or argument makes a generic, "A copy of the function is instantiated for each unique parameter", and `IntegerTuple(3)` and `IntegerTuple(2)` are distinct types (https://chapel-lang.org/docs/language/spec/generics.html). Arrays keep the rank as a param and the bounds in a run-time domain: "A domain expression may contain bounds which are evaluated at runtime" (https://chapel-lang.org/docs/language/spec/domains.html).
90	- Scientific. Fortran 2003: a derived type's `KIND` parameters are constants; its `LEN` parameters may be given at run time and live with the object (IBM XL Fortran, https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/xl-fortran-aix/16.1.0?topic=types-derived-type-parameters-fortran-2003). Extents are `LEN`-like: a field.
91	- Scientific. X10: classes take properties, "final instance fields", and a dependent type such as a rank-2 array is a constraint over them, checked by a constraint solver (Nystrom, Saraswat, Palsberg, Grothoff, OOPSLA 2008, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1449764.1449800). One field per object at run time.
92	- Scientific. Julia: values may be type parameters, `Array{T,N}`, `Val{N}`; "By passing `N` as a type-parameter, you make its 'value' known to the compiler", which specialises per value while the program runs; with a size computed at run time, `Val(n)` recreates "the same problem all over again", dynamic dispatch (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/performance-tips/). The nearest peer to this loader: code per value, made at run time.
93	- Typed functional. Haskell: `KnownNat` has "instances of the class for every concrete literal", `natVal` returns the number at run time, and `someNatVal` "converts an integer into an unknown type-level natural" (https://hackage-content.haskell.org/package/base-4.22.0.0/docs/GHC-TypeLits.html). Types are erased; a size travels as a dictionary; `someNatVal` is `NatReflect.reflect`.
94	- Typed functional. Idris 2: quantity 0 means a variable "is erased at run time"; a `Vect`'s length is kept only when used, where Idris 1 needed `n` "available at run time" (https://idris2.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/multiplicities.html).
95	- In one line: the peers that care about speed make a size a constant in specialised code (C++, Rust, Chapel, Julia) and keep a descriptor only where unspecialised code must read it (Swift, Haskell, Scala). This loader stamps every instantiation it runs (FACTS:18), so its sized code is always specialised: A is the specialised-only answer, B adds the descriptor.
