<!-- Established facts, one line each, with the source. Grouped by area. Read at session start; cite by area and line rather than restating in chat. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:95-129`).
- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.
- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (ledger row 69); making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which is not a ledger row and not on the worklist as a separate item (it falls under worklist item 2, compiler-path library parity).
- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64`, no `dadd`/`dmul` anywhere in the generated loop (shown in bytecode, `perf-probes/boxing/javap/`); arrays are library objects over `get`/`put`, not `double[]` (`repo-internals.md:129`).
- On microGPT-shaped array code boxing is the dominant representational cost, 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]` in Java models of the program's three kernels, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles: the compiler prelude lacks the array types, with `Array`, `Vector` and `Array3` undefined in `FlatArrays.fsi` (row 305, wider than row 72). On the interpreter, the only path that runs the kernels, 43.5% is the AST walk, 32.3% environment lookup, 5.2% type dispatch and 0% number representation (JFR on `krows`). The order that followed: an `RR64` array type in the compiler library (G2); the two one-line runtime defects (rows 302, 303, since fixed by rung 0); unboxing and `double[]`, designed into the first. A failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache (`258105b3e`; `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The boxing probe's scalar-loop reading, 156× primitive Java with boxing about 2% of it, is of the tree before rung 0's two fixes (rows 302, 303; `53362cb88`); of the costs it named, `countedseqloop`'s boxed indices and closure call (about 7%) and the representational rest (about 30%) are unaddressed (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed: the message is built only under the `debug` flag (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:248`; row 302; `53362cb88`; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip is fixed: the literal caches its `double` instead of re-parsing its text in `asRR64()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`; row 303; `53362cb88`; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The benchmark numbers on record from 2026-09-15 (`bench1t` 9.3441 s, `bench1h` 6.0732 s) were taken on a quieter machine; the 2026-09-17 before-run of the same unmodified tree measured 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s, so absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions and only a before/after pair taken in one session is (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars: the first `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler clears `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/`, and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`; the library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:170-179` restores it, about two minutes (observed 2026-09-17).
- The compiled path's bytecode cache can come up empty after a library-order rebuild that reports exit 0; re-running the same commands one at a time produced the jars (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
- Generic instantiations are stamped out at class-load time by ASM rewriting of template bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader.java`, `repo-internals.md:129`); whether `nat` parameters are baked into stamped classes is unprobed. Superseded 2026-09-24: a size is in the stamped class's name (`pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, `perf-probes/nat/java.md` § 1; `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`).
- Implicit parallelism: `for` is parallel unless every generator is `seq`; the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator are evaluated in parallel implicit threads (`tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`; row 265). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool; there is no explicit threading in any of our programs.
- The compile path's checker cannot check `nat` parameters at all (see "The checker and the one library" below). Sizes in types (`nat` parameters) are "instantiated at runtime" by the specification (`trait-parameters.tex`, natparams); they check shapes when a value is made or passed; no optimization is built on them anywhere. A `nat`-typed parameter does not unify statically with a run-time-built array (row 23); the interpreter matches at dispatch, and a mismatch reads "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (row 83). A literal size does unify (row 23's positive half).
- **The specification's own declaration of `Nothing` compiles on neither path, and the reason is name resolution, not codegen.** `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification/basic-lib/convenience.tex:49`) gives the identical single error from `fortress compile` and from `fortress walk`, both rc=255: `T is undefined`, at the `T` inside the extends clause (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-maybe/probes/WhereClauseNothing.fss`, `.txt`). A where clause on an object declaration does not bind a type variable used in that declaration's extends clause in either implementation. `CodeGen.forObjectDeclPrePass` would refuse the declaration a second time at codegen — `header.getWhereClause().isNone()` is one of its `canCompile` conditions (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:4088`) — but nothing reaches it. This is the mechanism behind `FortressLibrary.fss:1340-1341`'s "when we get where clauses working", and it is why both worlds must spell the empty case some other way.
- **An exported function fails exactly as an exported variable does when a component's name differs from the api it exports, and the failure is the repository's, not codegen's** (2026-09-20, rung X). `probes/FnApi.fsi`+`FnLib.fss`+`FnMain.fss` dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: FnApi`, alongside `P8Api$shared` and `P9Api$shared` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-export-var/probes/probes-preedit.txt:29,96,163`). Through the real entry points the divergence never reaches codegen at all: `fortress link P8Main` and `walk` on each of the three main components print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" (`probes/link-and-walk-preedit.txt:4-9,45-60`), so both execution paths assume the api and its implementing component share a name. The assumption is `Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`'s fallback to the api's own name (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/linker/Linker.java:72-76`) when nothing has been registered in its persisted map, and only the user can register one, by hand, through `LinkShell`'s `alink`/`clink` verbs (`linker/LinkShell.java:41-70`; `linker/README:28-40` describes the intended design). `Specification/basic/components/overview.tex:33-35` settles it — a reference to an imported api is "resolved to a component that exports that api" — and the team reserved the codegen half of the repair in three comments in one file (`CodeGen.java:411-441`, `:1856`, `:6599-6606`). Gated as an expected failure by `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test`.
- **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it** (2026-09-22, rung C, `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/probes/SpanAbsorb.fss` and `SpanAbsorb.txt`; ledger row 359). `createSpan` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Fortress.rats:145-157`) trims back over space characters only. A declaration ending in `end` is unaffected. So a comment-only edit to the library is not neutral at the syntax-tree level: rung C's widened three spans (the scalar block's first `-` in both files, `SUFFIX_SUM` in the `.fsi`), besides shifting every position below each insertion, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics must map positions back first (`compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py`, `remap-lines.py`). No answer changed.
- **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees** (rung I, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md`, section 4.1): `throw new FortressError((FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(name))` from inside a `builtinPrimitive` method reaches `Evaluator.forTry` unchanged (`MethodClosure.java:85-86` has no `catch`) and matches `catch e IntegerOverflow`; `Int.overflow()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:256-259`) is the helper and `WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException` the name. Measured by the 25 `overflows(...)` assertions of `ProjectFortress/tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, whose helper catches nothing but `IntegerOverflow`. Before this rung no native raised one; the interpreter's mapping of every other Java exception is unchanged (`FunctionClosure.java:188-196`), so row 336's division by zero and row 347's `Int.rc` still end the run.

## The checker and the one library

- Only 211 of `FortressLibrary.fss`'s 4,518 lines (4.7%) are the 108 `builtinPrimitive` native bindings; the rest is plain Fortress. Whole interpreter library: 427 bindings across nine files. The interpreter's glue classes take the evaluator's boxed values and cannot be reused by the compiled path; the compiler's natives are static Java methods, and `nativeHelpers/` already ships 355 of them, covering about 79 of the 108 by another name. Source: `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`, measured 2026-09-16.
- `fortress compile Library/FortressLibrary.fss` as it is: 1,417 errors, all in DISAMBIGUATE, all name collisions because both preludes are in scope; an artifact. With `FortressLibrary` made the prelude (a driver over `Shell`'s public entry points, no tracked file changed): disambiguation passes with zero errors; the type checker then reports 92 errors in the library's own apis (36 `X excludes Y but it extends Y`, 26 `types exclude each other`, 26 `Integral[\I\]` bound failures, in the comparison and numeric tower) and then **crashes: `Not yet implemented`** in `STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` (STypesUtil.scala:546-559) for `nat`, `int`, `bool`, `dim` and `unit` static parameters. Desugar and codegen are never reached. Source: `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`, measured 2026-09-16.
- **The Scala type checker does not implement `nat` static parameters at all**: a six-line program with a `nat` parameter fails on the compile path (`Not yet implemented` inferred, `ClassCastException` explicit) and runs on the interpreter. The interpreter's library has 81 such declarations, C4's vocabulary 30; `CompilerLibrary` has one, the empty `Matrix`. <!-- What Pavol has decided, stated, or already knows, with dates; in his words or a close paraphrase. Read at session start so that none of it is re-explained to him. Standing directives about how we work are in explorations/protocol.md and are not repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- The revival's toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression; Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources; "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability" (2026-09-15).
- The APL side quest began as a curiosity (2026-09-10), became a ladder to learn APL (09-11, he has not read the book), was redirected to native code, not an interpreter in an interpreter (09-12), and got microGPT as its target on 09-13; the ladder "was to keep you busy and expand the probe". The remaining APL ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued (09-15).
- Hoped for a diamond from the Hsu-style flat program; got "a few lumps of coal"; the rewrite (rung 4b) was to get closer, and the vocabulary is where any polishing happens.

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
- The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here"; this goes on the priority list (2026-09-15). The first measurement (the scalar loop) said boxing was about 2% of the gap; Pavol objected that the loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator) and asked for a fairer test; the fairer test agreed with him: on array-shaped code boxing is 6.3-6.5× and the dominant representational cost, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles at all today (FACTS, execution model). The order now on record: the compiler library's array type first, the two one-line runtime defects second, unboxing designed into the first.
- The type checker runs only on the compile path; he wants it usable on interpreter programs and considers that low-hanging fruit (2026-09-15). It is item 0.1 of `performance-roadmap.md` (2026-09-08), which the coordinator had not indexed; see FACTS, deficit.
- Hsu's critique of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".

## Decisions on record

- 2026-08-23, recovered from the transcript on 2026-09-23 (`coordinator/lineage.md`): the third-party Java 9 port gets no credit and no mention — "we can lose the porcupines credit since you seem to have not really been informed by their changes"; "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere"; the revival's toolchain was rebuilt from the original tree with a few mechanical fixes, the port only showed that a revival was possible. And his plan the same day, not carried out: rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main`. On 2026-09-23, told that CLAUDE.md's opening still described the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history: "This is incorrect. Where does this come from? Use archeology to find correct facts and correct the record" — corrected in CLAUDE.md, the other files left for his decision.
- 2026-09-14: C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
- 2026-09-15: redo rung 4 as the focused base (done); do the vocabulary swap with shared `nat` dimensions (in progress); the ledger is not split, two views are derived (done); the ledger review is the next major step after the swap; the remaining APL ground is closed.
- 2026-09-15: "fleshing out the standard library" is a very important task: first fix the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch, then extend the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them. Open question he has not answered: whether this means editing the sealed `Library/` (the standing rule is never; worklist item 4 "unseal the linear-algebra layer" names the rows) or building the layer in our own tree; the coordinator assumes our own tree until he says otherwise.
- 2026-09-16: the goal restated: finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed spec (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not redesign the language; the measuring stick is one program, microGPT compiled to bytecode and running fast; a pure-Java microGPT will be written later as the floor to measure against; the tree is tagged at the unsealing point and the next phase modifies the original sources with the lessons of the explorations.
- 2026-09-16: the mathematical notation (Fortify, the 2D rendering) is his verdict "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, and the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress. Do not spend work on it unless he asks.
- 2026-09-16: before unsealing he wants the territory map (`coordinator/map/`): repository and language architecture, the pipeline phases, test coverage per layer, the gaps on the path in order with the cost of leaving each, the development loop's slow spots, a touch-this-affects-that map, and where the design intent is written (papers, not only the spec).
- 2026-09-16: development-loop performance is a first-class concern; when an iteration waits too long on something, find the cause and fix it.
- 2026-09-17: the tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at `75cca6683` (the map's last commit); commits after it may edit the original sources. Order he accepted: the compile-path ladder baseline first (every interpreter test and the 29 not-working library tests through `fortress compile` and `run`, phase reached and missing names ranked), then the two one-line runtime fixes, then `nat` checking, then the compiler library grown from the team's own drafts, test-driven: every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and the full suite stays green.
- 2026-09-17, a standing preference Pavol stated twice in one session after two designs reached for a retreat: when something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch he refused bisection of commits — "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle he refused a stop — "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one". What still reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.
- 2026-09-17, clarified by Pavol when the batched-climb design asked whether that sentence fixed the gate's frequency: it does not. What it fixes is test-driven discipline and the permanence of checks — the worker writes the test first, **verifies that it actually fails**, then makes the fix, then proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on. The unacceptable process it rules out is the one-off validation script: proving once, by hand, that the interpreter and the compiler agree on a program and then going ahead without leaving a permanent check in the gate. Whether the suite is run per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per-batch is in line with the rule.
- Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run).

- 2026-09-18, after the coordinating session's container died: the work continues in the blinded run's container, on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it. Transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded` — "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts? I think it would just unnecessarily complicate the matters" — and the two lineages are joined at analysis time. The backup is repaired before anything else runs. The repair batch is re-run from the start, since recovering the dead run's agent state is not available. The recovery procedure is documented as a lesson about Claude Code in a remote container, kept with the backup documentation, not in the gap ledger.
- 2026-09-18, on the workflow before the repair batch is re-run: workers commit and push to their own `wip/` branches as they work — "perfectly reasonable. I'm giving you my explicit yes" — and the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls", with skeptics on Opus and the escalation when "we are returning back with a redesign"; the judge inherits the session's model so that running out of Fable credits means switching the session, not editing the script; workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof". Agreed to the three escalation points (a refusal, a stop, a red gate) and to no Fable pass before every edit.

- 2026-09-19, after climb batch 1 landed: the six process decisions for batch 2 are taken as `coordinator/process-decisions-review-1.md` amended them, on the coordinator's recommendation and Pavol's "go" (he did not read the full text: "Are there strong recommendations and clear wins … pick a good default? … go"): every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test; the eight script changes, a five-kilobyte gate summary diffed against the last, the gate run beside the review, no full logs committed, no rung-chain scheduling; the one-thread pin written into `fastTrack` and the four-thread `atomic` runs gating (a timeout re-run once); the `_WIcontains` key implemented in the harness; a ladder-regression stage over the measured pass list with the two microGPT programs held at their phase; and the six gaps the review found. `Maybe` stays as landed and `floor`/`ceiling` keep the float result; row 330 stays open as a note. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run still needs his explicit go.

- 2026-09-19: interpreter performance is irrelevant to every decision — "interpreter of Fortress, which is hundreds times slower than the Python interpreter, is irrelevant for any performance discussions"; "we cannot judge anything performance related in Fortress while we do not have a compiler". No edit to C4 for speed (the tuple-split measurement is an interpreter number only), and no performance decision of any kind until microGPT runs compiled.
- 2026-09-19, on the FlatArrays review's repair that turned `mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)` into `planeSum(mask, …)`: "NO. That's not Fortress!" The model's text is the notation the project exists for; an operator in it does not become a function call to satisfy the interpreter's overload check. The edit was stopped before it landed. Any repair that would change a line of the model is shown to him as a diff before it is built, and the vocabulary is repaired around the notation, not the other way round.
- 2026-09-19, answering the open question of 2026-09-15 (own tree or the sealed `Library/`): "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround; the library's own practice is the standard.
- 2026-09-19, on `coordinator/array-design.md`'s four questions: storage is `double[]`, unboxed — "we must go to double array for performance. There is again no question about this. If this should have been high performance language, it cannot be boxed." And the `nat` sizes are not sidestepped or layered in later: "I don't know [that] we can sidestep the nat issue. That is a central design point that they are using." ## The library's arrays and algebra

- `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` are the only sized array traits; `Array3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, …\]` carries no algebraic trait (row 292; `FortressLibrary.fsi:1465, 1583, 1657` since the library commits of climb batches 3 and 3.5).
- `Vector` and `Matrix` inherit `+`, `-`, unary `-` and `zero` from `AdditiveGroup`, nothing else; `×` reaches no array by design because juxtaposition is the inner product and the array traits exclude `AnyMultiplicativeRing` (rows 64, 109, 293); a carrier that extends the ring is accepted unchecked, changes juxtaposition to elementwise and breaks `+` (vocabulary review v02, v02b).
- The library's products are declared with shared `nat`s (`Matrix[\T,n,m\]` × `Matrix[\T,m,p\]`, `FortressLibrary.fsi:1508-1516`); C4's own products were not, which is habit; the focused base's `FlatArrays2` states them (twelve declarations including the per-rank elementwise `×` and `/`, 25 of 29 nats agreeing; 39 declarations), and a wrong-shape call is refused at dispatch, uncatchable for an overloaded name (row 83), as a unification error naming the nat for an unoverloaded one (`apl/mg/checks/mismatch_probe.out`).
- Two declarations of one name differing only in the element type, or a rank-specialised declaration beside an index-generic one, are refused at load ("at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types"; `apl/mg/checks/model_run.out.0`, `elemwise_nat_probe.out.0`); two apis' overloads of one name are checked as one family, so two vocabularies cannot stand in one component (`diag_fwd_two_vocabularies_rejected.out.0`).
- The shipped `RR64` does not satisfy the specification's algebraic bound `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` (vocabulary review, probe `v04b_groupbound.out.0`); `T extends Number` is the bound that works for every element type and rank (row 295).
- The library's scalar-extension block for `+ - MIN MAX` over arrays is generic since `02d09a39f` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4511-4521`, `.fsi:2550-2560`); no reshape, plane, gather, outer product or ravel exists in the library (vocabulary review, section A).
- An array is a trait with `get`/`put`; a view is an object implementing it over other storage, the language's own idiom; the library's row slice `m[i,:]` costs 5× a six-line user view; a diagonal as a `Matrix` view costs 13-54× the operator (vocabulary review v20, v07).
- The element type is `Number` only for `Vector`/`Matrix` (row 24); irrelevant to numeric microGPT, decisive for Run B's autodiff value and for APL characters.

## The territory map

- Tasks and transactions are implemented twice, `interpreter/evaluator/` and `runtimeSystem/`, independently (B.11). Row 302's fix is in the compiled world's copy only.
- `import java` also works on the interpreter path through `ForeignComponentWrapper` + `ClosureMaker`; no test uses it (B.12). Corrected 2026-09-20 (`perf-probes/prelude/import-java-interpreter.md`): wired and unfinished, it does not work; four gaps, all on the interpreter's side: `NamingCzar.fortLib` is fixed to the builtin api, which declares none of `ZZ32`/`RR64`/`JavaString` in that world (`NamingCzar.java:294-295`); a second `import java` from one package falls through `Driver.ensureApiImplemented` to a `ClassCastException` (`Driver.java:464-466`, "temp hack till we knit in natives properly"); the foreign name is never rewritten (`ForeignComponentWrapper.java:31,38`) and `BaseEnv.java:531-533` bugs on the qualified reference; and `ClosureMaker` emits a call into the compiler's `nativewrapper_cache`, which the interpreter neither writes nor loads. So one binding file cannot serve both worlds; the one-library variant is one shared text with one small builtin component per world behind a single api, which makes the api-to-differently-named-component link (ledger row 320's class-name half, `Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`) live work.
- Codegen refuses any declaration carrying a where clause or a contract (`CodeGen.java:2937, :2941, :4076, :4078, :4983, :4985`); not in the ledger (flagged, Pavol's call). `atomic <expr>` has no visitor, `atomic do … end` compiles; `spawn`, `label`/`exit`, object expressions, array literals and comprehensions, local function declarations have no visitor (`spec-to-implementation.md` §3).
- The checker (`IndexBuilder.scala:187-189`) refuses `type` aliases, `test` and `property` on both paths. Coercion is the one mechanism the compiler path has and the interpreter does not (no `Coercion`/`coerce` under `interpreter/`; row 19).
- **A generic object referenced without its static arguments is a static error on the compiled path, and the checker never consults the expected type for it** (2026-09-19, `explorations/compiler-probes/maybe-inference/inference.md`): `b: Box[\ZZ32\] = Box` fails with `Ill-formed type: Box`; a bare `Empty` as a call argument or a field default fails with `T is not in the kind env`, an internal `bug()` from `TypeAnalyzer.scala:766` reported at the declaration's span; the same forms with the static argument written compile and run on both paths. The decision is in the checker's `SVarRef` case, `typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:624-641`, whose `:639-640` keeps the uninstantiated type under the team's own `TODO: handle missing static args`; static-argument inference exists only for arrows (`STypesUtil.scala:912-930`, called from application and coercion), and a parametric empty case reached by `coerce` still fails bare. Under `walk` the same forms are `InterpreterBug: Couldn't figure out Empty[\T\](uninstantiated) <: Opt[\ZZ32\]`. Consequence for row 331: a parametric `Nothing[\T\]` would serve the corpus's `Nothing[\ZZ32\]` and never the specification's bare `= Nothing`; the non-parametric object plus `coerce` that the prelude uses is the only shape that compiles, so `Maybe` stays as landed. Incidental: `typecase` over a user-declared generic object crashes code generation (`Error trying to close method scope`, `CodeGen.java:2802`), row 340. Corrected the same day by the minimal reproducer (`compiler-probes/maybe-inference/probes/TcPlain.fss`): neither the generic object nor `typecase` alone is the trigger; a `typecase` used directly as a function or method body whose value needs an implicit coercion (`IntLiteral` to a declared `ZZ32`) makes ASM's stack-map frame computation fail (`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` under `MethodWriter.visitMaxs`, relabelled by the `catch (Throwable)` at `CodeGen.java:2801-2802`); wrapped in `do … end` the same body compiles, and every gated use of the shape returns `()` so never reaches the coercion.
- The gate: two corpora, hand-ported, sharing no file name; only `parser_tests/` is read by both; no test compares the paths on one program; interpreter tests pass on "no exception and no `fail` in output" (`FileTests.java:367-371`), compiler run tests on exit code plus `PASS`. `fortress.unittests.noopt=true` (`default_repository/configuration:51`) hides 226 tests and leaves the 43-file bytecode optimizer with zero. Every `testSystem` shard runs `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (`build.xml:1184`), so no gated test sees concurrency; `TransactionJUTest`'s multi-threaded half is commented out (`TestTask.java:43-44`). No `nat`-parameterised program is compiled or run; the cache round trip is not asserted (`ASTJUTest.java:654`). 121 `.fss` inside green directories are dark; `linker_tests`, `compiler_regressions`, `BirdyLib`, the `not_working_*` directories are orphaned (`map/test-coverage.md`).

## The container

- The process cost of the climbs and the batches — the eight-rung climb's wall clock and its gate share, the limits of parallelism on this box, and each batch's agents, tokens, tool calls and span — is measured in `explorations/coordinator/iteration-cost.md`, `coordinator/repair-batch-review.md` and the batch records; the conclusions it produced are in `POSITIONS.md` and in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, and the entries themselves are in `FACTS-history.md`.
- The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling kills long runs; check runs go under the `Monitor` tool (1800000 ms), sequential, nothing else running when a number is to be kept.
- The disk allowance fills with parser-generation temp directories: every run that imports a grammar generates a Rats! parser into a fresh `/tmp/fortress<random>rats` directory (`RatsUtil.getTempDir`, `syntax_abstractions/rats/RatsUtil.java:138-146`, via `IOUtil.createAndMarkTempDirectory`), 5.8 MB each, never deleted; 723 of them (4.2 GB) filled the allowance on 2026-09-15 and broke a worker's tool output mid-run ("no space left on device"). Deficit until fixed at the source (an edit under the sealed tree, or a `deleteOnExit`); mitigation in our tree: `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them when sourced, and `df` must be checked before any long run.
- The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling; `Monitor` for long runs (the microGPT-runs entry above).
- A container can be lost outright: the coordinating session of 2026-09-17 (`bdff267d-…`) died mid-workflow and could not be re-provisioned, because the branch it was created from was no longer found on the remote. Recovery moved into the blinded run's container, which already had the checkout and toolchain. Cost: four workflow agents (~798k tokens), their worktrees, and the 13 hours after the last transcript snapshot at 20:31. Everything through `2ab1d6d8` was pushed and safe, and `REPAIR-BATCH.md` kept the batch runnable. Mechanism, the three traps and the recovery procedure: `explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md`.
- The transcript backup fires on the main session's Stop, not on any agent's completion, and swallows all errors: a session inside one long turn is not being backed up and a failed push is silent. Workflow-agent transcripts were outside its globs until 2026-09-18; oversized transcripts now split at 64 MiB, and the wrapper packs loose objects because the clone ships `gc.auto=0`.
- **The Workflow harness runs two agents at once on this box** (measured 2026-09-18, four one-command agents in one `parallel()`: agents 0 and 1 started 19:14:08, agents 2 and 3 at 19:14:31 after the first pair finished at 19:14:23; `batched-climb-plan.md` §2). `model: 'opus'` in `agent()` resolves to a fixed model identifier, readable in each agent transcript's `message.model` field and not written here (protocol §4); an agent with no `model` inherits the session's. A subagent's floor is about 45k tokens before it does anything (183k for the four). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (33,022 tokens read by agents 1–3) and not the first user message (11,010 written by each), because a cache read lands only at a breakpoint the harness placed and a shared prefix inside one message is not one.
- The VM can be restarted under a live session with the disk intact: 2026-09-18 23:22 UTC, 25 minutes into the repair batch's re-run, kernel build string fc-v33 → fc-v37, one JVM running (16 GB, no swap, 4 CPUs: not a memory death). Worktrees, uncommitted edits and agent transcripts survived; the Workflow run and its agents did not, and a run is relaunched, never resumed; the `wip/` branches held every pushed milestone (`remote-container.md` § The 2026-09-18 restart).
- **A user interrupt of the coordinating session's turn kills a background Workflow run** (2026-09-19): climb batch 1's first run, `wf_a29fd04b-a9a`, launched 07:15 UTC, lost both its rung agents at 07:46:42, the second Pavol's interrupt cut the turn that a check-in trigger had just started; both agent transcripts end at that timestamp mid-work, no result line reached the journal, and the harness no longer knew the task. The Agent tool's workers are not affected (the review worker launched after the interrupt ran to completion). The `wip/` branches held F's three and M's three milestones and M's worktree its uncommitted report, so the relaunch at 08:25 from the same base continued under the prefix's continuation clause. Cost: about 40 minutes of two workers. Rule: while a Workflow runs, a check-in must not be interrupted mid-turn; and a batch is relaunched, never resumed, after any such death.
- **A manual compaction issued between turns leaves a running Workflow alive** (found 2026-09-19 by a worker in the archived transcript of session `bdff267d`, `transcripts` branch, parts file `001.jsonl`): the eight-rung climb's run `wf_73833dfb-d25` (launched 2026-09-17 06:00:57 UTC) survived two `/compact` commands, boundaries 10:47:33 (442,504 tokens before, 130 s) and 14:25:25 (177,831 tokens, 153 s), both typed while the session sat between turns; rung 5's commit landed 84 s after the first boundary, rungs 6-8 and the final re-run followed, and the run's completion notification arrived 14:39:09 with all eight rungs. This container's three compactions (09-18 18:38, 22:54; 09-19 06:38) coincided with no run. So the rule is: compact between turns, never send during a turn; the 09-19 death was a mid-turn interrupt, not a compaction. Caveat: that run's journal and agent transcripts are not in the backup, so the agents' survival is inferred from their commits and the session's own status turns.
- **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` is the one script every probe and gate runner sources, and it is verified from its new home** (2026-09-24, after `7bc8177a3` moved `experiment/` under `explorations/`): it derives `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own location two levels up, and re-running the two shadow experiments that source it, `reviews/mie-probes/forest/forest-run.sh` (423 s) and `perf-probes/nat/runtime/run-all.sh` (669 s), reproduced every committed count and probe output (`checker-count.txt`'s six counts, stock 103 and forest 37 among them, and captures r1-r5 byte-identical); the only differences were dates, timings and line numbers shifted by the library commits `c2b4e2c95` and `d6faad28f` made after the captures. astra's scripts keep their own `experiment/` paths, which name astra's tree.

## Where the work stands

The goal is to finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed specification (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not to redesign the language, with one program as the measuring stick: microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast (the root `CLAUDE.md` § Project goal; `coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-16).

The live thread is the one library. The interpreter's library (`FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`) is to become the library the compiler checks, and the work is to bring the compiled checker to accept it (`coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-21). Between that library and bytecode stands the checker, not desugaring or code generation; it reports 103 errors on the library, the count since climb batch 3, and a batch's count may only fall from it or declare its rise (`coordinator/FACTS.md` § The checker and the one library). Two decisions are in front of Pavol. First, the route on the checker's multiple instantiation exclusion, the rule that no type may be two different instantiations of one generic, which 61 of the 103 errors come from: route A keeps the rule and flattens the library's numeric tower, with the interpreter taught coercion; route B drops the rule; route C takes the forest rule of the group's 2012 patents; the brief recommends A (`reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md` § 1 and § 5). content.text:
Row 30 is recorded in POSITIONS, the docket and ledger row 333, and pushed (`8ba96424f`). Now the two results again, from the beginning.

## What the route C experiment measured

**The problem it was testing.** The library's number types form a tower: ZZ32 inside ZZ64 inside ZZ. Each level is declared as `Integral` applied to its own name. Because ZZ32 also extends ZZ64, ZZ32 ends up being `Integral[\ZZ32\]` and `Integral[\ZZ64\]` at the same time. The compiled checker has a rule that forbids exactly that: one type may not be two different applications of one generic. About 60 of the library's 103 checker errors come from this rule.

**The two routes.** Route A keeps the rule and flattens the tower, so no type is two things at once, and teaches the interpreter coercion to make up for the lost inheritance. Route C keeps the tower and softens the rule the way the team's 2012 patents describe: a type may be several applications of one generic as long as those applications line up in a chain, which the tower's do.

**What the worker did.** It built route C completely as a shadow beside the tree and ran it on small probe programs and on the whole library. Nothing touched `main`.

**Finding 1: the softened rule alone is unsafe.** Say ZZ64 has its own `+` and ZZ32 has its own faster `+`. A call written against the ZZ64 level but handed a ZZ32 value can land on the wrong body, and compiled code then crashes with a JVM linkage error. I have been calling this the specialisation hole. To close it, C needs a second rule the patents do not contain: at every level of a chain, the declarations must agree on their return types. The worker derived that rule from Naden's write-up. With it, the hole probes are refused at compile time instead of crashing at run time. Whole C is about 190 lines in five files.

**Finding 2: the new rule refuses part of the tower.** It refuses about 25 declaration pairs, mostly ZZ64's operators seen from the ZZ32 level, and MIN and MAX on Number and QQ. Making the whole tower pass needs two more things. Seven declarations the library never wrote, such as a TIMES on ZZ32. And the checker must treat `Integral[\ZZ32\]` and plain `ZZ32` as the same type. The patents allow that only when the trait says `comprises T`, meaning "nothing is this trait except T itself". Writing that clause on the eight traits that need it makes the checker overflow its stack, with or without route C. So full C is blocked behind a checker defect nobody has examined.

**Finding 3: three problems no checker rule reaches.** A chain whose middle level adds nothing of its own dies at run time in compiled code, because the code generator writes no forwarding method for a middle level. The checker picks the top of a chain where the interpreter picks the bottom, so the two paths can answer differently on one program. And the interpreter refuses the specialised pairs outright and overflows on `comprises T` the same way. Each is separate work in the code generator or the interpreter.

**Finding 4: the cheap C gives up the middle of the tower.** C-lite allows a specialised body only at the bottom of a chain. It refuses ZZ64's operators and the MIN family on Number and QQ. In plain terms, the middle levels could not have their own fast bodies. That is the opposite of what you said matters: specialisation is a must.

**Finding 5: what switching to C later would cost.** C's checker half laid over a flattened library gives exactly the stock checker's errors, so that half can be added at any time. But I told you the reversal was one library rung in reverse, and that was too cheap. It also needs the call-site fix, the code generator's forwarding method, interpreter work, a way past the overflow, and the seven declarations. The correction is in FACTS.

In one sentence: C can be built and its checker half is cheap, but full C is blocked on a checker overflow and needs code-generator and interpreter work the record never counted, while the cheap C loses specialisation where the tower needs it most.

## What the size probes found

**The setting.** A size in a type, the 3 in `Vector[\RR64, 3\]`, is a `nat` parameter. The shadow work taught the checker to handle them. The open question was what the run time does with the 3. Compiled generic code is a template, and the loader stamps out one class per use, named with the arguments, so `Vec⟦3⟧` is a class. Design A treats a size the way the run time already treats an operator passed as a static argument: a piece of the class name and nothing more. Design B gives each size literal a tiny run-time object, so a size is a real value the run time can hold and pass, as a type argument is.

**The brief's condition.** It recommended A only if "a dispatched overload arm generic in a size" needs no more under A than reading the size out of a class name. The words: overloading is several functions under one name, chosen by argument type. When the choice cannot be made at compile time, because the argument is typed `Any`, compiled code chooses at run time by testing the value's class. That chooser is the dispatcher, and each candidate function is an arm. An arm generic in a size is one written for any size, `f[\nat s\](v: Vec[\s\])`, next to arms for fixed sizes and a catch-all. Ledger row 214 has this shape working in the interpreter.

**Probe one, that arm.** Under A the dispatcher tests whether the value belongs to a class named with the arm's own letter, `Vec⟦s⟧`. No such class ever exists, so the test always fails and the catch-all is chosen. Wrong answer, silently. The fix is 70 to 90 lines by reading, not built, with two design questions inside it. Under B the dispatcher refused to compile any sized arm at all, but 29 lines fix that and all four probe programs answer right. So the brief's condition failed, and its default A fell with it.

**Probe two, the fourth gap.** A method inside a sized object reads its own size, `len() = s`. Under A the object's class was named with the template's letter instead of the number, so the read failed. Seven lines in the loader fix it, but they change how every template's constants are handled, take a branch the team's own comment calls a problem, and have not been through the gate. Under B there is no such gap.

**Probe three, a type test on a size.** Asking at run time "is this a `Vec[\3\]`" works under both designs.

**A find that matters whichever design wins.** The checker rung of the size wall refuses that overload set, because it throws every size parameter away before comparing two overloads. Four lines fix it, and they go into that rung's brief.

**What A still has.** A size in an extends clause costs it nothing, and it needs no class per size literal. B has to generate one class per distinct literal, about 30 unwritten lines; the library uses four literals in 85 places. Built and unbuilt lines as they stand: A has 35 built and 70 to 90 not built; B has 60 built and about 30 not built. Both need the same 25 lines for a size used as a value, and the checker's four.

**Not settled under either.** The inner product's shared size: `DOT` takes two vectors of one size, and something must check at dispatch that both sizes match. And a bound the desugarer gives every size parameter, `extends Object`, which B's dispatcher happens to skip.

In one sentence: A's recommendation rested on a condition the measurement broke; B was right on everything probed with fewer unbuilt lines, and A's remaining advantage is the classes per size literal it saves.

Both decisions are ready as asks, one per message, each with my recommendation. The route ask comes first unless you say otherwise.

## 1. The flat world in five lines

- The flat world is route A. Today every number sits on one chain, `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: AnyIntegral <: QQ <: RR64 <: Number` (keep, terms). Under A the links go: `ZZ32` is no longer a `ZZ64`, nor `ZZ64` a `ZZ`, nor an integer a `QQ`, nor `QQ` an `RR64`; the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` become siblings under `Number`, and `AnyIntegral` stays the integers' common parent (keep § 1; the sketch :6

content.text:
The route ask.

**What we decide.** Which route the compiled checker takes on the rule that no type may be two applications of one generic, the rule about 60 of the library's 103 errors come from. Route A keeps the rule and flattens the tower. Route C keeps the tower and softens the rule as the patents describe.

**What A does, in three pieces of work.**

- **The interpreter learns coercion.** The specification lets a wider type declare a `coerce` that converts a narrower value when nothing else fits. The compiled path has this, the interpreter does not. The rung adds it at the interpreter's dispatch, about 150 to 200 lines in six Java files. Route A is recorded and pushed (`a00710be9`). The size ask.

**What we decide.** How the compiled run time carries a size, the 3 in `Vector[\RR64, 3\]`, once the checker accepts sizes. Design A: a size is a piece of the stamped class's name and nothing more, the path an operator passed as a static argument already takes. Design B: each size literal gets a tiny run-time object of its own, so a size is a value the run time can hold, pass and compare, as a type argument is.

**What B does.** The compiler emits one small class per distinct size literal a program uses, loaded on demand. The dispatcher, the loader's extends-clause piece and the size-reading methods then treat a size exactly as they treat a type argument. Of that, 60 lines are built and measured under the shadow; the piece that emits the class per literal is about 30 lines by reading, not built, and mechanical. The library uses four literals.

**What A does.** The loader exempts sizes from needing a run-time class, and everything that needs the size as a value reads it back out of a class name. Of that, 35 lines are built. The dispatcher's fix is 70 to 90 lines by reading, not built, and carries two design questions that would need answering first. Its fourth-gap fix, 7 lines, changes how every template's constants are handled and takes a loader branch the team's own comment calls a problem.

**What both need.** The 25 lines for a size used as a value, `s` inside a body, built and equal under both. The checker's 4-line fix, in the checker rung's brief either way. And one open item under both: the inner product's shared size, two vectors of one size checked to match at dispatch, unmeasured.

**What it produces.** With B, the four dispatch programs answer right, a size-generic arm reads its size, a sized object reads its own size, and a type test on a size works. With A, the same only after the two unbuilt pieces and their questions.

**What it touches.** The compiler's code generator, the overload dispatcher and the two loader files under `ProjectFortress/src/`, on the compiled path only. Nothing in the library, nothing in the interpreter, nothing the checker rung touches, so the checker rung goes into batch 4 whichever design you choose.

**What it costs.** One rung, the run-time size rung, in the batch after batch 4, briefed from the probes and gated by the five existing sized compiler tests plus new ones for the four probe programs.

**What a yes to B commits you to.** A class per size literal in every compiled program, which is the design where sizes and types are the same kind of thing at run time. That is also the shape the array work needs later, a size the run time can compare when a `double[]` sits under a sized vector.

**What a yes to A commits you to.** Two design questions decided before the rung is briefed, the loader change through the gate, and sizes staying a special case that every new run-time feature has to parse out of a name.

My recommendation: design B.

content.text:
You are thinking in the right space, and the name you are after is the nine steps of protocol § 6: refresher, what each path does today measured, what the specification says, where it sits beside the other kinds, what the library already does, the peers by family, the history in the commits, the derivation from your principle, then the decision in your words. The size brief already follows those steps (`explorations/reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`), but it was written before the probes, so its data is stale where the probes changed it. One Opus worker is revising it now with the probes' data and a new section that measures the run-time cost, and it writes the measurement note beside the probes. It launched at 14:53 UTC. Nothing is committed until I review it, and the size decision waits for it.

Meanwhile, the plain answers as far as the record supports them. What is measured is marked; the rest is read from the mechanism and the worker is measuring it.

**What A resembles.** Operators. Fortress lets a generic take an operator as a static argument, `Op[\+\]`. The run time carries such an argument as a symbol inside the stamped class's name and gives it no run-time descriptor of its own. Design A extends that exemption to sizes. That is the existing mechanism you remembered.

**What B's classes are and what they cost.** For each distinct size literal a program uses, B makes one small class that holds the integer, made when the loader first meets that size and kept for the program's life. The cost is one class load per distinct size, once, a few hundred bytes each. The library uses four literals. Measured: start-up under A and B was the same within noise.

**Why the hot path is the same under both.** Under both designs the code that does the work is the stamped class, `Vec⟦RR64,3⟧`, an ordinary JVM class whose methods the JIT compiles like any Java method. Inside its body the size is emitted as the constant 3, under both designs, by the value-position piece. B's small class is consulted only where the run time needs the size as a datum: choosing among overloads by size at a dispatched call, or making a new sized instantiation from inside generic code. At those same places A has to parse the number out of the class name's text, which is more work, not less. So A is lighter only in creating no classes; on the hot path they are equal; where a size is read at run time, B is the lighter one. This paragraph is by reading. The worker times a hot loop under both and shows the bytecode.

**Shape checks, where and how often.** At compile time: the checker, now that the shadow taught it sizes, verifies that the shared dimension of a matrix product matches, and refuses a mismatch before anything runs. content.text:
You are right that the name carries the information under both designs, and that decoding a name is cheap and widely done. That is not what the two designs differ on. Both stamp the class `Vec⟦RR64,3⟧`, both keep the 3 in that name, and under both the code inside that class has the 3 as a constant. The difference is what the run time holds beside the name when it has to reason about a static argument as a value.

**How this run time already works for types.** For every type argument, the compiled run time keeps a small descriptor object, its run-time type information. All of the generic machinery is written against those objects: the dispatcher reads a value's arguments through them, the closure loader receives them to stamp the right arm, generic code passes them on when it instantiates something with its own parameters, and type tests inside generic code use them. Names are used for identity and for loading; objects are used for reasoning. That is the same split Swift makes, as far as I know it: mangled names are the compact spelling in the binary, decoded once into metadata objects that the run time then passes around, never demangled on every generic call. I say that from memory of Swift's design, not from a check in this session.

**What A and B decide.** Sizes today have no such object. B gives a size the same object a type has, so every existing path carries it unchanged. That is why the dispatcher fix was 29 lines and then all four programs were right. A keeps sizes name-only, so every place the run time needs a size as a value has to get its own separate route: decode the name in the dispatcher, carry the result through the closure loader by a new channel, add getters some other way. Those are the two design questions inside A's unbuilt 70 to 90 lines. The fourth gap was another instance of the same thing: the descriptor could not name its object class correctly because A's size had no object to substitute.

**Why B's object is a class per literal, not just a number.** The loader reaches every descriptor by its class name and substitutes names when it stamps a template. A class per literal is the shape that fits that machinery with no new special case. It is a holder for one integer, loaded once.

**So what is being weighed.** Not run-time cost. Whether a size is the same kind of thing as a type inside the run time, carried by the machinery that already exists, or a second kind of thing with its own plumbing added feature by feature. The probes found A failing at two places for that reason, and the array work will add more places that need a size as a value, the shared dimension of a product among them.

Your instinct that A is lighter holds for one thing only: it makes no classes. The worker is measuring what that is worth in bytes and milliseconds, and what a dispatched call costs under B.

**What it does with a size in a type, today.** The compiler mangles a size into
the instantiation name: `NamingCzar` maps `KindNat` and each `IntArg` to the
tag `Naming.XL_INTNAT` (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:1826-1832`, `:1888-1910`).
Nothing reads it back. The runtime's generic RTTI class holds one field per
static parameter, all typed as type RTTI, and the only kind the runtime
consults is `opr` (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1600-1622`;
`Naming.java:95-108`); `XL_INTNAT` is declared at `Naming.java:213` and that is
its only runtime mention. Measured consequence: a `nat` used in *value*
position compiles to a `getstatic` of a class the loader cannot produce and
dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError`
(`array-design-review.md` §1b, probe 6). And the code generator refuses a size
in an `extends` clause before that, with
`CompilerError("Only emitting RTTI for types right now")`
(`CodeGen.java:5793`).

Section 6 in one paragraph: the size is mangled into the instantiation name
(`NamingCzar.java:1826-1832`, `:1888-1910`) and nothing reads it back — the
runtime consults only the operator kind (`Naming.java:95-108`), the generic
RTTI class has no size field (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1600-1622`), a
size in an `extends` clause is refused outright
(`CodeGen.java:5793`), and a size in value position compiles to a reference the
loader cannot satisfy (`array-design-review.md` §1b, probe 6). So the first
sized object that compiles will need work in Java after the checker work in
Scala; the review counts at least three gated batches where the design counted
---JAVA---

  `CodeGen.java:5784` must push the size in the extends-clause path, about 10: **3 files, about 60 lines of code, 17 of them written and
  working.**

It makes sense, and you have put your finger on the thing my asks compressed away. The answer to your direct question first.

**There is an existing run-time object, and it already has the slot.** Every stamped type, `Vec⟦RR64,3⟧`, has a descriptor object with one slot per static parameter, all typed as references to other descriptors. The team's code generator already counts a size among those parameters, so the descriptor's factory already takes an argument for the 3 (`CodeGen.java:5317-5328`). What is missing is not the slot. It is an object to put in it, because 3 has no descriptor today, and the run time fills every slot with a descriptor found by class name. That is what B adds: a descriptor for the number. So your "of course, extend the run-time object" is design B, and B is what the team's own code assumes.

**What "class per number" means.** The run time finds a descriptor by its class name and the descriptor must answer that name. So the descriptor for 3 lives in a class named `3$RTTIc`, a holder for one integer, made by the loader the first time a program uses 3 as a size, one holder per distinct number used as a size in the program. Nothing in arithmetic points to it. The 3 in a loop body is a constant under both designs. The holder is only what sits in the type descriptor's slot, so the dispatcher and the closure loader can read a value's size the way they read its element type.

**Why A was discussed at all.** The run time has one exception to the descriptor rule: an operator passed as a static argument is baked into the class name with no descriptor. The first probe worker built A, sizes as a second such exception, at fewer lines than B. A Sonnet archaeology worker is now on your question, launched at 15:16 UTC, reading history only, output beside the size notes. Two things I can say now, and what I cannot.

**What an operator argument is, and why it plausibly got no descriptor.** An operator static parameter is the name of an operator, `+`, not a type. 131 explorations/perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md
<!-- Why the compiled path treats an `opr` static parameter differently from a `nat`/`type` one, and how that split entered the tree. Written for Pavol, 2026-09-24, by a delegated worker from a read-only pass over the git history, the specification and the interpreter; nothing was built or run. -->

# Why operators are different, and how that came about

## 1. The commits, in order

The interpreter's operator parameter is the oldest of the three mechanisms.
David Chase (`dr2chase`) opened it within the project's first year:
`1d618873a` "First cut at opr parameters, including tests" (2007-08-14),
after `35a704241`/`b7e67e060` the same week. Its name-substitution
mechanism (§2) was reworked once: `1fefb37c7` "Replaced OprInstantiator
reflection-visitor with a NodeUpdateVisitor" (2008-09-04).

The compiled path's version is a single, continuous effort by the same
author, opened more than four years later and closed in about ten weeks:

- `a5a06c65c` "Some steps towards opr parameters…" (2011-12-08) adds
  `LEFT_HEAVY_ANGLE`/`RIGHT_HEAVY_ANGLE` — "marks Opr parameters in RTTI
  types" — and `oprArgAnnotatedRTTI`, the bracket-name channel, before any
  of the run time's other kind-handling exists.
- `3b7bda65e` "More SMOPing towards opr parameters" (2012-01-13) deletes a
  block of per-kind Unicode dingbats (bool, dim, nat, opr, type, unit) each
  marked "seem to be unused", replacing all six at once with the string
  tags `XL_BOOL`/`XL_INTNAT`/`XL_OPR`/`XL_TYPE`/`XL_UNIT`/`XL_DIM`
  (`Naming.java:212-217`) — `opr` and `intnat` born as siblings, same block.
- `b2fe1437e`, same day, "Refactoring to get opr-static-param data
  available for RTTI class creation".
- `bcf08dae8` "More work in opr parameters, still busted somehow in
  instantiation" (2012-01-18) adds `isOprKind` (`Naming.java:95-109`, in
  the `XlationData` inner class) — the run time's *only* per-kind
  predicate, used to leave `opr` out of the RTTI machinery. No reason is
  given beyond "still busted".
- `49e0373b8` "Working towards instantiating RTTI for opr-parameterized
  types" (2012-01-26) adds `RTTI.java` itself, the abstract descriptor
  class every type's descriptor now extends: the general descriptor
  mechanism was built to make the `opr` case work, and ended up serving
  every other kind too.
- `0b4584c03`/`8af8941d9` (01-27, 01-29) "Closer to…"; `fb32dcc9d`
  "Initial opr parameter test working…" (01-30) closes the run.
  `726d806e0` (01-24, Tristan King) is the one commit by someone else.

**Sizes were not part of this design.** `XL_INTNAT` is a same-commit
sibling of `XL_OPR` (`3b7bda65e`) but gets none of the rest: no
heavy-angle channel, no `isOprKind`-style exclusion, ever. A `nat` static
parameter defaults into the same "every static parameter gets an RTTI
field" treatment as a `type` parameter (`InstantiatingClassloader.java
:1600-1622`) — not a decision made for a size, but the absence of one:
nothing ever carved sizes out the way `opr` was carved out. The size probes
(`perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md`, `runtime.md`) later found this default
wrong for a literal used in value position.

## 2. What an operator parameter is for

The specification says an operator parameter is not a value channel.
`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:173-174`: "Unlike other static
parameters, operator parameters may be used in both type context and value
context" — but "value context" means as the *name* of an operator method
to call directly (`x MYOP y`), never as a value handed to a function.
`:224-226`: "any declarations that may be associated with an actual
operator name that is passed for an operator parameter are *irrelevant* to
the behavior of the operator parameter… the subtrait inherits methods
whose names are the actual operator names instead of the operator
parameter names." An operator argument is a compile-time synonym,
substituted into the declaring trait's own method names at instantiation.

The interpreter matches this, and had since 2007. An operator argument
evaluates to an `FTypeOpr`, a named, memoized `FType`
(`interpreter/evaluator/types/FTypeOpr.java:44-46`) whose `unifyNonVar` is
simply `bug(…, "Unimplemented -- unify opr parameter …")` — never needed,
since unification on an operator never happens. `EvalType.forOpArg`
(`EvalType.java:316-317`) is exactly this: `return
FTypeOpr.make(NodeUtil.nameString(b.getId()));`. Instantiating a generic
with an operator argument, `FTypeGeneric.Factory.make`
(`FTypeGeneric.java:156-180`) pulls every `opr` argument *out* of the
arguments that identify the instantiation, builds a name-to-name map, and
hands it to `OprInstantiaterVisitor` to rewrite the trait/object's own AST,
substituting the actual operator's name throughout the body — the same
idea `oprArgAnnotatedRTTI` re-derives on the compiled path four years
later, from the same author.

By contrast `trait-parameters.tex:83-86` on `nat`/`int`: "These parameters
are instantiated at runtime with numeric values… may be used… to appear in
any context that a variable of type N32 can appear, except that it cannot
be assigned to." A size is specified as a genuine run-time value; an
operator is specified as a compile-time name. They were never meant to be
treated alike — the compiled path's present sameness (both fall into the
RTTI-bearing default) is an accident of what got built, not a reading of
the spec.

## 3. Does the run time ever need an operator as a value?

No site was found, interpreter or compiled path, where an operator
argument is dispatched on, compared, or type-tested at run time. The
compiled path's own comment says as much where it builds a generic RTTI
factory: `InstantiatingClassloader.java:2683`, "Push nulls for opr
parameters in the factory call" — an operator's slot in the RTTI
constructor is filled with a null, because nothing downstream reads it.
Name substitution at stamping — baking the operator's name into the
mangled class/method name, once, at instantiation — is everything the
mechanism does with it, on both paths, in every commit found.

No file in `Papers/`, and no comment longer than a line or two anywhere in
`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/*.java`, discusses
unifying `opr` with the other kinds or names its RTTI exclusion as a
considered choice; `isOprKind`'s commit message reads as debugging, not
design. `Specification/basic-lib/`'s "big operators" (`BIG SUM`,
`__bigOperator` in `FortressLibrary.fss:1121`) are a reduction syntax over
ordinary operator methods; they do not touch operator static parameters.

## 4. The worker's reading, not a decision

author, opened more than four years later and closed in about ten weeks:

  types" — and `oprArgAnnotatedRTTI`, the bracket-name channel, before any
  of the run time's other kind-handling exists.

  block of per-kind Unicode dingbats (bool, dim, nat, opr, type, unit) each
  marked "seem to be unused", replacing all six at once with the string
  tags `XL_BOOL`/`XL_INTNAT`/`XL_OPR`/`XL_TYPE`/`XL_UNIT`/`XL_DIM`
  (`Naming.java:212-217`) — `opr` and `intnat` born as siblings, same block.
- `b2fe1437e`, same day, "Refactoring to get opr-static-param data
  available for RTTI class creation".
- `bcf08dae8` "More work in opr parameters, still busted somehow in
  instantiation" (2012-01-18) adds `isOprKind` (`Naming.java:95-109`, in
  the `XlationData` inner class) — the run time's *only* per-kind
  predicate, used to leave `opr` out of the RTTI machinery. No reason is
  given beyond "still busted".
- `49e0373b8` "Working towards instantiating RTTI for opr-parameterized
  types" (2012-01-26) adds `RTTI.java` itself, the abstract descriptor

content.text:
The archaeology landed and is committed (`ceecf70dd`, `explorations/perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md`). The answer to your three questions, in plain words.

**How the split came about.** One person, David Chase. He built operator parameters into the interpreter in the project's first year, 2007, as name substitution: an operator argument is pulled out of the instantiation's arguments and its name is written into the body. Four years later, over ten weeks from December 2011 to January 2012, he built the compiled path's version the same way: a name channel in the class name, and a single predicate that leaves operators out of the descriptor machinery. The commit that adds that predicate says only "still busted", so no design reason is on record. The descriptor base class every type's descriptor extends was written in that same run, to make the operator case work, and ended up serving every kind. Sizes got their tag in the same commit as operators and were then never touched: no channel, no exclusion. They fell into the descriptor treatment by default, not by a decision either way.

**Why operators are different.** The specification says so. An operator parameter is a compile-time name, substituted into the declaring trait's method names, and the declarations of the actual operator are "irrelevant". A size parameter is the opposite: "instantiated at runtime with numeric values", usable wherever a variable can appear. Both paths follow that for operators: nothing anywhere dispatches on, compares or type-tests an operator argument, and in the compiled descriptor factory the operator's slot is filled with a null that nothing reads. So the two kinds differ in what the run time must do with them, and unifying them would build a descriptor for a thing the language defines as having no run-time identity.

**Should we unify.** No, and not now. Nothing in either library and nothing on the microGPT path uses an operator parameter. The question goes into a ledger row with this note beside it, taken up if something on the path ever needs one. It is not a nine-step question, since the specification already answers the semantic part.

**One flag.** The worker's closing reading favours design A for sizes, on the ground that a size's one real need is value position. That weighs the wrong thing: value position costs the same under both designs, and the probes' finding was the other need, reading a size from a value's type at a dispatched call, where A fails. The specification's own words, a size is a run-time value, point the same way as the probes. That is my reading against the worker's, marked as such in FACTS, and the size ask still waits for the revised brief, which is in flight.
