# Facts on record

## Execution model

- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:95-129`).
- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.
- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (ledger row 69); making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which is not a ledger row and not on the worklist as a separate item (it falls under worklist item 2, compiler-path library parity).
- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64`, no `dadd`/`dmul` anywhere in the generated loop (shown in bytecode, `perf-probes/boxing/javap/`); arrays are library objects over `get`/`put`, not `double[]` (`repo-internals.md:129`).
- On microGPT-shaped array code boxing is the dominant representational cost, 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]` in Java models of the program's three kernels, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles: the compiler prelude lacks the array types, with `Array`, `Vector` and `Array3` undefined in `FlatArrays.fsi` (row 305, wider than row 72). On the interpreter, the only path that runs the kernels, 43.5% is the AST walk, 32.3% environment lookup, 5.2% type dispatch and 0% number representation (JFR on `krows`). The order that followed: an `RR64` array type in the compiler library (G2); the two one-line runtime defects (rows 302, 303, since fixed by rung 0); unboxing and `double[]`, designed into the first. A failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache (`258105b3e`; `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The boxing probe's scalar-loop reading, 156× primitive Java with boxing about 2% of it, is of the tree before rung 0's two fixes (rows 302, 303; `53362cb88`); of the costs it named, `countedseqloop`'s boxed indices and closure call (about 7%) and the representational rest (about 30%) are unaddressed (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed: the message is built only under the `debug` flag (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:248`; row 302; `53362cb88`; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip is fixed: the literal caches its `double` instead of re-parsing its text in `asRR64()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`; row 303; `53362cb88`; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`) (full entry in FACTS-history.md).
- The benchmark numbers on record from 2026-09-15 (`bench1t` 9.3441 s, `bench1h` 6.0732 s) were taken on a quieter machine; the 2026-09-17 before-run of the same unmodified tree measured 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s, so absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions and only a before/after pair taken in one session is (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars: the first `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler clears `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/`, and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`; the library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:170-179` restores it, about two minutes (observed 2026-09-17).
- The compiled path's bytecode cache can come up empty after a library-order rebuild that reports exit 0; re-running the same commands one at a time produced the jars (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
- Generic instantiations are stamped out at class-load time by ASM rewriting of template bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader.java`, `repo-internals.md:129`); whether `nat` parameters are baked into stamped classes is unprobed. Superseded 2026-09-24: a size is in the stamped class's name (`pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, `perf-probes/nat/java.md` § 1; `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`).
- Implicit parallelism: `for` is parallel unless every generator is `seq`; the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator are evaluated in parallel implicit threads (`tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`; row 265). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool; there is no explicit threading in any of our programs.
- The compile path's checker cannot check `nat` parameters at all (see "The checker and the one library" below). Sizes in types (`nat` parameters) are "instantiated at runtime" by the specification (`trait-parameters.tex`, natparams); they check shapes when a value is made or passed; no optimization is built on them anywhere. A `nat`-typed parameter does not unify statically with a run-time-built array (row 23); the interpreter matches at dispatch, and a mismatch reads "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (row 83). A literal size does unify (row 23's positive half).
- **The specification's own declaration of `Nothing` compiles on neither path, and the reason is name resolution, not codegen.** `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification/basic-lib/convenience.tex:49`) gives the identical single error from `fortress compile` and from `fortress walk`, both rc=255: `T is undefined`, at the `T` inside the extends clause (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-maybe/probes/WhereClauseNothing.fss`, `.txt`). A where clause on an object declaration does not bind a type variable used in that declaration's extends clause in either implementation. `CodeGen.forObjectDeclPrePass` would refuse the declaration a second time at codegen — `header.getWhereClause().isNone()` is one of its `canCompile` conditions (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:4088`) — but nothing reaches it. This is the mechanism behind `FortressLibrary.fss:1340-1341`'s "when we get where clauses working", and it is why both worlds must spell the empty case some other way.
- **An exported function fails exactly as an exported variable does when a component's name differs from the api it exports, and the failure is the repository's, not codegen's** (2026-09-20, rung X). `probes/FnApi.fsi`+`FnLib.fss`+`FnMain.fss` dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: FnApi`, alongside `P8Api$shared` and `P9Api$shared` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-export-var/probes/probes-preedit.txt:29,96,163`). Through the real entry points the divergence never reaches codegen at all: `fortress link P8Main` and `walk` on each of the three main components print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" (`probes/link-and-walk-preedit.txt:4-9,45-60`), so both execution paths assume the api and its implementing component share a name. The assumption is `Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`'s fallback to the api's own name (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/linker/Linker.java:72-76`) when nothing has been registered in its persisted map, and only the user can register one, by hand, through `LinkShell`'s `alink`/`clink` verbs (`linker/LinkShell.java:41-70`; `linker/README:28-40` describes the intended design). `Specification/basic/components/overview.tex:33-35` settles it — a reference to an imported api is "resolved to a component that exports that api" — and the team reserved the codegen half of the repair in three comments in one file (`CodeGen.java:411-441`, `:1856`, `:6599-6606`). Gated as an expected failure by `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test`.
- **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it** (2026-09-22, rung C, `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/probes/SpanAbsorb.fss` and `SpanAbsorb.txt`; ledger row 359). `createSpan` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Fortress.rats:145-157`) trims back over space characters only. A declaration ending in `end` is unaffected. So a comment-only edit to the library is not neutral at the syntax-tree level: rung C's widened three spans (the scalar block's first `-` in both files, `SUFFIX_SUM` in the `.fsi`), besides shifting every position below each insertion, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics must map positions back first (`compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py`, `remap-lines.py`). No answer changed.
- **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees** (rung I, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md`, section 4.1): `throw new FortressError((FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(name))` from inside a `builtinPrimitive` method reaches `Evaluator.forTry` unchanged (`MethodClosure.java:85-86` has no `catch`) and matches `catch e IntegerOverflow`; `Int.overflow()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:256-259`) is the helper and `WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException` the name. Measured by the 25 `overflows(...)` assertions of `ProjectFortress/tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, whose helper catches nothing but `IntegerOverflow`. Before this rung no native raised one; the interpreter's mapping of every other Java exception is unchanged (`FunctionClosure.java:188-196`), so row 336's division by zero and row 347's `Int.rc` still end the run.

## The checker and the one library

- Only 211 of `FortressLibrary.fss`'s 4,518 lines (4.7%) are the 108 `builtinPrimitive` native bindings; the rest is plain Fortress. Whole interpreter library: 427 bindings across nine files. The interpreter's glue classes take the evaluator's boxed values and cannot be reused by the compiled path; the compiler's natives are static Java methods, and `nativeHelpers/` already ships 355 of them, covering about 79 of the 108 by another name. Source: `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`, measured 2026-09-16.
- `fortress compile Library/FortressLibrary.fss` as it is: 1,417 errors, all in DISAMBIGUATE, all name collisions because both preludes are in scope; an artifact. With `FortressLibrary` made the prelude (a driver over `Shell`'s public entry points, no tracked file changed): disambiguation passes with zero errors; the type checker then reports 92 errors in the library's own apis (36 `X excludes Y but it extends Y`, 26 `types exclude each other`, 26 `Integral[\I\]` bound failures, in the comparison and numeric tower) and then **crashes: `Not yet implemented`** in `STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` (STypesUtil.scala:546-559) for `nat`, `int`, `bool`, `dim` and `unit` static parameters. Desugar and codegen are never reached. Source: `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`, measured 2026-09-16.
- **The Scala type checker does not implement `nat` static parameters at all**: a six-line program with a `nat` parameter fails on the compile path (`Not yet implemented` inferred, `ClassCastException` explicit) and runs on the interpreter. The interpreter's library has 81 such declarations, C4's vocabulary 30; `CompilerLibrary` has one, the empty `Matrix`. So the sized-array vocabulary cannot pass the compile path's checker today, and the static dimension checking the `nat` design promises is not implemented anywhere. Source: `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`, measured 2026-09-16.
- **Between the interpreter's library and bytecode stands the checker, not desugaring or code generation** (2026-09-20, `perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen.md`, the library pushed through DESUGAR and CODEGEN with the checker's failures caught per top-level declaration, validated on `CompilerLibrary.fss` where the method reproduces the ordinary compile exactly): of `FortressLibrary.fss`'s 446 top-level declarations the checker passes 237 clean, reports errors on 97 and crashes on 112 (81 `makeInferenceArg` nyi, 29 `TraitType→IntExpr`, the `nat` gap); DESUGAR and OVERLOADREWRITE then report zero diagnostics on all of it; CODEGEN emits 275 and refuses 313, of which only **5 are on declarations the checker checked clean** (four a numeric static argument, one a method call on an intersection-typed receiver); the rest are missing annotations on unchecked declarations (227), the two missing visitors `Juxt` (53) and `Label` (1), `nat` static arguments (14), malformed overload sets (7); `canCompile` refused nothing and no native binding was missing. Two obstacles the earlier counts did not show: the compile path's own `extends Object` pre-desugaring (`Shell.java:371-386`) adds 712 of the 960 checker errors in the prelude apis and 618 of 1,204 in the component, rejecting every generic instantiated at a tuple type, more than the 93 tower errors; and overload dispatch generation does not terminate on this library's exclusion graph (1,046 s, stopped by hand), so it was switched off for the measurement.

- **Two constraints of the test and native machinery, measured by rung S** (`6bec1b004`): (1) the native-wrapper generator wraps every method of a class named by `import java`, private ones included, and fails the whole import on any parameter or result type with no Fortress counterpart (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java:215-225`, `:250-258`; a `Class<?>` parameter: `compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/probes/judge-shape-wrapper-error.txt:6`), so a helper in a `nativeHelpers` class needs a Fortress-mappable signature even when private (row 368). (2) In the junit harness a link or compile *exception* of a component whose name contains `XXX` is reported `OK Saw expected exception` whatever the `.test` file is called (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:346-360`), so the `<Name>Link.test` half of the split expected-failure shape guards against a regression reported as diagnostics but not one reported as an exception; and a `run` stage whose `run_out_contains` is unmet fails even in an `XXX` file (`:534-537`, `:583-585`), so a program that dies before printing its marker needs `run_out_does_not_contain` instead (`compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/probes/xxx-union-check-lines.txt`).
- **Three heaps run the interpreter, and a gated test can pass at two of them and die at the third**: `bin/fortress` gives the JVM `-Xmx256m` unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set (`bin/fortress:28-29`, row 67), the testSystem harness 768 MB (root `build.xml:131`, `junitMem`, the `systemShard` macro's `maxmemory` at `:1181`), and the climb's shared `JAVA_FLAGS` 4 GB (`explorations/experiment/env.sh:8`). Rung I's `ZZ 3 LSHIFT 2147483647` passed at 768 MB and 4 GB and ended the run with an uncatchable `OutOfMemoryError` at 256 MB, because `BigInteger.shiftLeft` allocates about 268 MB before its range check throws (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/probes/skeptic/SkBigAlloc.txt`); its skeptic found it by running the test at the launcher's heap, and the repair checks the bit length first (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md`, section 4.4). A claim about a run-time failure mode near a memory limit is measured at 256 MB.

## Landed semantics

- The compiled world's mutable-variable cell holds `fortress.AnyType.Any`, the language's top type, not `runtimeValues.FValue`: `FValue` is an abstract class (`runtimeValues/FValue.java:13`) and a compiled closure is not one of its subclasses, so a mutable variable of arrow type failed the verifier. The defect was already in the tree for *local* mutable variables, which have always been stored in such a cell (`compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/probes/P15LocalArrow.fss`, `P16LocalArrowTask.fss`: `VerifyError` on `49ee5e91`, `f(1) = 3` after R1), and R1 fixed both kinds by widening the payload (`runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java:18-32`, `runtimeSystem/Transaction.java:20,27-28,144,152,226`).
- **A numeral's value reaches the compiled world intact as of the repair batch of 2026-09-18.** `CodeGen.forIntLiteralExpr` chose the numeral's representation by `BigInteger.bitLength()` against `<= 32` and `<= 64`; `bitLength()` counts no sign bit, so a non-negative numeral of bit length exactly 32 or exactly 64 was truncated into a signed slot and arrived wrapped negative — `4294967295` and `18446744073709551615` both became `-1`, against `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-86` (a numeral of digits has the value of its digits in radix ten, with nothing bounding it) and `basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:368-370,398-401` (wrapping and saturating have their own operator spellings and "operations on type $\mathbb{Z}$ never need to wrap or saturate"). The bounds are now `<= 31` and `<= 63`, exact for both signs, and `FIntLiteral.asNN64` reads the decimal string a numeral of bit length 64 now keeps. Where the compiled run contradicted `walk` in silence it now agrees with it: `4294967295` at `ZZ` prints `4294967295` on both paths, and `a = 4294967295; b = 1; println (a + b)` prints `4294967296` on both (ledger row 317, `compile-ladder/repair-r2-literal-wrap/REPORT.md`).

## The library's arrays and algebra

- `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` are the only sized array traits; `Array3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, …\]` carries no algebraic trait (row 292; `FortressLibrary.fsi:1465, 1583, 1657` since the library commits of climb batches 3 and 3.5).
- `Vector` and `Matrix` inherit `+`, `-`, unary `-` and `zero` from `AdditiveGroup`, nothing else; `×` reaches no array by design because juxtaposition is the inner product and the array traits exclude `AnyMultiplicativeRing` (rows 64, 109, 293); a carrier that extends the ring is accepted unchecked, changes juxtaposition to elementwise and breaks `+` (vocabulary review v02, v02b).
- The library's products are declared with shared `nat`s (`Matrix[\T,n,m\]` × `Matrix[\T,m,p\]`, `FortressLibrary.fsi:1508-1516`); C4's own products were not, which is habit; the focused base's `FlatArrays2` states them (twelve declarations including the per-rank elementwise `×` and `/`, 25 of 29 nats agreeing; 39 declarations), and a wrong-shape call is refused at dispatch, uncatchable for an overloaded name (row 83), as a unification error naming the nat for an unoverloaded one (`apl/mg/checks/mismatch_probe.out`).
- Two declarations of one name differing only in the element type, or a rank-specialised declaration beside an index-generic one, are refused at load ("at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types"; `apl/mg/checks/model_run.out.0`, `elemwise_nat_probe.out.0`); two apis' overloads of one name are checked as one family, so two vocabularies cannot stand in one component (`diag_fwd_two_vocabularies_rejected.out.0`).
- The shipped `RR64` does not satisfy the specification's algebraic bound `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` (vocabulary review, probe `v04b_groupbound.out.0`); `T extends Number` is the bound that works for every element type and rank (row 295).
- The library's scalar-extension block for `+ - MIN MAX` over arrays is generic since `02d09a39f` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4511-4521`, `.fsi:2550-2560`); no reshape, plane, gather, outer product or ravel exists in the library (vocabulary review, section A).
- An array is a trait with `get`/`put`; a view is an object implementing it over other storage, the language's own idiom; the library's row slice `m[i,:]` costs 5× a six-line user view; a diagonal as a `Matrix` view costs 13-54× the operator (vocabulary review v20, v07).
- The element type is `Number` only for `Vector`/`Matrix` (row 24); irrelevant to numeric microGPT, decisive for Run B's autodiff value and for APL characters.

## The container

- The process cost of the climbs and the batches — the eight-rung climb's wall clock and its gate share, the limits of parallelism on this box, and each batch's agents, tokens, tool calls and span — is measured in `explorations/coordinator/iteration-cost.md`, `coordinator/repair-batch-review.md` and the batch records; the conclusions it produced are in `POSITIONS.md` and in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, and the entries themselves are in `FACTS-history.md`.
- The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling kills long runs; check runs go under the `Monitor` tool (1800000 ms), sequential, nothing else running when a number is to be kept.
- The disk allowance fills with parser-generation temp directories: every run that imports a grammar generates a Rats! parser into a fresh `/tmp/fortress<random>rats` directory (`RatsUtil.getTempDir`, `syntax_abstractions/rats/RatsUtil.java:138-146`, via `IOUtil.createAndMarkTempDirectory`), 5.8 MB each, never deleted; 723 of them (4.2 GB) filled the allowance on 2026-09-15 and broke a worker's tool output mid-run ("no space left on device"). Deficit until fixed at the source (an edit under the sealed tree, or a `deleteOnExit`); mitigation in our tree: `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them when sourced, and `df` must be checked before any long run.
- The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling; `Monitor` for long runs (the microGPT-runs entry above).
- A container can be lost outright: the coordinating session of 2026-09-17 (`bdff267d-…`) died mid-workflow and could not be re-provisioned, because the branch it was created from was no longer found on the remote. Recovery moved into the blinded run's container, which already had the checkout and toolchain. Cost: four workflow agents (~798k tokens), their worktrees, and the 13 hours after the last transcript snapshot at 20:31. Everything through `2ab1d6d8` was pushed and safe, and `REPAIR-BATCH.md` kept the batch runnable. Mechanism, the three traps and the recovery procedure: `explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md`.

<!-- What Pavol has decided, stated, or already knows, with dates; in his words or a close paraphrase. Read at session start so that none of it is re-explained to him. Standing directives about how we work are in explorations/protocol.md and are not repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- The revival's toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression; Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources; "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability" (2026-09-15).
- The APL side quest began as a curiosity (2026-09-10), became a ladder to learn APL (09-11, he has not read the book), was redirected to native code, not an interpreter in an interpreter (09-12), and got microGPT as its target on 09-13; the ladder "was to keep you busy and expand the probe". The remaining APL ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued (09-15).
- Hoped for a diamond from the Hsu-style flat program; got "a few lumps of coal"; the rewrite (rung 4b) was to get closer, and the vocabulary is where any polishing happens.

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
- The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here"; this goes on the priority list (2026-09-15). The first measurement (the scalar loop) said boxing was about 2% of the gap; Pavol objected that the loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator) and asked for a fairer test; the fairer test agreed with him: on array-shaped code boxing is 6.3-6.5× and the dominant representational cost, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles at all today (FACTS, execution model). The order now on record: the compiler library's array type first, the two one-line runtime defects second, unboxing designed into the first.
- The type checker runs only on the compile path; he wants it usable on interpreter programs and considers that low-hanging fruit (2026-09-15). It is item 0.1 of `performance-roadmap.md` (2026-09-08), which the coordinator had not indexed; see FACTS, deficit.
- Hsu's critique of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".

## Decisions on record

- 2026-08-23, recovered from the transcript on 2026-09-23 (`coordinator/lineage.md`): the third-party Java 9 port gets no credit and no mention — "we can lose the porcupines credit since you seem to have not really been informed by their changes"; "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere"; the revival's toolchain was rebuilt from the original tree with a few mechanical fixes, the port only showed that a revival was possible. And his plan the same day, not carried out: rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main`. On 2026-09-23, told that CLAUDE.md's opening still described the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history: "This is incorrect. Where does this come from? Use archeology to find correct facts and correct the record" — corrected in CLAUDE.md, the other files left for his decision.
- 2026-09-14: C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
- 2026-09-15: redo rung 4 as the focused base (done); do the vocabulary swap with shared `nat` dimensions (in progress); the ledger is not split, two views are derived (done); the ledger review is the next major step after the swap; the remaining APL ground is closed.
- 2026-09-15: "fleshing out the standard library" is a very important task: first fix the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch, then extend the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them. Open question he has not answered: whether this means editing the sealed `Library/` (the standing rule is never; worklist item 4 "unseal the linear-algebra layer" names the rows) or building the layer in our own tree; the coordinator assumes our own tree until he says otherwise.
- 2026-09-16: the goal restated: finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed spec (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not redesign the language; the measuring stick is one program, microGPT compiled to bytecode and running fast; a pure-Java microGPT will be written later as the floor to measure against; the tree is tagged at the unsealing point and the next phase modifies the original sources with the lessons of the explorations.
- 2026-09-16: the mathematical notation (Fortify, the 2D rendering) is his verdict "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, and the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress. Do not spend work on it unless he asks.
- 2026-09-16: before unsealing he wants the territory map (`coordinator/map/`): repository and language architecture, the pipeline phases, test coverage per layer, the gaps on the path in order with the cost of leaving each, the development loop's slow spots, a touch-this-affects-that map, and where the design intent is written (papers, not only the spec).

trait AnyMatrix end

trait Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]
        extends { AnyMatrix, Array2[\T, 0, s0, 0, s1\], AdditiveGroup[\Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]\] }
        excludes { AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    opr +(self, v:Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] =
        ivmap[\T\](fn (i:(ZZ32,ZZ32),e:T):T => e + v.get(i))
    opr -(self, v:Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] =
        ivmap[\T\](fn (i:(ZZ32,ZZ32),e:T):T => e - v.get(i))
    opr -(self): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = map[\T\](fn (e:T):T => - e)
    scale(t1: T): Matrix[\T,s0,s1\] = map[\T\](fn (e:T):T => t1 e)
    mul[\ nat s2 \](other: Matrix[\T,s1,s2\]): Matrix[\T,s0,s2\] = do
        res = matrix[\T,s0,s2\]()
        mma(a:ZZ32,i:ZZ32,b:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,c:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):() =
            if k>=i AND k>=j then
              if k=1 then
                pr : T = get(a,b) other.get(b,c)
                (* If this were atomic, we could parallelize j-partition. *)
                res.put((a,c), res.get(a,c) + pr)
              else
                (k0,k1) = partition(k)
                (mma(a,i,b,j,c,k0),mma(a,i,b,j,c+k0,k1))
              end
            elif j>=i then
                (j0,j1) = partition(j)
                mma(a,i,b,j0,c,k)
                mma(a,i,b+j0,j1,c,k)
            else
                (i0,i1) = partition(i)
                (mma(a,i0,b,j,c,k),mma(a+i0,i1,b,j,c,k))

content.text:
Three parts, in your order.

**The myopic view.** I recall it; no archaeology needed. What is on record: a watch-list line in the protocol and a POSITIONS entry saying that a fork put to you names the library's own way first, and a fork resting on a rule that refuses something says what the library does instead. That fixes the one step I skipped. It does not fix the mechanism that carried the two shapes for five days: the first review measured two shapes and wrote them into the file's comment, every later brief said "drop what the library serves", and every worker and I read the record as the space of solutions instead of the language as the space. The record was trusted where it should have been treated as one reading.

What I propose, three rules:

- **A brief states the problem, never the shape.** "Diag's product costs s times the arithmetic; restore it" is a problem. "Drop what the library serves" or "subtype or operator" is a shape, and a worker given a shape never looks past it.
- **Alternatives come from a clean worker.** Before a fork reaches you, one worker that has not read the record's framing gets the problem statement and the library sources and is asked to list every mechanism the language offers for it, with the library's own precedent for each, rejecting none. The blinded workers of August found what the informed ones missed, so this is a shape we know works. Cost: one Opus worker per fork, well under an hour.
- **A refusing rule is a question, not an answer.** When a rule stops a shape, the next sentence in any brief or reply is how the library itself lives under that rule. The interpreter's overload rule stops two generic operators; the library lives under it by overriding methods, in hundreds of places.

Recommendation: write the three into protocol § 6, replacing the watch-list line's rule with them, on your yes.

**The rest of the list.** Rows 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, then the four ledger homes 374 to 377, one per message, once the diagonal probe has landed and the size worker is launched behind it. I start with row 40 in the message after that.

**The batch.** The two probes in flight do not gate batch 4. The size probes prepare the run-time size rung, which you placed in the batch after; the diagonal probe is row 39's own. What still stands between now and the launch is the same as before batch 3: the remaining rows decided, so that their small fixes join the batch as a rung, then the manifest written by workers for your reading, then your go. No other prep is owed.

Sorry. Again, plainly.

**What went wrong.** The first review measured two ways to build the diagonal and wrote them into the file's comment. Every later brief and every later reader, me included, started from those two. Nobody went back to the library to ask how it handles the same situation. That is the failure.

**What is already recorded.** One protocol rule: before I put a choice to you, I check how the library does the same thing, and if a rule blocks one option I say what the library does under that rule.

**What I think we should add.** Three things.

1. When I brief a worker, I describe the problem, not the solution I expect. "Diag's product is too slow, restore a fast one" is fine. "Drop what the library serves" is not, because it tells the worker where to stop looking.
2. Before a design choice comes to you, one extra worker gets only the problem and the library sources, not our earlier notes, and lists every way the language and library offer to solve it. We did this in August with the blinded workers and it worked. It costs one Opus worker, under an hour.
3. When some rule blocks an option, the brief or my reply must also say how the library itself gets around that rule. In this case the interpreter blocks two generic operators, and the library gets around it by overriding methods.

If you say yes, I write these three into the protocol.

**The list.** After the diagonal probe lands and the size worker starts, I take row 40, then 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, then the four ledger homes, one per message.

### 6d. The compiled representation of a nat-sized `double[]` array

Where the nat lives, two places, both needed: in the stamped class's name, `Vector⟦FRR64,16⟧` and `Vector⟦FRR64,4192⟧` being different classes, which the loader already produces from the mangled name (probe 6) and which is what makes the nat a fact for the checker and for dispatch; and as a run-time field of the native store (`dim_x` in the `FZZ32Vector` shape), because nothing today turns the name back into a value, the store's `get`, `put` and `|self|` need the number, and the `double[]` carries its own length. One class per distinct size is the price; microGPT's sizes are six literals and a computed 4192.

What the loader must do with a nat argument beyond what it does: supply a value for a nat in value position inside a template. Either the instantiater rewrites the `getstatic <Component>$n.ONLY` reference into a constant when it stamps `⟦…,5,…⟧` (an instruction-level substitution in `Instantiater`, the job the expando stub at `InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172` was left for), or the code generator emits a read from the run-time type descriptor, which today refuses `IntArg` (`CodeGen.java:5783`). Under the two-place representation the library's value uses of a nat are few (`i s1 + j` in `__DefaultArray2`, the `N[\s0\]` witness in `subarray`) and the store's field can serve the first; the second is explicit-only. So the value mechanism is a `.java` rung of its own, needed for the full port and not for the first kernels. Default: the field first, the name-to-constant substitution when the port reaches `subarray`.

Run-time sizes: `array[\RR64\](n)` with `n` computed cannot name its class at compile time. Either a native helper builds the stamped name from the integer and asks the loader for `Array1⟦FRR64,0,4192⟧` by that string, which is a string from a number and unprobed, or the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` as it already does in the model (`FlatArrays.fss:14-17`) and only literal and symbol sizes get sized classes. Default: the second; it is what the model writes today, and the `reflect` group of §6c is then the one library pattern the compiled world does not reproduce until the first is probed.

### 6e. The checker edit and the shadow route, assessed

The plan (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` §c-§f): a third track beside types and operators in the constraint solver, `Formula.scala` (711 lines) taking most of the diff, `TypeAnalyzer.pEqv` and its cast guard, `STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg`, `ExportChecker.equalIntExprs`, `TypeWellFormedChecker` rejecting arithmetic in a static argument; about 24 functions in five Scala files, 200-300 lines; no Java; the five nat compiler tests stay green; no catalogued test flips. Two items the plan did not close and this document's probes sharpen: the object crash of §6a is reproduced by a four-line object with no `extends`, so it is on the path of the very first sized declaration; and the code generator's `IntArg` refusal in `extends` is reached by every storing object.

The shadow route (`next-climb.md:102-104`; the recipe of `perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh`): copies of the five files compiled with `scala.tools.nsc.Main` into `shadow-classes`, placed first on the class path; the gate can be run with the shadow overlaid on `ProjectFortress/build`, as the template fix was (its 31 lines went green that way, `33-testfast.out`, `34-testsystem.out`). What it buys: the two unknowns, the object crash's source and the export checker's reach, are found without a sealed-tree edit, and the design of the inference variable can be tried as a reserved-name `IntRef` (the plan's option B) before the AST node (option A) is added, which a shadow cannot do because the AST is regenerated by `ant compileAll`. What it costs: a second toolchain path per iteration, and a prototype that differs from the real edit in that one representation. Assessment: the tree is unsealed and the batch script already runs `.scala` rungs under the full gate with the test written first, so the shadow is not a gate substitute; it is worth one worker session for the two unknowns and nothing more. Default: one shadow session for the object crash and the export checker, then the rung in 

The first failing test under `PLAN.md`'s rule, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NatInfer1.fss` with its `.test` naming `link`, `run`, `run_out_contains=PASS`: `object Box[\nat k\](v: ZZ32) end`, `unbox[\nat k\](b: Box[\k\]): ZZ32 = b.v`, `run() = if unbox(Box[\3\](7)) = 7 then println("PASS") end`; it fails today with `Not yet implemented` (probe 5 is the same shape). Beside it `NatObject1.fss` (a nat object instantiated with a literal, failing with the `ClassCastException`), `NatValue1.fss` (a nat in value position, failing at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError`), and the negative `XXXNatMismatch1.fss` (`same(Vec[\4\], Vec[\3\])`, `compile_err_equals` the mismatch message), which today compiles by the `pTrue()` hole and must be refused after.

=====
## 7. The decision tree, with two questions closed

Question 1, boxed or `double[]`: closed by Pavol, `double[]`. Consequence: the `RR64` store is a hand-written class on the `FZZ32Vector` pattern, never a stamped generic (§2), and the boxed `Object[]` store exists only for element types that have no native store.

Question 4, where sizes live: closed by Pavol, in the type as the team designed. Consequences: the checker rung of §6e precedes the first sized declaration; the export checker and the object crash are on the path, not optional; every distinct size is a stamped class; the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array` until the string-from-number route is probed (§6d, default).

Question 2, open: what implements the library's sized traits under `double[]`?
Branch "native stores per element type under the library's generic objects": `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]` keeps its shape and its `mem` field is the `RR64` store for `RR64`, `FZZ32Vector` for `ZZ32`, the boxed store otherwise, chosen by the factory from the run-time type tag; the interpreter's own layering with `PrimitiveArray` replaced; one unprobed link, the non-generic store trait under the generic `Array` (§4c).
Branch "the loader picks a `double[]` template per instantiation": the expando route; `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,4192⟧` would load a different class than `PrimitiveArray⟦FZZ32,4192⟧`; nothing of it exists, and the instantiater's only tool is name substitution.
Default: the first; it needs one probe and no loader change, and it is the library's own structure.

Question 3, open: where do the loops run unboxed?
Branch "inside native whole-array operations": Java helpers over `double[]` for the contractions and elementwise maps; a box per operation; no code-generator change; the user lambdas of `fill`, `map`, `rows` still box per element.
Branch "in generated code": the code generator learns `D` locals, `daload`/`dastore`, `dadd`/`dmul` for statically `RR64` code; every rung `.java` under the full gate; unlocks unboxed loops written in Fortress.
Default: natives first, with the kernel measurement in the first array rung; generated-code unboxing as PLAN's step 4, once the measured residue says what it is worth.

Question 5, open, from the third ruling: the library's unused nats (`.fsi:1496-1523`). Branch "default an unconstrained nat to `0`" keeps the library's text; branch "refuse and delete the dead parameters" edits six library declarations. Default: the first, the plan's own recommendation, and the only reason the checker rung would otherwise touch `Library/`.

Where microGPT's 26 operations go is not a question after the third ruling: into `CompilerLibrary` in the library's own style, whose precedent for scalar extension is the `ZZ32` block at `FortressLibrary.fss:4477-4517` (`opr +(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], y: ZZ32)` beside `AdditiveGroup.+`, the same overloading shape the review found illegal by the letter and the interpreter accepts), for maps `map(f)` over `replica`, for structure the view objects, and for products the shared-nat operators of §6c.

## 8. What happens right after the choice

First, the checker rung (`.scala`, full gate): the four tests of §6e, the shadow session for the two unknowns, then the edit of `nat-checking-plan.md` §f with option A. What it moves: no ladder file by itself (the plan's census), no microGPT component; it unblocks every sized declaration.

Second, the array rung (`.java`, full gate), the first failing test `library_tests/Vector1.fss`: `v = vector[\RR64,3\](fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.5 i); if v[1] + v[2] = 4.5 then println("PASS") end`, failing today at disambiguation on `Vector`; then the `RR64` store class and helper, the non-generic store trait under `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` (the probe of §4c first), `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, `Array`, `Array1`, `Vector` and `__DefaultVector` in the library's spelling, the factories; in the same rung `kdot` compiled over a native `dot` and timed against `KDotPrim`. What it moves: the ladder's `Array` 6, `array` 2 and `Array1` 6 past disambiguation; of the eighteen microGPT components, the 8 stopped on `Array` and the 2 on `Vector` reach the checker.

Third, library-only rungs: `Array2`, `Matrix`, the transposed views and the shared-nat products (`kmat` timed); `Array3`; the scalar extension and elementwise maps for `RR64` arrays in the `ZZ32` block's style, which is where the compile path's overloading check on the model's operator pairs is measured; `Char` (5 components) and the immutable variant (`ImmutableArray`, 3 components and 26 ladder files) in whichever order the counts rank them.

The claim (§6c): "Every one of these is a symbol or a literal; no arithmetic occurs inside white brackets anywhere in the library or in the two microGPT programs … So the minimal checker, symbols and literals unified by equality, covers all 81". The nat plan's census (`nat-checking-plan.md` §d) counted "an operator inside white brackets" and found 0.

The `ZZ32Vector` precedent proves that a hand-written class can implement a trait's `DefaultTraitMethods`, be a `NamingCzar` special type, and reach Java natives through `import java`, and `FZZ32` proves it under instantiated generic supertraits (finding 9). Reading row 40's ground: the array design's three open questions and what the review and later decisions did to them. Row 40 is next.

**Row 40.** On 09-19 the array design note (`coordinator/array-design.md`) left three questions you had not answered standing at the worker's defaults, and nothing was built on them:

1. Which object holds the `double[]` for each element type: the worker's default was the library's own generic array objects with a native store chosen by the run-time type of the elements.
2. Where a size lives at run time: the default was a field on the store, with the size in the class name later.
3. What a factory called with a computed size returns: the default was the unsized `Array`, as the model writes today.

What happened since. The adversarial review of 09-20 refuted default 1 by probe (the checker refuses that store selection) and said default 3 is what makes the model fail the checker, since the model's types are unsized. Default 2 it called right and forced. Then your later decisions changed the ground under all three: one library instead of the compiler's own (09-21), sizes at run time as descriptor objects, design B (09-24), and route A for the tower (09-24). And on 09-22 you put the array decisions after the switch-over, with plain explainers prepared beforehand.

So no decision was taken here. The three questions are open, and the note they sit in is stale in its premises.

What I propose: close row 40 as "not a decision taken"; the three questions come to you with the array fork after the switch-over, each prepared by workers in the nine-step shape, with the alternatives from a clean worker under the new rule. Recommendation: close it that way.

Not sure I like it. Uh, I took the answer that I criticized you for and gave it Opus 55 to review about tone. This is what it told me:

***

Yes, several.

**Aphorism as rule-writing.** "A refusing rule is a question, not an answer." "A brief states the problem, never the shape." These are slogans. Protocol rules need operational conditions: what triggers them, what output is required, and who checks it. The third rule's own gloss is more useful than its headline, which suggests the headline is there for cadence rather than content.

**Absolutes and unearned generalization.**
- "a worker given a shape never looks past it": it's stated as a law, but it rests on one episode.
- "The blinded workers of August found what the informed ones missed, so this is a shape we know works": n=1 promoted to "we know."
- "in hundreds of places" and "well under an hour" are estimates presented as facts.

**Agentless self-diagnosis.** "The record was trusted where it should have been treated as one reading." The error gets spread across "the mechanism," "every later brief," and "every worker and I." It owns the one skipped step, then passive voice absorbs the larger failure.

**Chiasmus and polish in a status report.** "the record as the space of solutions instead of the language as the space" is shaped to sound like an insight. The plain version would be: "we only considered options the first review had listed."

**Ceremonial register.** "On your yes." "No other prep is owed." "I recall it; no archaeology needed." "Three parts, in your order." The tone is somewhere between legal and liturgical: formal deference on top, while it schedules your next several messages underneath ("I start with row 40 in the message after that").

**Private vocabulary with no gloss.** "Rung," "ledger homes," "POSITIONS entry," "watch-list line," and "manifest" are dense references that assume you're holding the full state. That may be fine if you are, but it doesn't flag any uncertainty about whether you are.

**It violates its own proposal.** Rule 1 says to state the problem and not the shape. Then the recommendation hands you a shape ("write the three into § 6, replacing…") and offers no alternatives.

The terseness itself isn't the problem. The problem is that the compression is spent on cadence and confidence rather than precision.

***

Thoughts?

content.text:
The review is right on most points. Going through them.

1. **Slogans as rules.** Right. The headlines were written for sound. The version in the protocol is the plain one: each rule says what triggers it and what must be written. What it lacks is who checks. Today that is me, at the moment I write a brief or an answer, and nobody else.
2. **Absolutes.** Right on all three. "Never looks past it" is one episode. "We know works" is stronger than the record: there were four blinded workers in August and September, and the review-patterns note records that their results held, but that is four cases, not knowledge. "Hundreds of places" I did not count. "Well under an hour" is wrong by our own record: the last two size workers took 72 and 45 minutes.
3. **Passive voice on the failure.** Right. The plain sentence is: I only considered the two options the first review had listed, and I did not open the library to ask how it builds a specialised product until your question forced me to.
4. **Chiasmus.** Right.
5. **Ceremonial register.** Mostly right. "On your yes" is this project's convention for a decision, but the rest was liturgy, and scheduling your next messages was presumptuous even though the order of rows was your instruction.
6. **Private vocabulary.** Partly. You know rung, ledger and manifest. "Ledger homes" I should have defined: the four ledger rows 374 to 377 that still need a gated test, a plain one or an expected-failure one.
7. **Violates its own rule.** Right. I proposed three rules and no alternatives, on the same day I wrote a rule against exactly that.

The reviewer's last sentence is the same thing you have told me since the 15th: the compression goes into confidence instead of precision. I accept it.

What to do with the protocol text now. Three options:

- A. Leave it as committed. The plain wording is already there without the headlines.
- B. Rewrite the three rules in the form the reviewer asks for: the trigger, the required output, and who checks it. Small edit, my own turn.
- C. B plus a mechanical check in the batch workflow script, so a brief that names a solution shape is refused before a worker sees it. One Opus worker for the script change, and the check would be crude, since telling a problem from a shape is a judgement.

Recommendation: B.

# The diagonal's product as an override of `mul`

Probe for row 39 of the re-approval table (POSITIONS 2026-09-24): the
microGPT vocabulary's `Diag[\nat s\]` stays a subtype of the library's
`Matrix[\RR64,s,s\]` and gets its row-scaling product back by overriding
`mul`, the method the library's `Matrix Matrix` juxtaposition and `DOT`
forward to (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2627-2633`; `mul` declared at
`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1590`, body `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2512-2553`).
Shape 3 (the override) was tried first and passed, so shape 1 (a plain
`Diag` and the old operator) was not built. Interpreter path only; no library
file and no model line changed. Runs on 2026-09-25 between 21:34:40Z and
22:20:30Z, every time below from `date -u`.

- Shape 3 loads and runs in both vocabularies at the first attempt. The
  interpreter refused nothing: no overload, override or return-type message.
- The api needs no `mul` line. Both `.fsi` files keep
  `object Diag[\nat s\](d: Vector[\RR64,s\]) extends Matrix[\RR64,s,s\] end`,
  and the override is reached from other components through that
  declaration. Listing `mul` in the api was not tried, because nothing called
  for a variation.

  run time the value is a `Matrix`, because `ivmap` fills

After a compaction, the same order, with three rules added on 2026-09-19: `FACTS.md` is read whole, in one pass; if the handover's first section says a batch is running, its decision record (`CLIMB-BATCH-*.md`) is read next and the run's `journal.jsonl` and the agents' last transcript timestamps are checked before anything is said about it; and nothing else is read by the coordinator itself — rung reports, agent transcripts, ledger rows and source are read by a worker that returns a summary, so the coordinator's context holds what governs the work and not the record of how it was found. A fourth rule, added the same day after a boot listed two directories into its context: whether a worker is still running is read from the harness's notice at the top of the turn and from the one output path the handover names (`test -f`), never by listing the scratchpad or the task directory, and every boot command bounds its output.

Rules for keeping it: a fact enters `FACTS.md` when it is established with a source (a ledger row, a file:line, a measured output), in the commit that establishes it; a position enters `POSITIONS.md` when Pavol states it, in the next commit, in his words or a close paraphrase with the date; nothing in either file is repeated to Pavol in chat unless he asks or the fact has changed; when an answer in chat would restate an entry here, the answer cites the entry and adds only what is new. Entries are never deleted; a superseded entry gets "superseded by …" appended. `FACTS.md` holds the current state: what governs the work now, how a mechanism behaves, the operational traps, each open "not settled" list. When a batch lands, the entry a rung earned is condensed to the fact or rule as it stands, with its rows, hash and report path, and the narrative of how it was established moves to `FACTS-history.md` verbatim, tagged with the date and the section it came from (Pavol, 2026-09-24).

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Fortress revival

This is @palimondo's revival of Sun/Oracle's **Fortress** programming language
(Guy Steele's HPC language, 2003–2012; interpreter + partial JVM compiler,
BSD-licensed). The repo is a 2018 GitHub fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git
conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository: 5,397 trunk commits
from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 (`a874948ac`), twelve old branches and the `1.0`
tag. The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a history walk from HEAD stops
early; see `research/authorship.md`. Everything after `a874948ac` is the
revival's own work (2026). Working mode: Claude explains the
codebase and produces documentation and experiments as we go; Pavol decides
what gets committed. The full collaboration protocol — roles, tone, how work
is presented, commit discipline, delegation — is in
`explorations/protocol.md`; read it at session start.
The coordinator's knowledge base — `explorations/coordinator/` (`FACTS.md`: what is
established, with sources; `POSITIONS.md`: what Pavol has decided and already knows) — is
read at session start and after every compaction, and updated in the same commit as the
work that establishes a fact or takes a decision; the current state of the work is in
`explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`.

## Build and run

```bash
apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant  # JDK 8, 11, 17 and 21 also build and gate green
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
export FORTRESS_HOME=<repo root>
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS                          # proxy trust-store options confuse ant's JVM forks
cd $FORTRESS_HOME && ant compileAll              # ~80 s
./bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss      # interpreter ("walk")
```

Toolchain traps: `build.xml` drives scalac through `scala.tools.nsc.Main`
directly, because Scala 2.13 dropped the `scala.tools.ant` tasks; ASM is
vendored in `ProjectFortress/third_party/asm/`, and Fortress's own
`asmbytecodeoptimizer.Opcodes` shadows `org.objectweb.asm.Opcodes` in that
package; sources are compiled as UTF-8. The versions, the emitted classfile
level and the runtime's ForkJoin pool are in
`explorations/modernization-plan.md`.

Facts that save time:

- **Both execution paths work.** `fortress <file>.fss` interprets directly.
  The bytecode compiler path (`fortress compile` + `fortress run`) has two
  traps: imported library components (`System`, `CompilerSystem`) must be
  explicitly `fortress compile`d into the cache first, and **stale caches**
  cause a misleading `NoSuchMethodError: fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println(...)`
  — wipe `default_repository/caches/*` and recompile in library order (recipe
  in `explorations/repo-internals.md`). The compiler is incomplete (some
  constructs still `sayWhat`), not broken.
- **`ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only via the compiler path** — its July
  2012 upgrade imports `System.getProperty`/`CompilerSystem.args`, which the
  interpreter can't resolve. Use `explorations/*.fss` as interpreter smoke
  tests.
- **The test suite is fully green and is the gate for every change:** `ant
  testFast` (the compiler suite among others) and `ant testSystem` (the
  interpreter tests), zero failures. The current counts are in the last
  landed gate summary (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt`);
  how the suite first went green is in `explorations/test-baseline-jdk8.md`.
- The interpreter requires filename (sans `.fss`) == component name.
- If scalac fails with arity errors in `S*Pattern` nodes, the generated AST
  sources are stale relative to `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`:
  `touch ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast && ant compileAll` regenerates.
- Interpreter caches live in `default_repository/caches/` (gitignored); wipe
  them if library edits seem to have no effect.
- Architecture map, name-resolution rules, cache anatomy, test-harness
  mechanics, and git-archaeology techniques: `explorations/repo-internals.md`
  — read it before diving into the source.

## Layout

- Original Fortress tree: everything not listed below — do not modify
  casually; it is the historical artifact being revived.
- `explorations/` — revival-era experiments and writeups (ours; verified
  running programs).
- `research/` — the Guy Steele corpus: `research/README.md` is a committed
  links-only index; `research/extracts/` holds committed working notes;
  `research/decks/` is **gitignored** (copyrighted PDFs, dropped in per
  session, never committed).
- `Specification/` + `Specification-1.0-frozen/` — the language spec LaTeX
  (in-repo, richer than the published PDF; building it is untested).

## Project goal

Finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed
specification (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not redesign the
language; the measuring stick is one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode
and running fast (Pavol, 2026-09-16, `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`).
The plan is `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`; where the work stands is the
first section of `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`; every known gap,
defect and design limit is a row of `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`.

Claims in the 2012 tree's own READMEs (root `README.txt` among them) describe
their era, not the current tree — verify against the code before acting on
them.

# Fortress revival

This is @palimondo's revival of Sun/Oracle's **Fortress** programming language
(Guy Steele's HPC language, 2003–2012; interpreter + partial JVM compiler,
BSD-licensed). The repo is a 2018 GitHub fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git
conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository: 5,397 trunk commits
from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 (`a874948ac`), twelve old branches and the `1.0`
tag. The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a history walk from HEAD stops
early; see `research/authorship.md`. Everything after `a874948ac` is the
revival's own work (2026). Working mode: Claude explains the
codebase and produces documentation and experiments as we go; Pavol decides
what gets committed. The full collaboration protocol — roles, tone, how work
is presented, commit discipline, delegation — is in
`explorations/protocol.md`; read it at session start.
The coordinator's knowledge base — `explorations/coordinator/` (`FACTS.md`: what is
established, with sources; `POSITIONS.md`: what Pavol has decided and already knows) — is
read at session start and after every compaction, and updated in the same commit as the
work that establishes a fact or takes a decision; the current state of the work is in
`explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`.

## Build and run

```bash
apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant  # JDK 8, 11, 17 and 21 also build and gate green
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
export FORTRESS_HOME=<repo root>
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS                          # proxy trust-store options confuse ant's JVM forks
cd $FORTRESS_HOME && ant compileAll              # ~80 s
./bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss      # interpreter ("walk")
```

Toolchain traps: `build.xml` drives scalac through `scala.tools.nsc.Main`
directly, because Scala 2.13 dropped the `scala.tools.ant` tasks; ASM is
vendored in `ProjectFortress/third_party/asm/`, and Fortress's own
`asmbytecodeoptimizer.Opcodes` shadows `org.objectweb.asm.Opcodes` in that
package; sources are compiled as UTF-8. The versions, the emitted classfile
level and the runtime's ForkJoin pool are in
`explorations/modernization-plan.md`.

Facts that save time:

- **Both execution paths work.** `fortress <file>.fss` interprets directly.
  The bytecode compiler path (`fortress compile` + `fortress run`) has two
  traps: imported library components (`System`, `CompilerSystem`) must be
  explicitly `fortress compile`d into the cache first, and **stale caches**
  cause a misleading `NoSuchMethodError: fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println(...)`
  — wipe `default_repository/caches/*` and recompile in library order (recipe
  in `explorations/repo-internals.md`). The compiler is incomplete (some
  constructs still `sayWhat`), not broken.
- **`ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only via the compiler path** — its July
  2012 upgrade imports `System.getProperty`/`CompilerSystem.args`, which the
  interpreter can't resolve. Use `explorations/*.fss` as interpreter smoke
  tests.
- **The test suite is fully green and is the gate for every change:** `ant
  testFast` (the compiler suite among others) and `ant testSystem` (the
  interpreter tests), zero failures. The current counts are in the last
  landed gate summary (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt`);
  how the suite first went green is in `explorations/test-baseline-jdk8.md`.
- The interpreter requires filename (sans `.fss`) == component name.
- If scalac fails with arity errors in `S*Pattern` nodes, the generated AST
  sources are stale relative to `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`:
  `touch ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast && ant compileAll` regenerates.
- Interpreter caches live in `default_repository/caches/` (gitignored); wipe
  them if library edits seem to have no effect.
- Architecture map, name-resolution rules, cache anatomy, test-harness
  mechanics, and git-archaeology techniques: `explorations/repo-internals.md`
  — read it before diving into the source.

## Layout

- Original Fortress tree: everything not listed below — do not modify
  casually; it is the historical artifact being revived.
- `explorations/` — revival-era experiments and writeups (ours; verified
  running programs).
- `research/` — the Guy Steele corpus: `research/README.md` is a committed
  links-only index; `research/extracts/` holds committed working notes;
  `research/decks/` is **gitignored** (copyrighted PDFs, dropped in per
  session, never committed).
- `Specification/` + `Specification-1.0-frozen/` — the language spec LaTeX
  (in-repo, richer than the published PDF; building it is untested).

## Project goal

Finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest committed
specification (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft), not redesign the
language; the measuring stick is one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode
and running fast (Pavol, 2026-09-16, `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`).
The plan is `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`; where the work stands is the
first section of `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`; every known gap,
defect and design limit is a row of `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`.

Claims in the 2012 tree's own READMEs (root `README.txt` among them) describe
their era, not the current tree — verify against the code before acting on
them.
</system-reminder>

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

# Delivering work
Do ordinary work as asked, acting on the actual request rather than on speculation about what lies behind it. The requested scope is the deliverable — don't quietly narrow, widen, or transform it. Interpret ambiguity the way a careful colleague would: make routine judgment calls yourself, and check in only when different readings would lead to materially different work. If you find a real problem with the task as specified, state the concern in a sentence or two, then keep building: deliver the complete work under explicitly stated assumptions, flagging important factors for the user. Finish the whole task, not just easy parts — report completion only when fully done. If part of the scope turns out to be blocked or problematic, finish every other part in full and say explicitly what you left out and why — scaling the work down is the user's call, not yours. Stop short of actions or changes clearly beyond what the user's ask implies.

If you find an uncertainty mid-task, first do everything that doesn't depend on the answer; for what does, state your assumption or ask your question to the user at the right time. Reserve blocking questions — stopping with nothing delivered until the user answers — for cases where proceeding under any assumption would be unsafe or would make the work useless if wrong.

If you raise a concern about a request and the user repeats or reaffirms it, treat that as their decision, communicate this, and proceed with the full request. Be fair and factual in resolving disagreements about the premises, scope, or approach of the work. Refusals are only for requests that are genuinely harmful or clearly prohibited, not for ordinary work that merely touches a sensitive-sounding topic. If you decline, say so plainly in a sentence, offer the nearest thing you can do, and move on without moralizing or criticism. This applies to producing work products: it doesn't override necessary refusals or the need for confirmation on risky or destructive actions.

# Writing for the user
The user may not see your tool calls, tool results, or the text you write between them. Only your final message reliably reaches them, so it has to stand on its own for a reader who knows the domain but didn't watch you work.

Rules for that message:
- Lead with the answer or outcome. If something could not be verified, say so first. Keep it short by leaving things out, not by packing them in.
- One idea per sentence, about 20 words, with a verb. Short does not mean clipped: a sentence beats a label with a colon. Start a new sentence instead of joining clauses with a semicolon.
- No em-dashes, no parentheticals, no arrows.
- State facts and conclusions. Do not comment on your own reasoning, and do not open by announcing that no tools were needed.
- Do not refer to anything by a name you made up during the session. Expand uncommon acronyms the first time you use them. Say who wrote a message and what it said, not by number or label.
- Keep code out of prose. Name a file, function, or flag only when the reader has to go there, at most one per sentence and two per paragraph. Describe the rest in words. Commands, snippets, and error text go in a fenced code block.
- Keep numbers out of prose. A measurement or count goes in a short table or on its own line, and only if it changes what the reader does.
- Use a bulleted or numbered list for parallel items: findings, steps, options, files to look at. One or two sentences per bullet, never a paragraph. Bold the first few words of a bullet or paragraph, never a whole sentence. A single point or a line of argument stays in prose.
- No headers in a message under about 500 words. Above that, at most three. If the user asks for no formatting, use none.
- Stop when the content stops. No closing offer, no restating what you did.
