<!-- The design sketch for the first reserved fork of PLAN.md, the array representation on the compile path, written 2026-09-19 by a worker for Pavol and revised the same day after his three rulings (§6 quotes them): unboxed double[] is decided, the sized types are built as the team designed them with the checker taught nat parameters, and library work copies the library's own patterns. It assembles what next-climb.md §3a said a sketch must hold, adds the nat plan the second fork needs, and ends in a decision tree for what is still open. Eight probe programs were compiled in a private cache (§9); no tracked file was changed. Every recommendation is labelled "default" and decides nothing. One line per paragraph. -->

# How arrays should be built in the compiled world

## 0. The words used below

Boxing: a number wrapped in a heap object so that it can be treated like any other object. On the compile path every `RR64` is an `FRR64`, a Java object with one `double` field (`compiler/runtimeValues/FRR64.java:14-19`); adding two of them allocates a third. "Unboxed" means the bare JVM `double`, which lives in a register or in a `double[]` and costs nothing to make.

Stamping: the compiler writes a generic declaration (`Box[\T\]`) once as a template class; when a program first uses `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader reads the template and rewrites it with the argument's name filled in (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178`, the general case at `:210-290`; `Instantiater.java:48` substitutes the names). One stamped class per distinct argument list.

`nat` parameter: a static parameter that is a natural number rather than a type, written `Vector[\T, nat s0\]`; it puts a size into the type so that `Matrix[\T,n,m\]` times `Matrix[\T,m,p\]` can be declared with the shared `m`. Inference: working out a static argument the program did not write, from the types of the call's arguments.

Descriptor: the JVM's spelling of a type in bytecode. `D` is a bare double, `[D` an array of doubles, `Lcom/sun/…/FRR64;` a reference to the boxed class. Whether a field is boxed or not is exactly which of these its descriptor is.

View: an object that implements the array protocol (`get`/`put`) over some other array's storage without copying, such as a row of a matrix or a transposed matrix.

Rank: the number of indices an array takes; a vector has rank 1, a matrix rank 2, `Array3` rank 3. Shadow: compiled copies of a few source files placed first on the class path, so an edit can be tried and gated without changing a tracked file (`perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh`).

Project units: a rung is one worker session plus one skeptic under the batch script (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`); batch 1 was four rungs, fifteen agents, 3 h 11 min, with the full gate run once at 830 s (FACTS, ladder section). A rung that touches a `.java` or `.scala` file forces the full gate pair, and a batch holds at most one such rung; a library-only rung may drop `ant testSystem` (`next-climb.md` §5). The regression net is the ladder's 85 passing files (`compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/pass-list.txt`).

### 6d. The compiled representation of a nat-sized `double[]` array

Where the nat lives, two places, both needed: in the stamped class's name, `Vector⟦FRR64,16⟧` and `Vector⟦FRR64,4192⟧` being different classes, which the loader already produces from the mangled name (probe 6) and which is what makes the nat a fact for the checker and for dispatch; and as a run-time field of the native store (`dim_x` in the `FZZ32Vector` shape), because nothing today turns the name back into a value, the store's `get`, `put` and `|self|` need the number, and the `double[]` carries its own length. One class per distinct size is the price; microGPT's sizes are six literals and a computed 4192.

What the loader must do with a nat argument beyond what it does: supply a value for a nat in value position inside a template. Either the instantiater rewrites the `getstatic <Component>$n.ONLY` reference into a constant when it stamps `⟦…,5,…⟧` (an instruction-level substitution in `Instantiater`, the job the expando stub at `InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172` was left for), or the code generator emits a read from the run-time type descriptor, which today refuses `IntArg` (`CodeGen.java:5783`). Under the two-place representation the library's value uses of a nat are few (`i s1 + j` in `__DefaultArray2`, the `N[\s0\]` witness in `subarray`) and the store's field can serve the first; the second is explicit-only. So the value mechanism is a `.java` rung of its own, needed for the full port and not for the first kernels. Default: the field first, the name-to-constant substitution when the port reaches `subarray`.

Run-time sizes: `array[\RR64\](n)` with `n` computed cannot name its class at compile time. Either a native helper builds the stamped name from the integer and asks the loader for `Array1⟦FRR64,0,4192⟧` by that string, which is a string from a number and unprobed, or the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` as it already does in the model (`FlatArrays.fss:14-17`) and only literal and symbol sizes get sized classes. Default: the second; it is what the model writes today, and the `reflect` group of §6c is then the one library pattern the compiled world does not reproduce until the first is probed.

### 6e. The checker edit and the shadow route, assessed

The plan (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` §c-§f): a third track beside types and operators in the constraint solver, `Formula.scala` (711 lines) taking most of the diff, `TypeAnalyzer.pEqv` and its cast guard, `STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg`, `ExportChecker.equalIntExprs`, `TypeWellFormedChecker` rejecting arithmetic in a static argument; about 24 functions in five Scala files, 200-300 lines; no Java; the five nat compiler tests stay green; no catalogued test flips. Two items the plan did not close and this document's probes sharpen: the object crash of §6a is reproduced by a four-line object with no `extends`, so it is on the path of the very first sized declaration; and the code generator's `IntArg` refusal in `extends` is reached by every storing object.

The shadow route (`next-climb.md:102-104`; the recipe of `perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh`): copies of the five files compiled with `scala.tools.nsc.Main` into `shadow-classes`, placed first on the class path; the gate can be run with the shadow overlaid on `ProjectFortress/build`, as the template fix was (its 31 lines went green that way, `33-testfast.out`, `34-testsystem.out`). What it buys: the two unknowns, the object crash's source and the export checker's reach, are found without a sealed-tree edit, and the design of the inference variable can be tried as a reserved-name `IntRef` (the plan's option B) before the AST node (option A) is added, which a shadow cannot do because the AST is regenerated by `ant compileAll`. What it costs: a second toolchain path per iteration, and a prototype that differs from the real edit in that one representation. Assessment: the tree is unsealed and the batch script already runs `.scala` rungs under the full gate with the test written first, so the shadow is not a gate substitute; it is worth one worker session for the two unknowns and nothing more. Default: one shadow session for the object crash and the export checker, then the rung in the tree with option A.

The first failing test under `PLAN.md`'s rule, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NatInfer1.fss` with its `.test` naming `link`, `run`, `run_out_contains=PASS`: `object Box[\nat k\](v: ZZ32) end`, `unbox[\nat k\](b: Box[\k\]): ZZ32 = b.v`, `run() = if unbox(Box[\3\](7)) = 7 then println("PASS") end`; it fails today with `Not yet implemented` (probe 5 is the same shape). Beside it `NatObject1.fss` (a nat object instantiated with a literal, failing with the `ClassCastException`), `NatValue1.fss` (a nat in value position, failing at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError`), and the negative `XXXNatMismatch1.fss` (`same(Vec[\4\], Vec[\3\])`, `compile_err_equals` the mismatch message), which today compiles by the `pTrue()` hole and must be refused after.

## 7. The decision tree, with two questions closed

Question 1, boxed or `double[]`: closed by Pavol, `double[]`. Consequence: the `RR64` store is a hand-written class on the `FZZ32Vector` pattern, never a stamped generic (§2), and the boxed `Object[]` store exists only for element types that have no native store.

Question 4, where sizes live: closed by Pavol, in the type as the team designed. Consequences: the checker rung of §6e precedes the first sized declaration; the export checker and the object crash are on the path, not optional; every distinct size is a stamped class; the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array` until the string-from-number route is probed (§6d, default).

Question 2, open: what implements the library's sized traits under `double[]`?
Branch "native stores per element type under the library's generic objects": `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]` keeps its shape and its `mem` field is the `RR64` store for `RR64`, `FZZ32Vector` for `ZZ32`, the boxed store otherwise, chosen by the factory from the run-time type tag; the interpreter's own layering with `PrimitiveArray` replaced; one unprobed link, the non-generic store trait under the generic `Array` (§4c).
Branch "the loader picks a `double[]` template per instantiation": the expando route; `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,4192⟧` would load a different class than `PrimitiveArray⟦FZZ32,4192⟧`; nothing of it exists, and the instantiater's only tool is name substitution.
Default: the first; it needs one probe and no loader change, and it is the library's own structure.

Question 3, open: where do the loops run unboxed?
Branch "inside native whole-array operations": Java helpers over `double[]` for the contractions and elementwise maps; a box per operation; no code-generator change; the user lambdas of `fill`, `map`, `rows` still box per element.
Branch "in generated code": the code generator learns `D` locals, `daload`/`dastore`, `dadd`/`dmul` for statically `RR64` code; every rung `.java` under the full gate; unlocks unboxed loops written in Fortress.
Default: natives first, with the kernel measurement in the first array rung; generated-code unboxing as PLAN's step 4, once the measured residue says what it is worth.

Question 5, open, from the third ruling: the library's unused nats (`.fsi:1496-1523`). Branch "default an unconstrained nat to `0`" keeps the library's text; branch "refuse and delete the dead parameters" edits six library declarations. Default: the first, the plan's own recommendation, and the only reason the checker rung would otherwise touch `Library/`.

Where microGPT's 26 operations go is not a question after the third ruling: into `CompilerLibrary` in the library's own style, whose precedent for scalar extension is the `ZZ32` block at `FortressLibrary.fss:4477-4517` (`opr +(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], y: ZZ32)` beside `AdditiveGroup.+`, the same overloading shape the review found illegal by the letter and the interpreter accepts), for maps `map(f)` over `replica`, for structure the view objects, and for products the shared-nat operators of §6c.

## 8. What happens right after the choice

First, the checker rung (`.scala`, full gate): the four tests of §6e, the shadow session for the two unknowns, then the edit of `nat-checking-plan.md` §f with option A. What it moves: no ladder file by itself (the plan's census), no microGPT component; it unblocks every sized declaration.

Second, the array rung (`.java`, full gate), the first failing test `library_tests/Vector1.fss`: `v = vector[\RR64,3\](fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.5 i); if v[1] + v[2] = 4.5 then println("PASS") end`, failing today at disambiguation on `Vector`; then the `RR64` store class and helper, the non-generic store trait under `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` (the probe of §4c first), `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, `Array`, `Array1`, `Vector` and `__DefaultVector` in the library's spelling, the factories; in the same rung `kdot` compiled over a native `dot` and timed against `KDotPrim`. What it moves: the ladder's `Array` 6, `array` 2 and `Array1` 6 past disambiguation; of the eighteen microGPT components, the 8 stopped on `Array` and the 2 on `Vector` reach the checker.

Third, library-only rungs: `Array2`, `Matrix`, the transposed views and the shared-nat products (`kmat` timed); `Array3`; the scalar extension and elementwise maps for `RR64` arrays in the `ZZ32` block's style, which is where the compile path's overloading check on the model's operator pairs is measured; `Char` (5 components) and the immutable variant (`ImmutableArray`, 3 components and 26 ladder files) in whichever order the counts rank them.

The regression net is the ladder's 85 passing files (`compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/pass-list.txt`).

### 6d. The compiled representation of a nat-sized `double[]` array

Where the nat lives, two places, both needed: in the stamped class's name, `Vector⟦FRR64,16⟧` and `Vector⟦FRR64,4192⟧` being different classes, which the loader already produces from the mangled name (probe 6) and which is what makes the nat a fact for the checker and for dispatch; and as a run-time field of the native store (`dim_x` in the `FZZ32Vector` shape), because nothing today turns the name back into a value, the store's `get`, `put` and `|self|` need the number, and the `double[]` carries its own length. One class per distinct size is the price; microGPT's sizes are six literals and a computed 4192.

What the loader must do with a nat argument beyond what it does: supply a value for a nat in value position inside a template. Either the instantiater rewrites the `getstatic <Component>$n.ONLY` reference into a constant when it stamps `⟦…,5,…⟧` (an instruction-level substitution in `Instantiater`, the job the expando stub at `InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172` was left for), or the code generator emits a read from the run-time type descriptor, which today refuses `IntArg` (`CodeGen.java:5783`). Under the two-place representation the library's value uses of a nat are few (`i s1 + j` in `__DefaultArray2`, the `N[\s0\]` witness in `subarray`) and the store's field can serve the first; the second is explicit-only. So the value mechanism is a `.java` rung of its own, needed for the full port and not for the first kernels. Default: the field first, the name-to-constant substitution when the port reaches `subarray`.

Run-time sizes: `array[\RR64\](n)` with `n` computed cannot name its class at compile time. Either a native helper builds the stamped name from the integer and asks the loader for `Array1⟦FRR64,0,4192⟧` by that string, which is a string from a number and unprobed, or the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` as it already does in the model (`FlatArrays.fss:14-17`) and only literal and symbol sizes get sized classes. Default: the second; it is what the model writes today, and the `reflect` group of §6c is then the one library pattern the compiled world does not reproduce until the first is probed.

### 6e. The checker edit and the shadow route, assessed

The plan (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` §c-§f): a third track beside types and operators in the constraint solver, `Formula.scala` (711 lines) taking most of the diff, `TypeAnalyzer.pEqv` and its cast guard, `STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg`, `ExportChecker.equalIntExprs`, `TypeWellFormedChecker` rejecting arithmetic in a static argument; about 24 functions in five Scala files, 200-300 lines; no Java; the five nat compiler tests stay green; no catalogued test flips. Two items the plan did not close and this document's probes sharpen: the object crash of §6a is reproduced by a four-line object with no `extends`, so it is on the path of the very first sized declaration; and the code generator's `IntArg` refusal in `extends` is reached by every storing object.

The shadow route (`next-climb.md:102-104`; the recipe of `perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh`): copies of the five files compiled with `scala.tools.nsc.Main` into `shadow-classes`, placed first on the class path; the gate can be run with the shadow overlaid on `ProjectFortress/build`, as the template fix was (its 31 lines went green that way, `33-testfast.out`, `34-testsystem.out`). What it buys: the two unknowns, the object crash's source and the export checker's reach, are found without a sealed-tree edit, and the design of the inference variable can be tried as a reserved-name `IntRef` (the plan's option B) before the AST node (option A) is added, which a shadow cannot do because the AST is regenerated by `ant compileAll`. What it costs: a second toolchain path per iteration, and a prototype that differs from the real edit in that one representation. Assessment: the tree is unsealed and the batch script already runs `.scala` rungs under the full gate with the test written first, so the shadow is not a gate substitute; it is worth one worker session for the two unknowns and nothing more. Default: one shadow session for the object crash and the export checker, then the rung in the tree with option A.

The first failing test under `PLAN.md`'s rule, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NatInfer1.fss` with its `.test` naming `link`, `run`, `run_out_contains=PASS`: `object Box[\nat k\](v: ZZ32) end`, `unbox[\nat k\](b: Box[\k\]): ZZ32 = b.v`, `run() = if unbox(Box[\3\](7)) = 7 then println("PASS") end`; it fails today with `Not yet implemented` (probe 5 is the same shape). Beside it `NatObject1.fss` (a nat object instantiated with a literal, failing with the `ClassCastException`), `NatValue1.fss` (a nat in value position, failing at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError`), and the negative `XXXNatMismatch1.fss` (`same(Vec[\4\], Vec[\3\])`, `compile_err_equals` the mismatch message), which today compiles by the `pTrue()` hole and must be refused after.

## 7. The decision tree, with two questions closed

Question 1, boxed or `double[]`: closed by Pavol, `double[]`. Consequence: the `RR64` store is a hand-written class on the `FZZ32Vector` pattern, never a stamped generic (§2), and the boxed `Object[]` store exists only for element types that have no native store.

Question 4, where sizes live: closed by Pavol, in the type as the team designed. Consequences: the checker rung of §6e precedes the first sized declaration; the export checker and the object crash are on the path, not optional; every distinct size is a stamped class; the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array` until the string-from-number route is probed (§6d, default).

Question 2, open: what implements the library's sized traits under `double[]`?
Branch "native stores per element type under the library's generic objects": `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]` keeps its shape and its `mem` field is the `RR64` store for `RR64`, `FZZ32Vector` for `ZZ32`, the boxed store otherwise, chosen by the factory from the run-time type tag; the interpreter's own layering with `PrimitiveArray` replaced; one unprobed link, the non-generic store trait under the generic `Array` (§4c).
Branch "the loader picks a `double[]` template per instantiation": the expando route; `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,4192⟧` would load a different class than `PrimitiveArray⟦FZZ32,4192⟧`; nothing of it exists, and the instantiater's only tool is name substitution.
Default: the first; it needs one probe and no loader change, and it is the library's own structure.

Question 3, open: where do the loops run unboxed?
Branch "inside native whole-array operations": Java helpers over `double[]` for the contractions and elementwise maps; a box per operation; no code-generator change; the user lambdas of `fill`, `map`, `rows` still box per element.
Branch "in generated code": the code generator learns `D` locals, `daload`/`dastore`, `dadd`/`dmul` for statically `RR64` code; every rung `.java` under the full gate; unlocks unboxed loops written in Fortress.
Default: natives first, with the kernel measurement in the first array rung; generated-code unboxing as PLAN's step 4, once the measured residue says what it is worth.

Question 5, open, from the third ruling: the library's unused nats (`.fsi:1496-1523`). Branch "default an unconstrained nat to `0`" keeps the library's text; branch "refuse and delete the dead parameters" edits six library declarations. Default: the first, the plan's own recommendation, and the only reason the checker rung would otherwise touch `Library/`.

Where microGPT's 26 operations go is not a question after the third ruling: into `CompilerLibrary` in the library's own style, whose precedent for scalar extension is the `ZZ32` block at `FortressLibrary.fss:4477-4517` (`opr +(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], y: ZZ32)` beside `AdditiveGroup.+`, the same overloading shape the review found illegal by the letter and the interpreter accepts), for maps `map(f)` over `replica`, for structure the view objects, and for products the shared-nat operators of §6c.

## 8. What happens right after the choice

First, the checker rung (`.scala`, full gate): the four tests of §6e, the shadow session for the two unknowns, then the edit of `nat-checking-plan.md` §f with option A. What it moves: no ladder file by itself (the plan's census), no microGPT component; it unblocks every sized declaration.

Second, the array rung (`.java`, full gate), the first failing test `library_tests/Vector1.fss`: `v = vector[\RR64,3\](fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.5 i); if v[1] + v[2] = 4.5 then println("PASS") end`, failing today at disambiguation on `Vector`; then the `RR64` store class and helper, the non-generic store trait under `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` (the probe of §4c first), `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, `Array`, `Array1`, `Vector` and `__DefaultVector` in the library's spelling, the factories; in the same rung `kdot` compiled over a native `dot` and timed against `KDotPrim`. What it moves: the ladder's `Array` 6, `array` 2 and `Array1` 6 past disambiguation; of the eighteen microGPT components, the 8 stopped on `Array` and the 2 on `Vector` reach the checker.

Third, library-only rungs: `Array2`, `Matrix`, the transposed views and the shared-nat products (`kmat` timed); `Array3`; the scalar extension and elementwise maps for `RR64` arrays in the `ZZ32` block's style, which is where the compile path's overloading check on the model's operator pairs is measured; `Char` (5 components) and the immutable variant (`ImmutableArray`, 3 components and 26 ladder files) in whichever order the counts rank them.

What the probes say. `p1_monostore.fss`: a generic `Arr[\T\]`, a monomorphic `DStore extends Arr[\RR64\]`, and `mk[\T\](x: T): Arr[\T\] = DStore()`. Refused: `Function body has type DStore, but declared return type is Arr[\T\]` (`p1_monostore.compile.out`). `p1b_typecase.fss`, the library's own idiom from `array1` (`FortressLibrary.fss:2240-2244`), `typecase w of () -> RR64 => DStore() else => BStore[\T\](x) end`: refused, `Function body has type OR(DStore,BStore[\T\]), but declared return type is Arr[\T\]` (`p1b_typecase.compile.out`). So the shape is one monomorphic storing object per native element type (`__RR64Vector[\nat s0\]() extends Vector[\RR64,s0\]` with `mem: RR64Store`) beside the generic boxed one, and the problem moves to the factory `vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]()`, which must return the monomorphic object for `T = RR64` inside a body the checker types with `T` abstract; the probes show it cannot. ### Decision A. What puts `double[]` under the library's sized traits

What we do: choose the mechanism by which `Vector[\RR64,16\]` gets a `double[]` store while `Vector[\T,16\]` for other `T` gets a boxed one.

What it changes: which `.java` rung the array work needs first, and whether the library's generic factories keep their text.

content.text:
**Row 40: the three array-design defaults**

**What the row is.** On 09-19 a worker wrote `array-design.md`, which asked five questions about how arrays should be built on the compiled path. You answered two of them: `double[]` storage, and sizes in the types as the team designed. The worker had marked its own answers to the other three as "defaults". I let those stand without asking you, so the post-mortem put them on the docket as row 40. Nothing was built on any of them.

**1. Which object holds the numbers, per element type.** The element type is what the array holds, such as `RR64` or `ZZ32`.
- **The library's way:** there is one generic storing object per rank (vector, matrix, 3-D). `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]` holds its numbers in a field `mem` of type `PrimitiveArray[\T,s0\]`, and that one store type serves every element type (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2210-2211`). For unboxed storage, the team left two pointers to the same idea: the class loader would write a `double[]` version of that store when it stamps the `RR64` instance. They are the list of unboxing cases in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:12-19` and the empty stub in `InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`.
- **The default:** keep the generic object and let its factory choose the store. The factory is the function that makes a new array, like `vector[\RR64,3\]()`. It would look at the element type while the program runs and pick a `double[]` store for `RR64` and a boxed one for anything else.
- **Since then:** the review showed by probe that the compiled checker refuses this shape, even when it is written the library's own way with `typecase`. The default is refuted.
- **Other languages:** Java boxes every generic element (`ArrayList<Double>`). C#, Rust and Julia store raw doubles, because they make one version of the code per element type. Scala chooses `double[]` at run time from a class tag, which is what the default copied.

**2. Where an array's size lives at run time.**
- **The library's way:** in the type. The matrix store is `PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1)\]`, meaning s0 times s1 is written inside the type (`.fss:2423`), and the interpreter reads the size from there.
- **The default:** the size goes in the class name, where the checker sees it, and also in a plain field on the store. There were two reasons for the field:
  - the checker's planned `nat` design refuses arithmetic like `(s0 s1)` inside a type;
  - nothing turned a size in a type back into a number.
- **Since then:** the review called this default right and forced. Design B's value-position piece will turn a size in a type into a number, but the `(s0 s1)` arithmetic is still refused, so a matrix store still needs the field.
- **Other languages:** Rust's `[f64; N]` and C++'s `std::array<double, N>` keep a fixed size only in the type. Their growable arrays, `Vec` and `std::vector`, keep it in a field.

**3. What type an array gets when its size is known only at run time,** for example a size computed from the data.
- **The library's way:** `reflect` turns a number known only at run time into a size type, so the array still gets a sized type (`.fss:2342`, `:2747`). `reflect` exists only in the interpreter. The team's comment at `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fss:39` says "we ought to build it in".
- **The default:** return the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, an array type with no size in it. That is what C4's vocabulary does today.
- **Since then:** the review found that this stops microGPT at the checker, because the library's products are declared only on sized types. Also, tonight's size probe showed a factory can build a size's descriptor from a number known only at run time (`RTTIsize.of`). A compiled `reflect` would need exactly that.
- **Other languages:** in Rust and C++, a size known only at run time gets the unsized type (`Vec`). Julia can build a sized type from such a size, and pays for it with dispatch at run time.

**What else has moved.** The one-library decision (09-20 and 09-21) replaced the design's plan to put microGPT's operations in the compiler's own library. On 09-22 you put the array decisions after the switch-over.

**The choices**
- **Close as no decision taken.** The three stop being defaults. There is nothing to revert, because nothing was built. The questions come back with the array design after the switch-over, in the protocol's way:
  - a clean worker lists every way the language and library offer, the library's own way first;
  - then the nine steps;
  - then your decision.

  This costs nothing now and commits you to nothing now.
- **Approve them as they stand.** The array rung's brief would then carry a store choice the checker refuses, and unsized arrays that stop microGPT at the checker.
- **Decide the three now.** Each would need the clean worker's list and the nine steps now, one or more Opus workers, even though the switch-over they depend on has not happened.

Recommendation: close row 40 as no decision taken.

content.text:
Yes, Fortress has `RR32`, a 32-bit float. We used `RR64` because of how we checked the ports, not because microGPT needs 64 bits.

**Why `RR64`**
- The reference is Karpathy's pure-Python microGPT. A Python `float` is a 64-bit double.
- Every port was checked against goldens, the expected values that the Python reference produced in float64 (`explorations/experiment/run-c-goldens/README.md`).
- The briefs' pass marks are float64 tolerances:
  - the loss must match to 1e-12;
  - the gradient and the first Adam step to about 1e-15 (`RUN_C_BRIEF.md:21-22`).
- `RR32` keeps about 7 significant digits, so a 32-bit port could never meet those marks.
- Your 09-19 ruling says "double array". I found nothing on record that discusses the element width itself. The point you were making then was unboxed against boxed.

**Your premise is right.** Nobody trains in FP64. Training usually does its math in BF16 or FP16 and keeps the master weights and optimizer state in FP32. Inference is often quantized lower still.

**What Fortress has today**
- In the interpreter, `RR32` is declared as `value object RR32 extends RR64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:47`), so it sits under `RR64` in the tower. Support for it is thin: the interpreter's library names `RR32` only 3 times.
- The compiler's library declares it as a sibling of `RR64` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:475`), with its own runtime class, `FRR32`. That is already the flat shape that route A gives the whole tower.

**What switching to `RR32` would mean for the goal**
- **Speed:** a `float[]` moves half the bytes of a `double[]`. Where the JIT vectorizes, each vector instruction handles twice as many values. microGPT's kernels are dot products that mostly wait on memory, so FP32 is the fair "fast" target. The pure-Java floor you asked for on 09-16 should use the same type.
- **Checks:** the goldens would need a float32 run of the reference, or checks with float32-sized tolerances.
- **The model's text:** `RR64` appears on 17 lines of `MicroGptFlat.fss`. Changing it is a model edit, which you see as a diff first. Alternatively, the vocabulary could be generic in the element type, so the model names the type in one place.
- **The library:** the array work would have to carry `RR32` as fully as `RR64`.

Recommendation: add the element width, `RR32` or `RR64`, to the array questions that come back after the switch-over, next to row 40's three.

Destination: the compiler's prelude is the specification's, `AnyType`, `FortressBuiltin`, `FortressLibrary`, and `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra` are deleted at the switch-over. From `main` at the batch-2 landing:

**Step 0, now: stop adding to the compiler prelude.** Nothing is in flight (the tree is clean; the nine `wip/` remotes are landed batches awaiting deletion). The fourteen fork-free rungs were forecast to move 38 files by one phase and no microGPT component, and every one is a declaration `FortressLibrary` already has. Codegen rungs continue, being compiler work under any library: `forTryAtomicExpr` (row 353), `LetFn` (row 304), `ObjectExpr`, the eleven-file array-literal crash at `Misc.scala:876`. Prelude rungs (`Char`, `Thread`, `round`/`truncate`, `IndexOutOfBounds`) stop. The landed rungs' tests stay; the ten `library_tests` files that use compiler-world spellings (`NothingObject`, `Character`, `ZZ32Vector`) are rewritten at step 5.

**Step 1, the first rung: the interpreter prelude through the checker, as a gate stage.** Edit: `fortress typecheck` gets a `-fortress-lib` switch, the mirror of `-compiler-lib` (`Shell.java:860-863`; `typecheck` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` unconditionally today), or the 46-line `perf-probes/prelude/WorldFlip.java` moves into the harness; a stage in `climb-batch-workflow.js` beside the ladder regression runs the checker over the three apis and what they import under a private cache, prints the per-api error table and the crash line, and lands the table as the comparand. What it proves: that the distance to one library is measured by every gate from now on, and that the world switch is four lines. Stop condition: two runs print the same table (93 errors, 48 sites, 12 apis, `Not yet implemented` at `STypesUtil.scala:557`); the count is red, the suite is green; no library line changes. This is the one place the test-first rule is met by a stage rather than a `.fss`, because no program can yet be compiled against that prelude; the stage is permanent, which is what the rule protects.

Same batch, rungs 2 and 3, the defects with no question attached: family C, the fifteen `RangeInternals.fsi` bounds (`I extends AnyIntegral` where `Integral[\I\]` is required), 26 errors; families D and F and the site that extends and excludes `Condition[\()\]` in one line (`FortressLibrary.fsi:2526`), 4 errors. Gated by `testSystem`, which runs this code. Expected: 93 → 63 at 23 sites, nothing new. Stop: a fix that would change a declared type rather than a bound.

**Step 2, three worker sessions in parallel, no gate.** (a) The exclusion trace: for each of the 23 sites, which of the four clauses fires, beside the spec lines above; output: the sites under a stated rule (library rungs), the sites under the contradicted clause (a checker rung), and the sites under the `comprises` clause, the only decision that reaches Pavol. (b) The `nat` shadow session the review's decision F specifies: where the crash is (Scala or Java, finding 6), the export checker on the six dead-nat declarations (decision E: E2 in the checker, E3 the six-line api diff shown to Pavol), `NatExtends1`, `NatStore1`, and the loader probe that decides decision A (A2, the team's direction, against A3). (c) The half-session probe: a two-declaration component bound with `import java`, run by the interpreter; decides the builtins' shape for step 5.

**Step 3, the `nat` rung, then the exclusion rungs.** PLAN step 4 in the tree, shadow-proven, `.scala` plus whatever `.java` the shadow found: one to two gated batches. Decision E lands inside it. Then step 2(a)'s rungs, zero to two, or the `comprises` decision first. Stop condition of the phase: the stage prints zero errors and no crash, and `FlatArrays.fsi` type-checks with no error of its own (already true but for `nat`, FACTS). Milestone: `fortress typecheck -fortress-lib` works on interpreter programs.

**Step 4, one worker session: the prelude through DESUGAR and CODEGEN once.** No run has ever reached them with this library; the size is not on record. Output: the hole list, each hole a codegen rung, most of them rungs the ladder needs anyway.

**Step 5, the switch-over: at least two gated batches, with the one-`.java`-rung rule relaxed for them (as B1 proposed for the interpreter batch).** Batch one, the natives, re-bound as 2(c) decided: the 29 of 108 without a helper written, the 231 of `FortressBuiltin` matched to the compiler's helpers. Batch two, the names: the 38 sources and the frozen stub re-pointed; the two `useCompilerLibraries()` collapsed to one world with the extends-`Object` setting kept; the compile recipe's five files made three; the five prelude files deleted; the at least 48 compiler-side tests that name compiler-world spellings (a rough grep) rewritten to the spec's (`Nothing[\T\]`, `Char`). Gate: the full suite, the atomic runs, and the ladder regression, where the 85 passes must hold and the 104 fork-blocked files are expected to move off `Array is undefined`. Not settled: whether `FZZ32` implements `FortressLibrary.ZZ32` or `FortressBuiltin.Int` (the interpreter's `Int` is a value object under the trait; the compiler's value class is the trait's implementation); and, if 2(c) says two components, the mechanism, which is the step row 320 found missing (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`).

**Step 6, decision D: a diff, no code.** The model's static types (D1 with D3, the review's default) shown to Pavol as the diff of `rmsn` and `step`'s signature, as soon as step 3 lands and before any array rung.

content.text:
I've recorded row 40 as closed with no decision taken, in POSITIONS and the boot note. The element width question (`RR32` against `RR64`) is also written down as open.

**The switch-over** is the point where the compiled path stops using its own small library and reads the interpreter's library instead.

- **Today there are two libraries:**
  - the interpreter's, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, which is the one the specification describes;
  - the compiler's own starter library, `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, which the team called a temporary hack in 2008.
- On 09-20 and 09-21 you decided there will be one library, the interpreter's. The switch-over is where that happens (step 5 of `coordinator/library-route-judgement.md`).

**What the switch-over does.** It takes at least two gated batches.
- **The natives.** These are the library functions implemented in Java. Each one gets a binding the compiled path can call. Most already have a compiled helper under another name, and the rest get written.
- **The names:**
  - the compiler is pointed at the one library;
  - the compiler's three library files are deleted;
  - the compiler-side tests that use spellings only the compiler's library has are rewritten to the specification's spellings and kept. Those spellings are `ZZ32Vector`, `NothingObject` and `Character`.
- **The gate:** the full suite plus the ladder regression. The array-blocked ladder files are expected to get past "`Array` is undefined" for the first time.

**What has to come before it.** The compiler's checker must accept the interpreter's library. Today it reports 103 errors there. The work to get there:
- batch 4:
  - interpreter coercion;
  - the specification rung;
  - the first rung of teaching the checker sizes (`nat`);
- the batch after that: flattening the numeric tower (route A), and the rest of the size work;
- then one pass of the library through the compiler's later stages, to list the holes code generation still has.

**What waits until after it.**
- The array design: row 40's three questions, the array decisions A, B and D, and the element width.
- Several ledger rows close at the switch-over itself. One example is the specification's `shift`, which reaches the compiled path only then.

Two points are not settled yet:
- whether the compiled `ZZ32` class implements the library's `ZZ32` trait or `FortressBuiltin`'s `Int`;
- if the builtins end up as two components, how an api gets linked to a component with a different name. That is ledger row 320's missing piece.

The next item on the list is the judge-tier ask. I'll put it to you in the next message unless you say otherwise.

You can run batch 4 without closing all of them. What decides it is whether an open row affects something the batch builds on, edits, or is judged by. Going through them:

**No bearing on batch 4.** These can be decided alongside the batch or after it.
- **Row 41:** the api-to-component link. That is linker work, and it comes up at the switch-over.
- **Row 44:** `TryAtomicFailure` revived in the compiler's library. That library is deleted at the switch-over.
- **Rows 42, 45 and 46:** a test added outside its brief, and ledger rows reclassified or left as rows. These are questions about the record, and batch 4 touches none of their files.
- **Homes 374–377:** which kind of gated test four known failures get. None of their files is in a batch 4 rung.

**Bear on batch 4 through the gate that judges it**
- **Row 47:** the four interpreter test shards are compared by their sum, not one by one. Batch 4 adds interpreter tests, and each added file shifts the other files between shards (FACTS § The harness and the gate). If the per-shard comparison came back, the gate would go red for no real reason.
- **Row 48:** the gate compares against the last landed batch's summary, not a fixed baseline. Batches 3 and 3.5 were judged and landed that way.

Both rules are what the gate does today. If you don't answer them, batch 4 runs under them as they stand.

There is one precedent to weigh. On 09-22 you said batch 3 would wait until the rows then open were decided. In the end batches 3 and 3.5 ran with rows 30 and 39–48 still open. I haven't found your word waiving that in the record.

The batch also needs two things before it launches:
- the judge-tier ask, because it changes the script;
- the manifest, which isn't written yet and comes to you for a go.

Recommendation: take rows 47 and 48 now, one message each, then the judge-tier ask, then batch 4's manifest; the other rows and the four homes can follow alongside the batch.

  - Factories. [read]
    - `__makeZZ32Vector(l1, d1, l2, d2)` is in the builtin api (`.fsi:589`, `.fss:1150`).

  Measured on a 5-element vector (probe `VecBasics`), a program can do the following:
  
  - `makeZZ32Vector(5)` prints `[0 0 0 0 0]`. `|v|` is 5, `nrows` is 5 and `ncols` is 0.
  - `v.fill(7)` gives `[7 7 7 7 7]`. `v.fill(fn (i) => i i)` gives `[0 1 4 9 16]`.
  - After `v[2] := 42`, `v[2]` is 42.
  - After `w = v.copy; w[0] := 99`, only `w` has changed.
  - The operators give these results:
    - `v + 1` gives `[1 2 43 10 17]`.
    - `v - 1` gives `[-1 0 41 8 15]`.
    - `v MAX 5` gives `[5 5 42 9 16]`.
    - `v MIN 5` gives `[0 1 5 5 5]`.
    - `PREFIX_SUM v` gives `[0 1 43 52 68]`.
  - `makeZZ32Vector(2, 3)` followed by `fill2(fn (i, j) => 10 i + j)` prints `(2,3)`, then the rows `0 1 2` and `10 11 12`.
    - `|m|` is 6, `nrows` is 2, `ncols` is 3 and `m[1,2]` is 12.
    - `m.shape` is `(2, 3)`.

  ## 3. From source text to the Java class
  
  This section follows `v[2] := 42; x = v[2]`, where `v: ZZ32Vector`.
  
  1. Names. The program sees `ZZ32Vector` and `makeZZ32Vector` through the prelude, without an import. [read]
  2. Desugaring. Before type checking, `v[2]` becomes a call of a method on `v` named `_[_]`, and `v[2] := 42` becomes a call of one named `_[_]:=` (`compiler/desugarer/AssignmentAndSubscriptDesugarer.scala:75-80`). Guy Steele wrote this in October 2011 (section 5). [read]
     - The code generator's own subscript case, `CodeGen.forSubscriptExpr` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:4924-4982`), still has vector-specific code (`:4970-4981`, "Unknow Vector type").
     - Its first statement is `if (x == x) throw new Error("Should not be a subscriptExpr here in codegen!")` (`:4932`), so all of that code is dead.
  3. The name mapping. `NamingCzar` (`compiler/NamingCzar.java`, about 2K lines) is the compiler's table of translations between Fortress names and JVM names.
     - Its *special table* maps a few builtin traits straight to hand-written classes, not to generated interfaces. The vector entries are `bl(fortLib, "ZZ32Vector", "FZZ32Vector")` and `bl(fortLib, "StringVector", "FStringVector")` (`:553-554`, in the table at `:538-555`). [read]
     - As a result, every slot whose Fortress type is `ZZ32Vector` (a local, field, parameter or result) has the JVM type `com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32Vector`. The lookups are at `:1443-1444` and `:1544`. [read]
     - The generated library methods confirm this: they are `getValue(FZZ32Vector, FZZ32)`, `\=_\{_\}(FZZ32Vector, FZZ32)` and so on, with `self` typed as the Java class. [measured, javap]
  4. The call. The receiver's type is in the special table, so `CodeGen.methodCall` emits `invokevirtual` on `FZZ32Vector` rather than `invokeinterface` on the interface (`CodeGen.java:604-610`). The table's own comment says this is its only use (`NamingCzar.java:558-566`). [read]
     - The program's bytecode has `invokevirtual FZZ32Vector."\=_\{_\}"(FZZ32)FZZ32` for `v[2]`, and `…"\=_\{_\}\!="(FZZ32, FZZ32)FVoid` for the assignment. These JVM names are mangled spellings of `_[_]` and `_[_]:=`. [measured, javap]
  5. The trait bodies. `CompilerBuiltin.fss` is compiled like any other Fortress component. [measured: listing and javap of `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`]
     - The trait `ZZ32Vector` becomes an interface, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32Vector`.
     - Its bodies go into an abstract class, `…$DefaultTraitMethods`. Each body is a static method that takes `self`, plus an instance method that forwards to it.
     - Descriptor classes `…$RTTIc` and `…$RTTIi` are also generated.
     - `FZZ32Vector` extends the abstract class at run time.
  6. The native bindings. The line `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{simpleIntVector.getIndexedValue => jIntVectorGet, …}` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:305-311`) names seven static methods of `nativeHelpers/simpleIntVector.java` (40 lines). [read]
     - Each of them forwards to the class in one line. For example, `getIndexedValue(FZZ32Vector v, int i)` returns `v.getIndexedValue(i)` (`:17-39`).
     - `simpleStringVector.java` (27 lines) does the same for strings (`:18-25`).
  
     Two parts of the compiler turn such a line into something callable:
     - `repository/ForeignJava.java` reads the Java class with ASM and makes up a Fortress api for it. [read]
       - For each Java parameter type it asks `NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType` for a Fortress type.
       - A class that extends the Fortress top type `fortress.AnyType.Any` goes through a chain of `else if`s. There, `FZZ32Vector` becomes the trait `ZZ32Vector` and `FStringVector` becomes `StringVector` (`NamingCzar.java:329-349`, with the vectors at `:337-340` and the `Any` test at `:304-319`).
       - So from Fortress, the helper `getIndexedValue(FZZ32Vector, int): int` looks like `(ZZ32Vector, ZZ32) -> ZZ32`.
     - `compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java` writes a wrapper class, `native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntVector`, into the cache directory `nativewrapper_cache`. The wrapper's methods take and return the compiled path's boxed values. [read]
       - For each parameter it looks up a converter. `FZZ32` has one: unbox with `getValue()` and box with `make` (`:139`).
       - A class that extends `Any` gets the empty converter and passes through as itself (`:250-270`, the pass-through at `:253-256`).
       - The wrapper's `getIndexedValue(FZZ32Vector, FZZ32)` calls `FZZ32.getValue()`, then the helper, then `FZZ32.make(int)`. [measured, javap of the wrappers]
       - The `StringVector` wrapper works the same way. It uses `FJavaString.make(String)` for results and `FJavaString.getValue()` for arguments. [measured, javap of the wrappers]
  7. One element read, as it runs. The stack trace of an out-of-range read shows seven frames between the program's `run` and the array access. [measured]
     - The frames are, from the outside in:
       - the `_[_]` instance method and its static body (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:1125`);
       - the `getValue` pair (`:1121`);
       - the generated native wrapper;
       - `simpleIntVector.getIndexedValue` (`:20`);
       - `FZZ32Vector.getIndexedValue` (`:64`).
     - The index arrives as a boxed `FZZ32`, and the result leaves as a new `FZZ32`.
     - `array-design.md` counted the same chain as four calls and one allocation per element read. [cited: `explorations/coordinator/array-design.md:41`, probe 2 at `:195`]
     - I did not measure whether the JIT removes any of this.
  8. The class loader. At run time the custom loader, `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`, loads nearly every class itself. For a name with no generic markers, such as `com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32Vector`, it reads the bytes and defines them unchanged (`:199-210`, `:286-289`). No stamping happens for the vectors themselves, because they are not generic. [read]
  9. Stamping does touch the vectors when one is used as a type argument.
     - Take `object Cell[\T\](x: T) end` and `Cell[\ZZ32Vector\](makeZZ32Vector(2))`. The program compiles, then dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError: com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32Vector$RTTIc`. The error is raised in the static initializer of the stamped function class for `Cell`'s constructor. [measured]
     - `Cell[\StringVector\]` fails the same way, with `FStringVector$RTTIc`. [measured]
     - The cause, from the code: the stamped code asks for the descriptor by appending `$RTTIc` to the class name (`runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:134-138`, `Naming.java:1043-1051`), but the vectors' nested class is named `RTTIv`. [read]
     - I ran a probe-only check. I compiled a copy of `FZZ32Vector.java` with one extra nested class, `RTTIc`, whose `ONLY` field returns `RTTIv.ONLY`, into a scratch directory, and put that directory first on the run class path. The same compiled program then ran and printed `[0 0]`. [measured; nothing in the tree was changed]

     - FACTS.md:38 and `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md:77` recorded the `ZZ32Vector` case earlier, without a cause. [cited] No row of `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md` names it. [measured by grep]
  10. Raw Java arrays in a native helper's signature. `NamingCzar` also maps the Java type `int[]` (descriptor `[I`) to `ZZ32Vector`, and it has a clause for `"[String"` (`:381-384`). [read] Neither works:

[read]
  11. The bytecode optimizer is an optional later pass that the test harness runs as an extra step (`tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:1006-1015`). [read; not run]

  ## 4. What has the same shape, what does not, and why
  
  What has the same shape [read]:
  
  - Seventeen classes in `runtimeValues/` extend a generated `DefaultTraitMethods`: `FBoolean`, `FCharacter`, `FFloatLiteral`, `FIntLiteral`, `FJavaBufferedReader`, `FJavaBufferedWriter`, `FJavaString`, `FNN32`, `FNN64`, `FRR32`, `FRR64`, `FString`, `FStringVector`, `FZZ`, `FZZ32`, `FZZ32Vector` and `FZZ64` (grep). Each one is the hand-written run-time class of one builtin trait.
  - Fourteen of those traits, plus void, are in `NamingCzar`'s special table (`:538-555`), so their Fortress type is lowered straight to the class. `IntLiteral`, `FloatLiteral` and `String` are not in the table.
  - Each class has a nested descriptor class with a static `ONLY` field.
  
  How the vectors differ [read]:
  
  - Contents.
    - The scalars wrap one final value. For example, `FZZ32` wraps a `final int` (`FZZ32.java:16`).
    - The two vectors are the only classes that hold a Java array, and the only ones whose contents change after construction.
    - `FJavaBufferedReader` and `FJavaBufferedWriter` wrap a Java stream object.
  - Native wrappers.
    - The scalars have converters in `FortressMethodAdapter.java:139-155`, so the wrapper unboxes them to `int`, `double` and so on.
    - The vectors have no converter. A helper receives the vector object itself (step 6 of section 3).
  - Descriptor names.
    - Thirteen classes name their nested descriptor `RTTIc`, which is the name the loader asks for.
    - The vectors use `RTTIv`. The buffered reader and writer use `RTTIjbr` and `RTTIjbw` (`FJavaBufferedReader.java:33`). I did not run the reader or writer as type arguments.
  - Foreign mapping.
    - The scalars map from Java primitive types through a table (`NamingCzar.java:436-459`).
    - The vectors map from their own classes through the `else if` chain (`:337-340`).
  
  What does not exist on the compiled path:
  
  - There is no vector of `RR64`, `ZZ64` or any other element type, and no generic array. `Array`, `Vector`, `Matrix` and `array[\T\]` are undefined there. [cited: ledger rows 72 and 305, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:303`, `:317`]
  - The interpreter's library works differently. [read]
    - Its arrays are generic Fortress types that carry sizes, such as `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2099`) and `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]` (`:2210`).
    - They sit over one generic native store, `PrimitiveArray[\T, nat s0\]`. Its `get` and `put` are interpreter natives (`LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss:18-26`).
  - The interpreter's library has the same prefix sum on `Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]`. It sits under the comment "Some random stuff related to arrays and the MCKPE benchmark" (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4489-4503`; Steele, `fc1937ae0`). The compiled block in `CompilerLibrary.fss:484-519` has the same shape for `ZZ32Vector`, and it came eight days after the interpreter's version. [read; git]
  
  Why, as far as the tree and the commit messages say [git]:
  
  - Flood's first commit message is "Simple Integer 1 dimensional arrays." (`f4973a717`).
  - `StringVector` was made for the program arguments.
    - Before `24717d4ad`, `CompilerSystem.args` was an object with native hooks. Its comment read: "Right now this is a massive hack, to make the native wrapper use array-like *notation* without actually supporting native-side arrays per se. This should be remedied as soon as is practical."
    - That commit replaced it with `args : StringVector`. Its message says: "Updated CompilerSystem.args to use them".
  - The 2-D support and the lower bounds came from two applications.
    - Statistics examples taken from R. The message of `cdda863b8` says: "Made them start at 1 instead of zero for compatibility with R examples. Start of SimpleKCoefficient test."
    - A knapsack benchmark. The message of `d535963cb` says: "supports knapsack code".
    - Neither program is in the tree now. Flood removed the R-derived `ProcFreqFinal_tests` directory in `7caf58ad9` (2011-11-10). No knapsack program exists (grep).
  - No commit message and no comment says why the type is monomorphic, why there is no `RR64` vector, or why the team wrote a Java class instead of a generic Fortress object.
    - The revival's own finding is that stamping renames and cannot give one instantiation a `double[]` field (walkthrough §6; `explorations/coordinator/array-design.md:69`).
    - That is an analysis made in 2026, not a reason the team gave.

  ## 4. What has the same shape, what does not, and why
  
  What has the same shape [read]:
  
  - Seventeen classes in `runtimeValues/` extend a generated `DefaultTraitMethods`: `FBoolean`, `FCharacter`, `FFloatLiteral`, `FIntLiteral`, `FJavaBufferedReader`, `FJavaBufferedWriter`, `FJavaString`, `FNN32`, `FNN64`, `FRR32`, `FRR64`, `FString`, `FStringVector`, `FZZ`, `FZZ32`, `FZZ32Vector` and `FZZ64` (grep). Each one is the hand-written run-time class of one builtin trait.
  - Fourteen of those traits, plus void, are in `NamingCzar`'s special table (`:538-555`), so their Fortress type is lowered straight to the class. `IntLiteral`, `FloatLiteral` and `String` are not in the table.
  - Each class has a nested descriptor class with a static `ONLY` field.
  
  How the vectors differ [read]:
  
  - Contents.
    - The scalars wrap one final value. For example, `FZZ32` wraps a `final int` (`FZZ32.java:16`).
    - The two vectors are the only classes that hold a Java array, and the only ones whose contents change after construction.
    - `FJavaBufferedReader` and `FJavaBufferedWriter` wrap a Java stream object.
  - Native wrappers.
    - The scalars have converters in `FortressMethodAdapter.java:139-155`, so the wrapper unboxes them to `int`, `double` and so on.
    - The vectors have no converter. A helper receives the vector object itself (step 6 of section 3).
  - Descriptor names.
    - Thirteen classes name their nested descriptor `RTTIc`, which is the name the loader asks for.
    - The vectors use `RTTIv`. The buffered reader and writer use `RTTIjbr` and `RTTIjbw` (`FJavaBufferedReader.java:33`). I did not run the reader or writer as type arguments.
  - Foreign mapping.
    - The scalars map from Java primitive types through a table (`NamingCzar.java:436-459`).
    - The vectors map from their own classes through the `else if` chain (`:337-340`).
  
  What does not exist on the compiled path:
  
  - There is no vector of `RR64`, `ZZ64` or any other element type, and no generic array. `Array`, `Vector`, `Matrix` and `array[\T\]` are undefined there. [cited: ledger rows 72 and 305, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:303`, `:317`]
  - The interpreter's library works differently. [read]
    - Its arrays are generic Fortress types that carry sizes, such as `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2099`) and `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]` (`:2210`).
    - They sit over one generic native store, `PrimitiveArray[\T, nat s0\]`. Its `get` and `put` are interpreter natives (`LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss:18-26`).
  - The interpreter's library has the same prefix sum on `Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]`. It sits under the comment "Some random stuff related to arrays and the MCKPE benchmark" (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4489-4503`; Steele, `fc1937ae0`). The compiled block in `CompilerLibrary.fss:484-519` has the same shape for `ZZ32Vector`, and it came eight days after the interpreter's version. [read; git]
  
  Why, as far as the tree and the commit messages say [git]:
  
  - Flood's first commit message is "Simple Integer 1 dimensional arrays." (`f4973a717`).
  - `StringVector` was made for the program arguments.
    - Before `24717d4ad`, `CompilerSystem.args` was an object with native hooks. Its comment read: "Right now this is a massive hack, to make the native wrapper use array-like *notation* without actually supporting native-side arrays per se. This should be remedied as soon as is practical."
    - That commit replaced it with `args : StringVector`. Its message says: "Updated CompilerSystem.args to use them".
  - The 2-D support and the lower bounds came from two applications.
    - Statistics examples taken from R. The message of `cdda863b8` says: "Made them start at 1 instead of zero for compatibility with R examples. Start of SimpleKCoefficient test."
    - A knapsack benchmark. The message of `d535963cb` says: "supports knapsack code".
    - Neither program is in the tree now. Flood removed the R-derived `ProcFreqFinal_tests` directory in `7caf58ad9` (2011-11-10). No knapsack program exists (grep).
  - No commit message and no comment says why the type is monomorphic, why there is no `RR64` vector, or why the team wrote a Java class instead of a generic Fortress object.
    - The revival's own finding is that stamping renames and cannot give one instantiation a `double[]` field (walkthrough §6; `explorations/coordinator/array-design.md:69`).
    - That is an analysis made in 2026, not a reason the team gave.

  ## 7. What works and what does not, today
  
  What works [measured; everything ran in a private cache on JDK 25]:
  
  - Integer vectors:
    - creating 1-D and 2-D vectors;
    - `fill`, `fill` with a function, and `fill2`;
    - reading and writing elements in both ranks;
    - `|v|`, `nrows`, `ncols` and `shape`;
    - `copy` of a 1-D vector;
    - `v + k`, `v - k`, `v MIN k`, `v MAX k` and `PREFIX_SUM v`;
    - printing, and string concatenation.
  - String vectors: creating one, `putValue`, `getValue`, `s[i]`, `|s|` and printing.
  - `CompilerSystem.args` with zero or more arguments, including an argument that contains a space.
  
  What does not work [measured unless marked]:
  
  - An out-of-range index throws a Java `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, not a Fortress exception.
    - The prelude does define a Fortress `IndexOutOfBounds` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:92`), but the vectors never throw it. [read]
    - I did not test whether a Fortress `try` can catch the Java exception.
  - In 2-D, a column index past the end of its row reads an element of another row, with no error. `m[0,4]` is `m[1,1]`.
  - `copy` of a 2-D vector returns a 1-D vector of `nrows` elements. From a 2×3 vector it returns size 2 with `ncols` 0. The source says as much: "Handles only 1D case" (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:1120`).
    - `+`, `-`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `PREFIX_SUM` all start from `copy`, so on a 2-D vector they give the same truncated 1-D result. [read, not run]
  - Vectors built from a range, whose lower bound is not 0, only partly work.
    - `makeZZ32Vector(1:3)` supports `v[1]` and `v[3]`.
    - But `println(v)` fails in `toString` with "Index -1 out of bounds for length 3".
    - `v.fill(0)` fails the same way, in `putIndexedValue`.
    - The cause: `toString`, `fill`, `fill2`, `copy` and the operators all iterate from 0, while element access subtracts the lower bound. [read: `FZZ32Vector.java:34`, `:46-47`; `CompilerBuiltin.fss:1131`, `:1137`, `:1143`; `CompilerLibrary.fss:486`, `:499`]
  - `3 - v`, with the scalar on the left, is a static error. [cited, SkVecScalarC.txt]
  - `s[i] := x` on a `StringVector` is a static error. `putValue` is the way to write.
  - A vector cannot be a generic's type argument. The run fails at load with `NoClassDefFoundError: …FZZ32Vector$RTTIc` or `…FStringVector$RTTIc` (section 3, step 9).
  - A native helper cannot take `int[]` or `String[]` in its signature (section 3, step 10).
  - `fill` and `fill2` cannot be written as statements. That is a static error unless the result is bound.
  
  Read from the code, not run:
  
  - There is no `for x <- v`, because neither trait is a generator. Neither declares `generate`, and neither extends a generator trait (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:563-587`).
  - There is no equality on vectors, no vector-vector arithmetic, and no `SUFFIX_SUM` (it is commented out, `CompilerLibrary.fss:491-496`).
  - `makeZZ32Vector(n)` with a negative `n` reaches `new int[n]` unchecked (`FZZ32Vector.java:26`). `d1 * d2` is not checked for overflow.
  
  ## 8. Relation to unboxed numeric arrays on the compiled path
  
  These are facts about the code. This section proposes no design.
  
  - `FZZ32Vector` is the only numeric store on the compiled path. Its storage is unboxed: one `int[]` (`FZZ32Vector.java:18`). [read]
  - Its traffic is boxed. [measured]
    - Each read receives an `FZZ32` index and returns a new `FZZ32`.
    - Each write receives two boxed values and returns the void value.
    - Seven frames lie between the program and the array. One of them is a generated wrapper that unboxes and reboxes (section 3, step 7).
  - Arithmetic on the elements is done on `FZZ32` objects. The code generator emits no primitive arithmetic for Fortress numbers (walkthrough §5). [cited]
  - The only check per access is the JVM's array bounds check (FACTS.md:38). [cited, and measured above]
  - The type carries no element type and no size. It is one monomorphic class. [read]
    - A new element type means a new trait, a new Java class and new table entries.
    - `explorations/coordinator/array-design.md:67` counts these as "the team's own five wiring sites". [cited]
  - A vector cannot be a type argument today, because of its descriptor class name (section 3, step 9). [measured]
    - So it cannot sit inside a generic Fortress object as a field of type `T`.
    - `perf-probes/nat/size-cost/SizedSum.fss:11-15` works around this by building its own vector inside the object. [cited]
  - Natives cannot take a raw `int[]` or `double[]` today, because the wrapper generator skips array descriptors (section 3, step 10). [measured]
    - A helper can take the vector object and reach its array through `getValue()`. Every existing helper works this way (`simpleIntVector.java`). [read]
  - There is no `double` counterpart. `RR64` is boxed as `FRR64`, which wraps one `double` (`runtimeValues/FRR64.java`). The wrapper table converts it to a `double` at a native boundary (`FortressMethodAdapter.java:144`). [read]
  - On 2026-09-19 Pavol decided that the `RR64` store is an unboxed `double[]` (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:41`).

This is the worker's explainer, checked against the tree. I opened the key citations, including the `RTTIv` descriptor class and the two 2011 commits. It is only in the scratchpad (`vectors-explainer.md`). Nothing from it is committed.

# FZZ32Vector and FStringVector

These are two small hand-written Java classes. They are the run-time objects behind the only two array-like types the compiled path has: `ZZ32Vector`, a vector of 32-bit integers, and `StringVector`, a vector of strings. Both types exist only in the compiled path's own library. Christine Flood wrote both classes in August and September 2011, and Guy Steele extended the integer one in October 2011.

Each claim below is marked: **[measured]** means the worker ran it today on JDK 25 in a private cache; **[read]** means read from the code.

**Terms**
- *Prelude*: the library components every program sees without an import. On the compiled path these are `AnyType`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerLibrary`.
- *Boxed*: every compiled Fortress value is a JVM object. A `ZZ32` is an `FZZ32` object wrapping one `int`.
- *Descriptor*: a per-type object that generated code uses for type tests and dispatch. By the loader's convention, the descriptor of class `X` is the static field `ONLY` of a nested class named `X$RTTIc`.
- *`DefaultTraitMethods`*: for each trait, the compiler generates an abstract class holding the trait's method bodies. A class that implements the trait extends it.
- *Native binding*: a line like `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{simpleIntVector.getIndexedValue => jIntVectorGet, …}`, which makes a static Java method callable as a Fortress function.

## 1. The two classes

**FZZ32Vector** (`compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32Vector.java`, 83 lines) [read]
- It extends the generated `CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32Vector.DefaultTraitMethods` and implements the `ZZ32Vector` interface (`:16-17`).
- The elements are in `private int[] val`: unboxed, in one flat Java array. The shape is in four ints: `lower_x`, `dim_x`, `lower_y` and `dim_y` (`:18-19`).
- One class serves two ranks. The comment at `:14-15` reads: "It's kind of a kludge, but one of these babies can pretend to be either 1-D or 2-D." `dim_y == 0` means 1-D.
- Element access (`:64-68`):
  - in 1-D, `val[i - lower_x]`;
  - in 2-D, `val[(i - lower_x) * dim_y + (j - lower_y)]`, which is row-major.
- The class checks no bounds itself. The only check is the JVM's own array bounds check.
  - In 2-D, a column index past the end of its row lands in the next row. In a 2×3 vector, `m[0,4]` returns the element at `m[1,1]`. [measured]
  - An index past the whole array throws Java's `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, not a Fortress exception, and the program ends. [measured]
- `dim()` is the total element count. `rows()` is `dim_x`, and `cols()` is `dim_y`, which is 0 in 1-D.
- Its descriptor class is named **`RTTIv`**, not `RTTIc` (`:79-82`). Section 3 explains why that matters.

**FStringVector** (`FStringVector.java`, 52 lines) [read]
- It is the same pattern, 1-D only, holding a `String[]` of plain Java strings.
- It has no lower bound, and no check beyond the JVM's.
- An unset element is Java `null`, and it prints as `null` with no error. [measured]
- Its `toString` puts a space after every element: `[a bc null ]`. [measured]
- Its `asString` is misspelled `asSring`, so nothing calls it. The typo was inherited from the class it was copied from, which Steele later fixed only in `FZZ32Vector`.
- Its descriptor class is also named `RTTIv`.

**What they inherit**
- At run time, the Fortress methods (`v[i]`, `fill`, `nrows` and so on) all come from the generated `DefaultTraitMethods` in the compiled prelude jar. The Java class adds only storage and access. [measured with `javap`]

## 2. The Fortress types

- Neither type is in the specification, and neither exists under `walk`. [measured by grep] The interpreter types its program arguments as `ImmutableArray[\String,ZZ32\]` instead.
- **`ZZ32Vector`** is declared in `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:563-580`.
  - It has no static parameters, so it names no element type and no size.
  - It has `shape`, `nrows`, `ncols`, `copy`, `v[i]`, `v[i,j]` and both assignment forms, `|v|`, `fill(x)`, `fill(f)` and `fill2(f)`.
  - `CompilerLibrary` adds `makeZZ32Vector` in four forms, and the operators `PREFIX_SUM`, `v + k`, `v - k`, `v MIN k` and `v MAX k`, with the scalar on the right only.
- What a program can do, measured on a 5-element vector:
  - `v.fill(fn (i) => i i)` gives `[0 1 4 9 16]`;
  - after `v[2] := 42`, `v + 1` gives `[1 2 43 10 17]` and `PREFIX_SUM v` gives `[0 1 43 52 68]`;
  - a 2×3 vector filled by `fill2` prints `(2,3)` and then its two rows.
- **`StringVector`** has `getValue`, `putValue`, `s[i]` and `|s|`. It has no `s[i] := x`, which is a static error. Its one real use is `CompilerSystem.args`, the command-line arguments. With the arguments `one "two words"`, `|args|` is 2 and `args[1]` is `two words`. [measured]

## 3. From source text to the Java class

Following `v[2] := 42; x = v[2]`:

1. **Desugaring.** Before type checking, `v[2]` becomes a method call named `_[_]`, and the assignment becomes one named `_[_]:=`. Steele wrote this in October 2011 (`AssignmentAndSubscriptDesugarer.scala:75-80`). The code generator's own vector code in `forSubscriptExpr` is dead: it opens with `if (x == x) throw new Error(…)` (`CodeGen.java:4932`).
2. **Name mapping.** `NamingCzar`, the compiler's table of Fortress-to-JVM names, has a special table that maps a few builtin traits straight to hand-written classes. It includes `ZZ32Vector → FZZ32Vector` and `StringVector → FStringVector` (`NamingCzar.java:553-554`). So every variable, field or parameter of type `ZZ32Vector` has the JVM type `FZZ32Vector`, and calls on it are emitted as `invokevirtual` on the class. [measured with `javap`]
3. **Trait bodies.** `CompilerBuiltin.fss` compiles like any component. The trait's bodies become static methods in the generated abstract class, and each body is one call to a native helper.
4. **Native bindings.** `nativeHelpers/simpleIntVector.java` (40 lines) forwards each call to the class in one line. The compiler makes a Fortress signature for each helper. It also writes a wrapper class into `nativewrapper_cache` that unboxes the `FZZ32` index to an `int` and boxes the result back. The vector object itself passes through unconverted.
5. **One element read, as it runs.** Seven stack frames lie between the program and the array access:
   - the `_[_]` method and its body;
   - the `getValue` pair;
   - the generated wrapper;
   - the helper;
   - `FZZ32Vector.getIndexedValue`.

   The index arrives boxed, and the result leaves as a new `FZZ32`. [measured] The worker did not measure whether the JIT removes any of this.
6. **Class loader.** The vector classes are not generic, so the loader defines them unchanged.
7. **As a type argument, it fails.** `Cell[\ZZ32Vector\](makeZZ32Vector(2))` compiles, then dies at load with `NoClassDefFoundError: …FZZ32Vector$RTTIc`, and likewise for `StringVector`. [measured]
   - Stamped code asks for the descriptor by appending `$RTTIc` to the class name (`MethodInstantiater.java:134-138`), but the vectors' descriptor class is `RTTIv`.
   - A probe-only copy of the class with an `RTTIc` added made the same program run and print `[0 0]`. [measured; nothing in the tree changed]
   - FACTS recorded this failure on 09-24 without a cause. No ledger row names it.
8. **Raw Java arrays at a native boundary don't work.** A helper taking `int[]` compiles, but its wrapper is silently empty, and the run fails with `NoSuchMethodError`. The wrapper generator skips every method with an array parameter, under the comment "We can't represent bytes, shorts or arrays yet" (`SignatureParser.java:45-55`). A helper taking `String[]` fails at compile time. [measured]

## 4. Same shape, and what differs

- Seventeen classes in `runtimeValues/` follow this pattern: a hand-written class for one builtin trait. Examples are `FZZ32`, `FRR64`, `FBoolean` and `FJavaString`.
- The two vectors differ from the rest in four ways:
  - they are the only ones holding a Java array, and the only ones whose contents change after construction;
  - they are the only ones with no unbox converter at a native boundary;
  - their descriptor class is `RTTIv`, where 13 of the others use `RTTIc`;
  - there is no vector of `RR64` or `ZZ64`, and no generic array. On the compiled path, `Array`, `Vector` and `Matrix` are undefined (ledger rows 72 and 305).
- The interpreter's library works differently. Its arrays are generic, sized Fortress types, such as `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]`, over one generic native store, `PrimitiveArray`.
- **Why**, from the commit messages:
  - Flood's first commit was "Simple Integer 1 dimensional arrays."
  - `StringVector` replaced "a massive hack" for the program arguments.
  - The 2-D support and lower bounds served R statistics examples ("start at 1 instead of zero for compatibility with R examples") and a knapsack benchmark. Neither program is in the tree now.
  - Nothing on record says why the type has no element type, why there is no `RR64` vector, or why the team wrote a Java class instead of a generic Fortress object.

## 5. History

- `f4973a717`, 2011-08-16, Flood: "Simple Integer 1 dimensional arrays." This is `FVector`, a 1-D `int[]` wrapper.
- `24717d4ad`, 2011-09-07, Flood:
  - renamed it `FZZ32Vector` and added `FStringVector` as a copy of it;
  - added both entries to the special table;
  - switched `CompilerSystem.args` to `StringVector`.
- `85c4b8a47`, 2011-09-07, Flood: 2-D arrays, with the wrong row stride.
- `cdda863b8`, 2011-09-21, Flood: `nrows` and `ncols`, and indices starting at 1 for the R examples.
- `fc1937ae0` and `05b0ceaa8`, 2011-10-04, Steele: the new subscript desugaring, and the `asString` typo fixed in one class only.
- `d535963cb`, 2011-10-12, Steele, "supports knapsack code":
  - general lower bounds, the stride fixed, the "kludge" comment;
  - on the Fortress side, `excludes`, `shape`, `copy`, `fill`, `fill2` and the assignment operators;
  - the four factories and the operator block.
- `8414723ac`, 2012-06-08, Chase: each `RTTIv` made to extend the generated trait descriptor. This is the last change to either Java file.
- `6b5517af6`, 2012-06-14, Chase: the arguments passed through `systemOps.getArgs`.

## 6. Tests

- Four gated tests run `FStringVector`, and all passed in the last suite run:
  - `Compiled2`, `Compiled4` and `Compiled7`, all through `CompilerSystem.args`;
  - the revival's `DefaultRenderRungS`, which checks that a `StringVector` prints `[a b ]`.
- `XXX3u`, `XXX6at` and `XXX6bi` only check that `(ZZ32Vector, ZZ32)->ZZ32Vector` appears in an error's list of `+` overloads.
- **No gated test creates, indexes or prints a `ZZ32Vector` at run time.**
- `other_compiler_tests/VectorTest2.fss` and `VectorTest3.fss` have no `.test` file, so the gate never runs them. Run by hand, they print `10` and `69`, which is right. [measured]

## 7. What works and what does not, today

**Works** [measured]
- Creating 1-D and 2-D integer vectors, `fill` and `fill2`, reading and writing elements, `|v|`, `nrows`, `ncols`, `shape`, 1-D `copy`, the five operators, and printing.
- String vectors, and `CompilerSystem.args`.

**Does not work**
- An out-of-range index throws a Java exception, not the prelude's own `IndexOutOfBounds`.
- In 2-D, a column overflow silently reads another row.
- `copy` of a 2-D vector returns a truncated 1-D vector ("Handles only 1D case", `CompilerBuiltin.fss:1120`). So the operators, which start from `copy`, give wrong results on 2-D. [read]
- For vectors built from a range, whose lower bound is not 0, `println` and `fill` fail with index -1. They iterate from 0 while element access subtracts the lower bound.
- `3 - v` is a static error, and so is `s[i] := x`.
- A vector cannot be a generic's type argument, because of the `RTTIv` name (section 3, item 7).
- A native helper cannot take `int[]` or `String[]`.
- Read from the code, not run:
  - there is no `for x <- v`, no equality on vectors, and no vector-vector arithmetic;
  - a negative size reaches `new int[n]` unchecked.

## 8. How this relates to unboxed arrays

These are facts about the code, not a design.
- `FZZ32Vector` is the only numeric store on the compiled path. Its storage is unboxed, but every access boxes: the index arrives boxed, a new `FZZ32` comes out, and seven frames lie between the program and the array.
- Arithmetic on the elements is done on boxed objects, because the code generator emits no primitive arithmetic for Fortress numbers.
- The type carries no element type and no size. A new element type means a new trait, a new Java class and new table entries.
- As a type argument it fails today, because of its descriptor's name. So it cannot sit in a generic object as a field of type `T`.
- Natives cannot take a raw `int[]` or `double[]` today. A helper takes the vector object and reaches its array through `getValue()`.
- `array-design.md` names `FZZ32Vector` as the precedent for the `double[]` store you decided on (09-19). It also records an unprobed step: a hand-written non-generic class sitting under a generic trait.

One finding here is new to the record: the cause of the type-argument load failure. I can commit the explainer as a note, with a FACTS line for that cause, if you want it on record.

and its fold; batch base `8590d7a9e`). The gate ran once on this tree and returned
`green: false` with an empty `failing` list and one `countsDown` line:
`COUNT DOWN system-2/SystemJUTest 97 -> 95`. Everything else it measures is clean:
`compileAll`, `testFast` (47 suites, 1422 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors), `testSystem`
(4 shards, 384 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors), 39 of 39 four-thread atomic runs `PASS`, the
85-file ladder byte-identical to its baseline, the eighteen microGPT components unmoved
(`gate/summary.txt`; `gate/ladder/comparison.txt` and `microgpt-comparison.txt` both
0 bytes). Nothing here is a build or a test run: I read, I ruled, and the numbered steps at
....

summaries prints the one red line the gate reported and nothing else. The corrected
function keeps `RED` and `EMPTY` per row, so a shard with a failure is still named by its
own row. The thirteen JS lines prescribed in step 3 below were decoded here exactly as the
script's string literals will produce them (`node` over the array, Node 22) and sourced,
and gave those six outputs; the wrapped `node --check` of step 5(b) passes today's file and
fails a copy with one stray parenthesis. The worker repeats both, but the texts are not
guesses.

The language specification has no view on a test harness; this is a decision about the
batch machinery under Pavol's standing rule for a red gate (rework the source of the
conflict holistically; dropping a rung only when its approach is wrong). No rung's
approach or code is at fault, so `drop` would be wrong and, at `:1153`, terminal. `stop` is
for the reserved forks and there is none. The candidates:

1. **Correct the criterion only.** `gate2` still runs the in-memory criterion against the
   stale comparand and the batch dies at `:1160` with a clean tree. Rejected alone.

These are two small hand-written Java classes. Each holds the elements of one of the only two array-like types the compiled path has: a vector of 32-bit integers and a vector of strings. They are the run-time objects behind the Fortress types `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`, and those types exist on
