The same compiled program then ran and printed `[0 0]`. [measured; n
188:    - Take a helper `static int sum(int[] a)` bound by `import java`. The program type-checks and compiles, and `jSum(makeZZ32Vector(3))` is accepted. But the generated wrapper class is empty, and the run fails with `NoSuchMethodError: … native.vecprobe.IntArr.sum(FZZ32Vector)`. [measured]
249:- Some changes are hidden behind a cut link. To find those, I scanned the file's content at every listed commit in date order and noted where a line first appears. The helper script is `strhist.sh` in the scratch directory.
#!/bin/bash
# usage: strhist.sh <file> <fixed-string>
# For every commit (all refs, full history) touching <file>, in author-date order,
# print the commits where the count of <fixed-string> in the file changes.
cd /home/user/fortress
f="$1"; s="$2"
prev=-1
git log --all --full-history --format='%H %at' -- "$f" | sort -k2 -n | while read H at; do
  c=$(git show "$H:$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -cF -- "$s")
  if [ "$c" != "$prev" ]; then
    echo "$(git log -1 --format='%h %ad %an [%p] %s' --date=short $H | cut -c1-140)  => count $c"
    prev=$c
  fi
done

- `import java` also works on the interpreter path through `ForeignComponentWrapper` + `ClosureMaker`; no test uses it (B.12). Corrected 2026-09-20 (`perf-probes/prelude/import-java-interpreter.md`): wired and unfinished, it does not work; four gaps, all on the interpreter's side: `NamingCzar.fortLib` is fixed to the builtin api, which declares none of `ZZ32`/`RR64`/`JavaString` in that world (`NamingCzar.java:294-295`); a second `import java` from one package falls through `Driver.ensureApiImplemented` to a `ClassCastException` (`Driver.java:464-466`, "temp hack till we knit in natives properly"); the foreign name is never rewritten (`ForeignComponentWrapper.java:31,38`) and `BaseEnv.java:531-533` bugs on the qualified reference; and `ClosureMaker` emits a call into the compiler's `nativewrapper_cache`, which the interpreter neither writes nor loads. So one binding file cannot serve both worlds; the one-library variant is one shared text with one small builtin component per world behind a single api, which makes the api-to-differently-named-component link (ledger row 320's class-name half, `Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`) live work.

- Codegen refuses any declaration carrying a where clause or a contract (`CodeGen.java:2937, :2941, :4076, :4078, :4983, :4985`); not in the ledger (flagged, Pavol's call). `atomic <expr>` has no visitor, `atomic do … end` compiles; `spawn`, `label`/`exit`, object expressions, array literals and comprehensions, local function declarations have no visitor (`spec-to-implementation.md` §3).

- The checker (`IndexBuilder.scala:187-189`) refuses `type` aliases, `test` and `property` on both paths. Coercion is the one mechanism the compiler path has and the interpreter does not (no `Coercion`/`coerce` under `interpreter/`; row 19).

+- **The compiled path's only array-like types are `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`, two hand-written Java classes declared only in its prelude and absent from the specification** (2026-09-25, `compiler-probes/vectors/vectors.md`, probes and captures under `compiler-probes/vectors/probes/`). `FZZ32Vector` holds an unboxed `int[]` with lower bounds and an optional second dimension (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32Vector.java:14-19`), `FStringVector` a `String[]`; `NamingCzar`'s special table lowers both types straight to the classes (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:553-554`); every element access is boxed and passes through seven frames, a generated native wrapper among them; no gated test creates or indexes a `ZZ32Vector` at run time. The load failure of a `ZZ32Vector` as a generic's type argument (the size-cost entry above, "no ledger row yet") is the descriptor class's name: both classes call it `RTTIv` (`FZZ32Vector.java:79-82`) while stamped code asks for `<class>$RTTIc` (`runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:134-138`), and a probe-only copy with an `RTTIc` alias runs (`probes/rttic-alias.patch`, `out-VecGeneric-rttic.txt`). A native helper cannot take a Java array: the wrapper generator skips every method with an array parameter (`compiler/nativeInterface/SignatureParser.java:45-55`). Written by Christine Flood (`f4973a717`, `24717d4ad`, 2011) and extended by Guy Steele (`d535963cb`, 2011-10-12).

- **A generic object referenced without its static arguments is a static error on the compiled path, and the checker never consults the expected type for it** (2026-09-19, `explorations/compiler-probes/maybe-inference/inference.md`): `b: Box[\ZZ32\] = Box` fails with `Ill-formed type: Box`; a bare `Empty` as a call argument or a field default fails with `T is not in the kind env`, an internal `bug()` from `TypeAnalyzer.scala:766` reported at the declaration's span; the same forms with the static argument written compile and run on both paths. The decision is in the checker's `SVarRef` case, `typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:624-641`, whose `:639-640` keeps the uninstantiated type under the team's own `TODO: handle missing static args`; static-argument inference exists only for arrows (`STypesUtil.scala:912-930`, called from application and coercion), and a parametric empty case reached by `coerce` still fails bare. Under `walk` the same forms are `InterpreterBug: Couldn't figure out Empty[\T\](uninstantiated) <: Opt[\ZZ32\]`. Consequence for row 331: a parametric `Nothing[\T\]` would serve the corpus's `Nothing[\ZZ32\]` and never the specification's bare `= Nothing`; the non-parametric object plus `coerce` that the prelude uses is the only shape that compiles, so `Maybe` stays as landed. Incidental: `typecase` over a user-declared generic object crashes code generation (`Error trying to close method scope`, `CodeGen.java:2802`), row 340. Corrected the same day by the minimal reproducer (`compiler-probes/maybe-inference/probes/TcPlain.fss`): neither the generic object nor `typecase` alone is the trigger; a `typecase` used directly as a function or method body whose value needs an implicit coercion (`IntLiteral` to a declared `ZZ32`) makes ASM's stack-map frame computation fail (`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` under `MethodWriter.visitMaxs`, relabelled by the `catch (Throwable)` at `CodeGen.java:2801-2802`); wrapped in `do … end` the same body compiles, and every gated use of the shape returns `()` so never reaches the coercion.

The explainer is in the repo, commit `363b3f62b`.

**Where it went.** Everything of ours lives under `explorations/`. The explainer is now `explorations/compiler-probes/vectors/vectors.md`, next to the earlier compiler probes. FACTS and INDEX have entries for it.

**What the worker did.**
- It was read-only on the tree. It changed no tracked file and wrote nothing into `default_repository/`.
- It did run experiments. For about 28 minutes it wrote and ran 13 small Fortress programs, compiled into private caches in the scratchpad. It also wrote two Java helpers and a probe-only copy of `FZZ32Vector` with the missing `RTTIc` added.
- All of that is now under `vectors/probes/`: the programs, their outputs, the helpers, the copy as a patch, and the scripts, re-pointed so they run from there.
- One run had no saved output: the copy with `RTTIc` added, run as a type argument. I re-ran it and saved the result. It prints `[0 0]`.
- The 204M of caches were rebuildable, so I deleted them together with the scratch copies.

The scratchpad as a whole holds about 7G across roughly 600 entries from this session. I've put a sweep of it on the list for after the batch.

**Row 47: how the gate compares the interpreter tests**

**The background.** `ant testSystem` runs the interpreter tests in four parts, called shards. It sorts the test files by name and deals them out in turn: the 1st to shard 0, the 2nd to shard 1, and so on. A file added anywhere shifts every file after it into a different shard. So the count in each shard changes even when nothing is broken (FACTS § The harness and the gate).

**What happened without you.** On 09-20, climb batch 2's gate went red on a single line: shard 2 went from 97 tests to 95. Nothing had failed. Two test files added on 09-19 had shifted the shards. A worker judging the red gate then changed the rule on its own:
- the four shards are now compared by their total, not one by one;
- a stronger check, comparing the actual test names, was put off rather than rejected.

Batches 3 and 3.5 ran and landed under the total rule. A failing test is red under any of these rules, because failures are checked separately.

**The choices**
- **Approve the total rule as it stands.** Nothing changes, and batch 4 runs as batches 3 and 3.5 did. The weakness: if a batch deleted one test and added another, the total would hide it. The skeptics and the review look for deleted tests, but the gate itself would not catch it.
- **Revert to one-by-one.** Batch 4 adds interpreter tests, and promoting row 379's expected-failure test renames a file. Either one shifts the shards, so the gate would go red with nothing broken.
- **Compare test names.** The gate would go red if any test that passed before is missing or failing, and would list new tests. This is the strongest check. It needs a change to the workflow script, and the stored summary would have to record test names, not only counts. It is one worker's job, and it lands before batch 4 launches.

Recommendation: approve the total rule for batch 4, and add the name comparison later as a script change put to you on its own.

content.text:
# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

- Read-only everywhere else. No builds and no gate runs; cheap measurements such as `git grep` are fine.
- Bound every command's output. Cite file:line for claims about the code.
- Plain English in the file: lists, not tables; numbers as K or M.
- Do not name any AI model in the file.

- The exact script changes needed before launch, if any, marked as either "red without it" or "advisable".

----
## Setting up a batch's worktrees

The workflow script cannot touch the filesystem before its first agent runs, so
the coordinator creates the worktrees and pushes the empty branches first, from
the commit `main` is at, which is then the script's `args.base`:

```sh
cd /home/user/fortress && BASE=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
for r in r1-atomic-static r2-literal-wrap; do
  git worktree add -b wip/repair-$r /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*} main
  cp -a ProjectFortress/build /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/ProjectFortress/   # javac incremental; scalac rebuilds anyway
  mkdir -p /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/tmp
  git push -u origin wip/repair-$r
done
```

Copy the build, never symlink it: a symlinked build makes `ProjectProperties`
resolve every cache path to the main tree (`batched-climb-plan.md` §4). After
the batch lands, the commit stage removes the worktrees and local branches; the
remote `wip/` branches are deleted in the GitHub UI.

You are examining one question for Pavol (@palimondo), who directs the revival of the Fortress programming language in `/home/user/fortress`. He is a programmer. Write in plain English, and define every term in the sentence that first uses it.

**The situation.** The revival has decided to change the language's rules. The compiled type checker keeps a rule, the "multiple instantiation exclusion": a type may not be a subtype of two different instantiations of one generic. The numeric tower is then flattened, and the interpreter learns coercion. Several sentences of the in-repo specification (`Specification/`, the LaTeX sources of the July 2012 draft) say otherwise. They allow a type to extend two instantiations, and some of their examples rely on that. So the specification will be edited. `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched.

Pavol's requirement for that edit, verbatim (2026-09-24): "our plan needs to update the spec with the change that we do and somehow properly record why we decided that way, so that there is no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation that would be confusing to people. We need to preserve the original historic record somewhere in a document with our reasoning why we did the switch and preserve the option to go the route C."

**The question.** In what form does the revised specification show that a passage was changed by the revival, and where do the original text and the reasoning live? This is a question of form, not of which sentences change.

**First step, before anything else.** List every way the specification's own sources, macros and build offer to show a change, and every way comparable language specifications use. Work from the sources:
- `Specification/`, its macros and its appendices;
- how `Specification/fortress.pdf` is built;
- the git history of `Specification/`, which shows how the original team revised its text from 2008 to 2012 and how the revival's two earlier specification commits did it.

Do not read the revival's planning notes about this question. They are in `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-4.md` and anything under `explorations/` that mentions "S1". The point is a list made fresh from the sources. You may read `explorations/protocol.md` (§ 6 has the method) and `explorations/repo-internals.md` for git archaeology techniques: the history has 146 severed parent links, so path-scoped `git log` misses commits, and that note says what to do instead.

**Then the nine steps of protocol § 6, adapted to a question of form.** Say which steps do not apply, and do not force them.
1. The refresher: what each form is.
2. What the specification does today: its change-marking machinery, and whether it is used, measured.
3. What the specification's prose says about its own revisions.
4. The numeric tower (probably not applicable).
5. What the team already did in the same family: their practice when they revised the text.
6. What peers do, by family:
   - language standards that carry a changes annex;
   - ones that keep an annotated edition beside the normative text;
   - ones that mark the text inline;
   - ones that keep the history outside the text.

   Cite a source for each, a URL or a document section.
7. The history in the commits.
8. The derivation from Pavol's requirement above, case by case, with what each form costs: in the PDF, for a reader, for keeping the original text recoverable, and for the option of reversing to route C later.
9. The options as they would be put to him, the specification's own way first, each with what it commits him to. End with a recommendation in one line, after the explanation, marked as your reading and not a decision.

**Rules:**
- Read-only on the tree. You may build the specification PDF only in a scratch copy outside the repository, and only if a claim about the rendered output needs it.
- Bound every command's output.
- Cite file:line for claims about the sources, and a commit hash for claims about history.
- Lists, not tables. Numbers of thousands or millions as K or M. Do not name any AI model.
- Write the result to `explorations/reviews/spec-change-form.md`, starting with a one-line header comment saying what it is, when and by whom it was written.
- Commit nothing. Run `git status --short` at the end.

**Your final report:** the list of ways, the recommendation, and the file's path.

lines: ## Boot note to the resumed coordinator

-**Update, 2026-09-24 08:59 UTC.** In flight since about 08:59 UTC, both Opus, both launched by the Agent tool (a message from Pavol does not kill them; a Workflow run is what a mid-turn interrupt kills): the route C shadow experiment, whose output is `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md` with patches and captures under `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c/`; and the run-time size design brief, whose output is `explorations/reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`. Neither is committed until the coordinator has reviewed it (the worker commits nothing). His go of that hour: "Recommendation accepted. Run 2 and 3 now" (POSITIONS 2026-09-24): the ledger rows one per message while they run, the exclusion route decided when the C data lands, then batch 4's manifest. Landed since the 07:10 note: the `experiment/` move (`7bc8177a3`) and its verification by re-running both shadow experiments from the new path (`582b4e17d`; FACTS § The container). The order below stands otherwise. Landed 09:21 UTC and committed: the size design brief (`explorations/reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`); its default is design A with the value-position piece in one rung, briefed only after one shadow session has probed the fourth gap and a dispatched overload arm generic in a size, and the checker rung of the size wall does not wait on the decision. Those two probes are the next worker to launch, after the route C worker finishes, because both build shadows in this one tree. Landed 11:12 UTC and committed: the route C experiment (`explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md`, `route-c/`; FACTS § The checker and the one library, the entry of 2026-09-24): C-full closes the specialisation hole with a 109-line return-type rule over every level of a chain, needs seven library declarations and an identification that only `comprises T` licenses, and `comprises T` overflows the checker; a chain without a specialisation dies compiled with `AbstractMethodError`; C-lite refuses the tower's inner half; the reversal cost on record is corrected upward. The route decision (item 2) is ready to be put to Pavol. In flight since 11:12 UTC, one Opus worker by the Agent tool: the size probes the brief asked for before the run-time rung is briefed (a dispatched overload arm generic in a size under A and B, the fourth gap's template, a type test on a size), output `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` with patches and captures under `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-probes/`. Landed 12:24 UTC and committed (FACTS § The checker and the one library, the entry of 2026-09-24 on the three size probes): design A's default falls to the brief's own stop condition, since under A a dispatched arm generic in a size silently picks the catch-all and its fix is about 70-90 unbuilt lines with two design questions, while design B is right on all four programs with 29 built lines and has no fourth gap; the checker rung of the size wall needs a four-line fix (`keep-size-params.patch`) that goes into its brief. So item (3), the size design, is Pavol's decision with the data, no default given; item (2), the route, likewise. Nothing is in flight. Row 30 of the re-approval table decided at his message of 13:49 UTC (the compiled `REM` guard approved as landed; POSITIONS 2026-09-24); the open re-approval rows are 39, 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47 and 48, then the four ledger homes 374-377, one per message. In the same message he asked for the route C experiment's results and the size probes' results again in plain words, because the first telling was too compressed; the retelling is a turn's final text, after which items (2) and (3) are put to him one ask per message. Route A decided at his message after the plain retelling ("Agreed. Route A it is."; POSITIONS 2026-09-24): item (2) is closed, and item (3), the size design, is the ask in front of him; batch 4's manifest follows it. In flight since 14:53 UTC, one Opus worker by the Agent tool, on Pavol's questions about the run-time cost of design B's classes and his request for the comparison in the nine-step form: it revises `explorations/reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md` in place with the probes' data and a new section "Run-time cost, measured", and writes `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` with `size-cost/run.sh` and captures under `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-cost/` (classes loaded and bytes, start-up, a hot loop timed under A and B with `javap` of the stamped body, a dispatched-by-size call under B, where shape checks happen and how often). Nothing committed until reviewed. The size decision waits for it; the re-approval rows can go on meanwhile. Two additions sent to that worker at Pavol's request: the revised brief's refresher explains the run time's descriptor machinery in plain words, and folds in the parts of `coordinator/map/compile-path-walkthrough.md` it rests on, since he has not read the walkthrough. Also in flight since 15:16 UTC, one Sonnet archaeology worker by the Agent tool on his question why an operator static argument carries no descriptor and whether the kinds should be unified, output `explorations/perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md`, read-only, nothing committed until reviewed. The archaeology landed at 15:26 UTC and is committed (`perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md`; FACTS § The checker and the one library, the entry after the size probes): an operator argument is a name by the specification and on both paths, a size a run-time value by the specification, sizes never carved out; its closing reading in favour of design A weighs value position alone and was flagged to Pavol. The size-cost worker is still in flight. The size-cost worker landed at 15:38 UTC and is committed (the brief revised in place; `perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` and `size-cost/`; FACTS § The checker and the one library, the entry after the operator archaeology): the designs differ by a few kilobytes at load and by nothing on the hot path; the brief's proposed default is now B, marked as not a decision. Nothing is in flight. The size ask is back in front of Pavol with the revised brief. **Design B decided at his message answered at 16:18 UTC ("B it is."; POSITIONS 2026-09-24), and no ledger row for the operator unification question ("I don't see a need"). Items (2) and (3) are closed. Put to him as a question in the same turn, awaiting his go: the two probes before the run-time size rung's brief (the factory variant of B against the loader emitter; `DOT`'s shared size on the compiled path), one Opus worker on the shadow stack, nothing on `main`. His go came at 16:20 UTC ("Go, then I compact you."), and the worker is in flight since then, by the Agent tool: output `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes.md` with programs, patches, `run.sh` and captures under `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes/`; nothing committed until the coordinator has reviewed it (`test -f` the note to see whether it has landed). The order after boot is: the re-approval rows 39, 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48 and the four ledger homes 374-377, one per message; then batch 4's manifest (interpreter coercion; the specification rung with its decision record; the size wall's checker rung with the four-line fix; row 379's and rows 380/381's fixes as rungs if they share no file), launched after the reset on his go; then the workflow option (b) ask, the inventory move list, the lineage cleanup, the GitHub issues plan, the cleaner pass. He asked for a compaction after this turn.** **Stopped at 16:29 UTC on Pavol's word ("Stop the workers."), seven minutes in, because 2 % of the week's usage was left with the reset due Friday about 10:00 UTC: nothing is in flight; the worker's partial files (three programs, a Java tool, a patch) were moved out of the tree to the scratchpad's `size-rung-probes-partial/` at 16:41 UTC so that nothing untracked sits in the tree, and are lost with the container; the two probes are relaunched with the same brief after the reset, on his go, beside batch 4's manifest; nothing else is spent until the reset.** **Row 39 decided at 18:31 UTC (POSITIONS 2026-09-24): the six scalar drops approved, the diagonal's specialised product restored by a probe of the override shape (`Diag extends Matrix` overriding `mul`, both vocabulary files, both check programs cold) that runs after the reset and before row 40; nothing is spent until Friday 12:00 CEST. The order after the reset is: that probe, then the two size probes relaunched, then rows 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48 and the homes 374-377, then batch 4's manifest.** **Booted 2026-09-25 after the weekly reset (Pavol: "Boot up. New usage quota is ready after weekly reset."). In flight since 21:31 UTC, one Opus worker by the Agent tool: the diagonal override probe of row 39 (shape 3, `Diag extends Matrix` overriding `mul`, in `run-c4/src/FlatArrays.{fss,fsi}` and `apl/mg/FlatArrays2.{fss,fsi}`, both check programs from an empty cache, the timed probe re-run as `v07b`; shape 1, the old operator, built only if the override is refused); output `explorations/run-c4/probes/vocabulary/diag-override.md` with `v07b_diag_override.fss`/`.out` beside it and the cold captures under `explorations/run-c4/cold-cache/diag-override/`; nothing committed until reviewed (`test -f` the note). The two size probes' relaunch is put to Pavol for his go in the same turn and starts after this worker lands, since both work in the one tree. Then rows 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, the homes 374-377, batch 4's manifest.** **His "Yes" to the size probes' relaunch came at 21:37 UTC; the brief is recovered from the transcript into the scratchpad (`size-rung-probes-brief.md`) and the worker launches when the diagonal probe lands.** **The diagonal probe landed and is committed (`405a31b0e`): the override passed at the first attempt in both vocabularies, row 39 is closed, ledger row 299 appended. In flight since 22:29 UTC, one Opus worker by the Agent tool: the two size probes under the brief of 2026-09-24 16:20 UTC with the relaunch addendum (the factory variant of design B against the loader emitter; `DOT`'s shared size on the compiled path); output `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes.md` with programs, patches, `run.sh` and captures under `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes/`; nothing committed until reviewed (`test -f` the note). Open in front of Pavol: row 40 of the re-approval table (the three array-design defaults; the coordinator's recommendation to close it as not a decision taken, the questions returning with the array fork after the switch-over), and the wording of protocol § 6's three rules of 2026-09-25 (option B, the trigger / required output / who checks form, recommended). You are examining one question for Pavol (@palimondo), who directs the revival of the Fortress programming language in `/home/user/fortress`. He is a programmer. Write in plain English, and define every term in the sentence that first uses it.

**The situation.** Pavol decided on route A for the compiled type checker (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-24, "Agreed. Route A it is."):
- The checker keeps the designers' "multiple instantiation exclusion" rule: a type may not be a subtype of two different instantiations of one generic.
- The library's numeric tower is flattened.
- The interpreter learns coercion.

The specification (`Specification/`, LaTeX sources of the July 2012 draft; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched) is to be revised to match. Some of the specification's own examples declare types that this rule refuses. Those examples cannot stay as they are.

**The question.** Which examples in the specification does the rule refuse, and what should each one become?
- The candidates Pavol has been told of include `Empty`, the specification's non-parametric `Nothing`, and an example about covariance. Find them, and any others, yourself from the sources.
- A related decision already on record: `POSITIONS.md` 2026-09-21, ledger row 331. The library keeps the parametric `Nothing[\T\]`. The specification's bare `Nothing` is future work, gated on `where` clauses binding a type variable in an `extends` clause, which neither path implements (`FACTS.md` § Execution model, the entry on `Nothing`).

**First step, before anything else.** List every way the language and the library offer to express what each refused example was showing. Work from the sources:
- the specification;
- the interpreter's library `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`/`.fsi` and the compiler's `Library/CompilerLibrary.*`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/*`;
- the team's papers under `Papers/`;
- the git history.

Do not read the revival's planning notes on this question. They are in `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-4.md` and anything under `explorations/` mentioning "S2". The point is a list made fresh from the sources. You may read `explorations/protocol.md` § 6 for the method, `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` for established facts, and `explorations/repo-internals.md` for the build, the two execution paths and git archaeology. The history has 146 severed parent links, and that note says how to work around them.

**Then the nine steps of protocol § 6, per example where they differ:**
1. The refresher: what the example means.
2. What each path does with it today, measured. Run it under `walk` and through `fortress compile`/`run`, in a private cache outside the repository. `repo-internals.md` gives the recipe and the stale-cache trap.
3. What the specification's prose says, including the same idea under another spelling.
4. Where it sits in the type hierarchy.
5. What the library already does in the same family. Name the library's own way first.
6. What peer languages do, by family. Cite a source for each.
7. The history in the commits.
8. The derivation from Pavol's principles:
   - route A;
   - the late implementation-informed positions outweigh the early specification text (`POSITIONS.md` 2026-09-23);
   - the library's practice is the standard (2026-09-19);
   - his requirement that the revision leave no open discrepancy and keep the original text and route C recoverable (2026-09-24).
9. The options as they would be put to him, each with what it commits him to. End with a recommendation in one line, after the explanation, marked as your reading and not a decision.

This decision touches the specification, the interpreter and the compiler, so a top-tier judgement will be made on your evidence afterwards. Keep what you measured apart from what you read or inferred, and mark each claim.

**Rules:**
- Read-only on the tracked tree. Probe programs and captures go under `explorations/reviews/spec-refused-examples/`, and caches go outside the repository.
- A climb batch is running on this machine in other worktrees. Run your probes one at a time. Do not run `ant` or the test suites. Do not touch `/home/user/fortress-*` or any `wip/` branch.
- Bound every command's output. Cite file:line for source claims, and a commit hash for history.
- Lists, not tables. Numbers of thousands or millions as K or M. Do not name any AI model.
- Write the result to `explorations/reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, starting with a one-line header comment saying what it is, when and by whom it was written.
- Commit nothing. Run `git status --short` at the end.

**Your final report:** the examples found, the list of ways for each, the recommendation, and the paths you wrote.

content.text:
I kept S2 separate from S1 and started it as its own Opus worker at 01:47 UTC, next to S1.

The reason is that they are different kinds of question. S1 is about form: how a changed passage is marked. S2 is about meaning: what the refused examples (`Empty`, the bare `Nothing`, the covariance example) should become. S2 needs the library, both execution paths and the history, while S1 needs none of that. Adding S2 to S1 would have slowed S1 and mixed the two.

How the S2 worker runs:
- Like S1, it hasn't seen the manifest's four options. It builds its own list from the sources first, then does the nine steps for each example.
- It runs small probes one at a time in private caches, so it doesn't compete with the batch for the machine.
- It writes to `explorations/reviews/spec-refused-examples.md` and commits nothing.

S2 touches the specification, the interpreter and the compiler. Under your rule of 09-20, that makes the final judgement top-tier work, either Fable with your yes or me on a clean context. I'll put that to you when the evidence lands.

input.summary: New rule: commit and push own files
input.message:
Rule change from Pavol, replacing "commit nothing": commit your own files as you go, and push.

How:
- Commit only the paths you wrote, in one command: `git add -- <your paths> && git commit -m '<message>' -- <your paths>`. Never `git add -A`, never a directory of caches, never a file you did not write.
- The commit message ends with exactly these two lines:
  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
  Name no AI model in the message.
- Before each push, run `git log --oneline origin/main..main`.
  - If it lists only your own commits, run `git push origin main && git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8`.
  - If it lists any commit that is not yours, do not push; just keep committing. A climb batch running on this machine commits to this same local main before its gate has passed, and a push would publish those commits.
- If git reports an `index.lock`, wait a few seconds and retry.
- Commit whenever your note reaches a state worth keeping, and at least at the end of each step.

Everything else in your brief stands.

  ### The examples the rule refuses
  1. **In `basic/trait-parameters.tex`, the language chapter's three where-clause examples.** A where-clause variable is a type name introduced by a `where` clause. Written in an `extends` clause, it means "for every T", so the type becomes a member of infinitely many instantiations.

## For Pavol

1. The stop at CLIMB-BATCH-4.md:77 ('A change in any interpreter test's output ... comes back to Pavol with the list') is met to the letter. Three tests print differently:
- XXXimmutableTopLevel: the Java line numbers of a printed NPE trace through LazilyEvaluatedCell.java and BaseEnv.java, both edited;

The judge does not lift this stop. The candidates:
- (a) read it as outside the stop's stated purpose, 'nothing should convert'. That is the reading of the worker, the skeptic and the judge, and it costs nothing.
- (b) hold rung C unmerged. No repair removes the change: any edit to those two files moves the printed line numbers.

2. Route A's price is wider than the example it was put to you with (price-keep-the-rule.md:89). 4. A scope decision by the judge, not under silence. The tuple-typed binding the skeptic found is repaired (home 1) rather than gated as an expected failure. It is repaired only for plain tuple types: varargs, keyword and arrow targets, and an overloaded function's tuple-typed parameter, stay unconverted and unmeasured.

lines: ## Boot note to the resumed coordinator

-**Update, 2026-09-24 08:59 UTC.** In flight since about 08:59 UTC, both Opus, both launched by the Agent tool (a message from Pavol does not kill them; a Workflow run is what a mid-turn interrupt kills): the route C shadow experiment, whose output is `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md` with patches and captures under `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c/`; and the run-time size design brief, whose output is `explorations/reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`. Neither is committed until the coordinator has reviewed it (the worker commits nothing). His go of that hour: "Recommendation accepted. Run 2 and 3 now" (POSITIONS 2026-09-24): the ledger rows one per message while they run, the exclusion route decided when the C data lands, then batch 4's manifest. Landed since the 07:10 note: the `experiment/` move (`7bc8177a3`) and its verification by re-running both shadow experiments from the new path (`582b4e17d`; FACTS § The container). The order below stands otherwise. Landed 09:21 UTC and committed: the size design brief (`explorations/reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`); its default is design A with the value-position piece in one rung, briefed only after one shadow session has probed the fourth gap and a dispatched overload arm generic in a size, and the checker rung of the size wall does not wait on the decision. Those two probes are the next worker to launch, after the route C worker finishes, because both build shadows in this one tree. Landed 11:12 UTC and committed: the route C experiment (`explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md`, `route-c/`; FACTS § The checker and the one library, the entry of 2026-09-24): C-full closes the specialisation hole with a 109-line return-type rule over every level of a chain, needs seven library declarations and an identification that only `comprises T` licenses, and `comprises T` overflows the checker; a chain without a specialisation dies compiled with `AbstractMethodError`; C-lite refuses the tower's inner half; the reversal cost on record is corrected upward. The route decision (item 2) is ready to be put to Pavol. In flight since 11:12 UTC, one Opus worker by the Agent tool: the size probes the brief asked for before the run-time rung is briefed (a dispatched overload arm generic in a size under A and B, the fourth gap's template, a type test on a size), output `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` with patches and captures under `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-probes/`. Landed 12:24 UTC and committed (FACTS § The checker and the one library, the entry of 2026-09-24 on the three size probes): design A's default falls to the brief's own stop condition, since under A a dispatched arm generic in a size silently picks the catch-all and its fix is about 70-90 unbuilt lines with two design questions, while design B is right on all four programs with 29 built lines and has no fourth gap; the checker rung of the size wall needs a four-line fix (`keep-size-params.patch`) that goes into its brief. So item (3), the size design, is Pavol's decision with the data, no default given; item (2), the route, likewise. Nothing is in flight. Row 30 of the re-approval table decided at his message of 13:49 UTC (the compiled `REM` guard approved as landed; POSITIONS 2026-09-24); the open re-approval rows are 39, 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47 and 48, then the four ledger homes 374-377, one per message. In the same message he asked for the route C experiment's results and the size probes' results again in plain words, because the first telling was too compressed; the retelling is a turn's final text, after which items (2) and (3) are put to him one ask per message. Route A decided at his message after the plain retelling ("Agreed. Route A it is."; POSITIONS 2026-09-24): item (2) is closed, and item (3), the size design, is the ask in front of him; batch 4's manifest follows it. In flight since 14:53 UTC, one Opus worker by the Agent tool, on Pavol's questions about the run-time cost of design B's classes and his request for the comparison in the nine-step form: it revises `explorations/reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md` in place with the probes' data and a new section "Run-time cost, measured", and writes `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` with `size-cost/run.sh` and captures under `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-cost/` (classes loaded and bytes, start-up, a hot loop timed under A and B with `javap` of the stamped body, a dispatched-by-size call under B, where shape checks happen and how often). Nothing committed until reviewed. The size decision waits for it; the re-approval rows can go on meanwhile. Two additions sent to that worker at Pavol's request: the revised brief's refresher explains the run time's descriptor machinery in plain words, and folds in the parts of `coordinator/map/compile-path-walkthrough.md` it rests on, since he has not read the walkthrough. Also in flight since 15:16 UTC, one Sonnet archaeology worker by the Agent tool on his question why an operator static argument carries no descriptor and whether the kinds should be unified, output `explorations/perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md`, read-only, nothing committed until reviewed. The archaeology landed at 15:26 UTC and is committed (`perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md`; FACTS § The checker and the one library, the entry after the size probes): an operator argument is a name by the specification and on both paths, a size a run-time value by the specification, sizes never carved out; its closing reading in favour of design A weighs value position alone and was flagged to Pavol. The size-cost worker is still in flight. The size-cost worker landed at 15:38 UTC and is committed (the brief revised in place; `perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` and `size-cost/`; FACTS § The checker and the one library, the entry after the operator archaeology): the designs differ by a few kilobytes at load and by nothing on the hot path; the brief's proposed default is now B, marked as not a decision. Nothing is in flight. The size ask is back in front of Pavol with the revised brief. **Design B decided at his message answered at 16:18 UTC ("B it is."; POSITIONS 2026-09-24), and no ledger row for the operator unification question ("I don't see a need"). Items (2) and (3) are closed. Put to him as a question in the same turn, awaiting his go: the two probes before the run-time size rung's brief (the factory variant of B against the loader emitter; `DOT`'s shared size on the compiled path), one Opus worker on the shadow stack, nothing on `main`. His go came at 16:20 UTC ("Go, then I compact you."), and the worker is in flight since then, by the Agent tool: output `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes.md` with programs, patches, `run.sh` and captures under `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes/`; nothing committed until the coordinator has reviewed it (`test -f` the note to see whether it has landed). The order after boot is: the re-approval rows 39, 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48 and the four ledger homes 374-377, one per message; then batch 4's manifest (interpreter coercion; the specification rung with its decision record; the size wall's checker rung with the four-line fix; row 379's and rows 380/381's fixes as rungs if they share no file), launched after the reset on his go; then the workflow option (b) ask, the inventory move list, the lineage cleanup, the GitHub issues plan, the cleaner pass. He asked for a compaction after this turn.** **Stopped at 16:29 UTC on Pavol's word ("Stop the workers."), seven minutes in, because 2 % of the week's usage was left with the reset due Friday about 10:00 UTC: nothing is in flight; the worker's partial files (three programs, a Java tool, a patch) were moved out of the tree to the scratchpad's `size-rung-probes-partial/` at 16:41 UTC so that nothing untracked sits in the tree, and are lost with the container; the two probes are relaunched with the same brief after the reset, on his go, beside batch 4's manifest; nothing else is spent until the reset.** **Row 39 decided at 18:31 UTC (POSITIONS 2026-09-24): the six scalar drops approved, the diagonal's specialised product restored by a probe of the override shape (`Diag extends Matrix` overriding `mul`, both vocabulary files, both check programs cold) that runs after the reset and before row 40; nothing is spent until Friday 12:00 CEST. The order after the reset is: that probe, then the two size probes relaunched, then rows 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48 and the homes 374-377, then batch 4's manifest.** **Booted 2026-09-25 after the weekly reset (Pavol: "Boot up. New usage quota is ready after weekly reset."). In flight since 21:31 UTC, one Opus worker by the Agent tool: the diagonal override probe of row 39 (shape 3, `Diag extends Matrix` overriding `mul`, in `run-c4/src/FlatArrays.{fss,fsi}` and `apl/mg/FlatArrays2.{fss,fsi}`, both check programs from an empty cache, the timed probe re-run as `v07b`; shape 1, the old operator, built only if the override is refused); output `explorations/run-c4/probes/vocabulary/diag-override.md` with `v07b_diag_override.fss`/`.out` beside it and the cold captures under `explorations/run-c4/cold-cache/diag-override/`; nothing committed until reviewed (`test -f` the note). The two size probes' relaunch is put to Pavol for his go in the same turn and starts after this worker lands, since both work in the one tree. Then rows 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, the homes 374-377, batch 4's manifest.** **His "Yes" to the size probes' relaunch came at 21:37 UTC; the brief is recovered from the transcript into the scratchpad (`size-rung-probes-brief.md`) and the worker launches when the diagonal probe lands.** **The diagonal probe landed and is committed (`405a31b0e`): the override passed at the first attempt in both vocabularies, row 39 is closed, ledger row 299 appended. In flight since 22:29 UTC, one Opus worker by the Agent tool: the two size probes under the brief of 2026-09-24 16:20 UTC with the relaunch addendum (the factory variant of design B against the loader emitter; `DOT`'s shared size on the compiled path); output `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes.md` with programs, patches, `run.sh` and captures under `explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes/`; nothing committed until reviewed (`test -f` the note).
